POLITICO https://www.politico.eu European Politics, Policy, Government News Tue, 13 Oct 2026 22:30:47 +0000 en hourly 60 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.9.10 OpenAI employee arrested and charged over hidden recording https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/13/openai-employee-arrested-and-charged-over-hidden-recording-01117275?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Tue, 13 Oct 2026 22:30:40 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9157583 Federal authorities arrested a Saudi national employed at OpenAI and charged him with planting a recording device in a company’s executive conference room, the Department of Justice announced Tuesday.

On or around Sept. 30, OpenAI discovered a sophisticated recording device inserted into the back of a television in an executive conference room located in one of its San Francisco offices. The company determined that the device was installed approximately a couple days prior, concealed in toilet paper. The contents of the device were encrypted, according to the DOJ.

The Department of Justice said in a news release that the employee, Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, was arrested Friday and appeared in federal court Tuesday. OpenAI confirmed the incident on social media and said that it was supporting the FBI’s investigation.

“We used our models to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier,” OpenAI said in its statement. “At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data.”

Alfozan used a “productivity tool” to inquire about the company’s meeting rooms, calendars, and “leadership and exec” locations, according to OpenAI’s complaint to the DOJ. A chatbot account associated with his spouse also indicated that the user submitted prompts in September relating to installing and remote accessing a recording device.

The DOJ said that CCTV footage showed Alfozan, who had been employed as an engineer by OpenAI since July 2025, near and inside the conference room on multiple occasions before the device was discovered. Meetings in the conference room “frequently involved discussions of highly confidential technical, commercial, and strategic information, including proprietary research, product plans, and business-development opportunities,” according to the complaint.

The company also discovered another recording device in one of Alfozan’s bags left in the office.

“We referred the matter to the FBI, and we’re grateful to the agents and prosecutors who moved quickly to make an arrest,” OpenAI said. “Our security program is designed to protect against a wide range of threat actors, from insider risks to cybercriminals to nation states, and this case is an example of how AI can help address these sophisticated security threats.”

The Saudi national, who has since been fired by OpenAI, faces a maximum penalty of five years in prison, a $250,000 fine and three years of supervised release if convicted, according to the DOJ.

“For us it is a matter of national security,” U.S. Attorney Craig H. Missakian for the Northern District of California said in a statement. “This arrest highlights our relentless efforts in partnership with the FBI to identify and prosecute those who seek to steal our technology, as alleged in the complaint.”

The British prime minister urged international allies to strengthen sanctions on Russia and called on President Vladimir Putin to agree to an energy ceasefire ahead of Zelenskyy’s visit to Downing Street. ]]> en From no cards to many: Europe warns Trump not to waste Ukraine’s leverage https://www.politico.eu/article/trump-europe-ukraine-leverage-war-russia-oil/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Tue, 13 Oct 2026 17:56:33 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9152606 WARSAW — Ukraine has more leverage than a year ago — and European leaders are warning Donald Trump not to squander it by pressuring Kyiv to ease up on Russia.

“In less than two years we went from the stage of no cards to the stage of don’t play your cards,” Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha told an audience at the Warsaw Security Conference. “That’s a true achievement.”

Last year, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy was ambushed in the Oval Office by Trump, who ridiculed him for having “no cards” to play against Russia.

Trump’s recent demand that Zelenskyy “better damn well stop” Ukraine’s refinery attacks, and his call for Ukraine to install a new leader, amount to a recognition that Kyiv does indeed have significant leverage in the fight.

Kyiv’s refinery campaign is helping create a growing fuel shortage across Russia and is also harming the Kremlin’s ability to finance the war. But European leaders fear that Trump’s desperation to lower fuel prices ahead of next month’s U.S. midterm elections by pressuring Kyiv to stop its attacks could weaken Ukraine’s hand without persuading Russia to end the war.

Sybiha’s comments drew loud applause at the Warsaw conference and underscored growing tensions among Kyiv, Washington and Ukraine’s European allies after Trump said the U.S. had agreed with Vladimir Putin to buy Russian diesel.

The dispute between Washington and Kyiv overshadowed a Warsaw event that is normally strongly pro-American, given Poland’s status as a key U.S. ally.

“Ministers and heads of state won’t say so outright what they think about the Americans, but they certainly think a lot of things — the negotiations with Putin are yet another stab in the back for the Ukrainians,” said a French lawmaker, speaking on condition of being granted anonymity.

“You end the war by persuading the aggressor to limit his level of ambition, not by asking the victim to capitulate,” said Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski.

His German counterpart Johann Wadephul underlined that Berlin is pushing the Trump administration to fully impose energy sanctions approved by the U.S. Congress.

On Sep. 18, Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Russia and Iran Sanctions Act of 2026, codifying existing US sanctions against Russia and expanding the scope for applying secondary sanctions, tariffs and restrictions, including against the energy sector.

“This is not the time to lower the sanctions regime, but to strengthen it,” Wadephul said.

U.K. Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband echoed that call, saying Trump should exert pressure on Russia to agree to an energy ceasefire under which both warring nations would stop hitting each other’s oil, gas, electricity and other assets.

Russia has so far refused to take such a step.

“Let us take seriously this issue of the energy ceasefire that President Trump has talked about, not simply a refinery ceasefire but a broad energy ceasefire, because in the last week alone we’ve seen 200 Russian attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure,” Miliband said.

Trump pressures Ukraine

The U.S. president said on Monday that Putin is keener to end the fighting than Zelenskyy — despite the Kremlin not agreeing to any ceasefire.

“I think actually Putin wants to make a deal more than Zelenskyy,” Trump said.

Since Trump announced an energy ceasefire — blindsiding both Kyiv and Moscow — Ukraine has paused bombing Russian refineries even as Russian attacks continue.

While Trump wants the attacks to stop, Ukraine’s European allies are keen to cripple Russia’s war effort.

“Ukraine is attacking refineries, which is having an effect, and data centers, which is also having an effect,” Sikorski said. He also called on Poland’s MAGA-aligned President Karol Nawrocki to use his influence with Trump “to explain to him that Putin is the aggressor and Zelenskyy is the victim of aggression.”

Wadephul added that he had talked to Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov during the U.N. General Assembly in New York last month, and saw no interest from him in ending the war.

“A lot of people in Europe and especially in Germany were asking us and me, ‘Why don’t you talk to the Russians?’ So now I had that conversation, and you saw the result,” he said. “It’s a very dire result. And it shows that Russia right now is not ready for ceasefire.”

During the same Warsaw event, Sybiha was forced to deny rumors that Washington may have stopped sharing intelligence with Kyiv in retaliation for its campaign of deep strikes against Russian oil refineries.

“You are asking me if we are getting intelligence data from the American side. Yes, we continue this cooperation,” he said. 

Concerns about a potential cut-off in U.S. intelligence grew on Tuesday after Ukraine’s threat detection system failed to detect ballistic missiles that battered Kyiv overnight. Sybiha said the failure was due to a “special type of weaponry which was used by the Russian side.”

Zelenskyy also underlined the need for continued intelligence sharing. “There was also a rather treacherous ballistic missile strike on Kyiv — five missiles that hit civilian infrastructure. Unfortunately, there was no warning from our partners regarding this strike. Intelligence on Russian ballistic missile launches helps save lives.”

Sybiha stressed that Kyiv needs to continue strengthening its ability to fend off Russia’s constant air attacks while Ukraine’s troops push back against Russian forces on the front lines.

“The future of Europe and the global security architecture is now being decided in Ukraine,” he said.

Chris Lunday and Laura Kayali contributed to this report.

How Maroš Šefčovič talked his way to a China trade breakthrough

Europe’s trade chief has won a first concession from Beijing. Now he must convince EU leaders that dialogue can deliver more.

By Camille Gijs and Carlo Martuscelli
in Brussels

Illustration by Natália Delgado/POLITICO

When Maroš Šefčovič set out his strategy for engaging with China to European Union ambassadors in July, he had a warning for governments urging tougher action on trade against Beijing.

“Sometimes, it’s even popular to start a trade war, but it’s very difficult to finish it,” the EU trade chief recalled later in an interview with POLITICO.

Three months on, Šefčovič has secured a first breakthrough, reaching a deal in Beijing last week to sharply reduce imports of Chinese hybrid cars. The symbolic win marks a small step toward stabilizing a trading relationship that Brussels believes has reached a dangerous tipping point.

The agreement, which will initially cap imports at 350,000 vehicles a year, marks a significant concession from Beijing, whose carmakers have been flooding the European market with increasingly competitive vehicles. 

For Šefčovič, who negotiated last year’s tariff truce with Donald Trump, the agreement suggests his strategy of engagement backed by the threat of tougher trade measures may be starting to pay off.

Šefčovič agreed to launch the trade dialogue at a meeting with Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao in Brussels in late June.

By focusing initially on cars — an area where the EU has leverage as one of the few major markets still open to Chinese manufacturers — the Slovak commissioner hoped to secure a confidence-building win before tackling thornier questions, from critical raw materials to China’s vast industrial overcapacity.

At the same time, he worked to coalesce European governments behind a parallel effort to strengthen the bloc’s trade defenses, reinforcing his negotiating position with the threat of tougher action to bring down the EU’s €1 billion-a-day trade deficit with China.

The hybrid deal, however, is only the opening move in a much bigger contest.

EU leaders meet in Brussels on Thursday to take stock, weighing the benefits of continued engagement against demands for more aggressive action to protect European industry from a surge in Chinese imports.

The meeting will test whether a commissioner who has made a career of finding compromises with difficult partners can maintain Europe’s support for a strategy whose success is far from assured.

“You have to deal with the same partner across the table,” Šefčovič said of the risks of starting a trade war, in the interview with POLITICO in August. “So if you can avoid this, it would be much better.”

Market power

Šefčovič’s opening move was to focus on an area where Europe still has leverage: access to its market of 450 million people.

China’s fiercely competitive manufacturers have become global powerhouses, but they are struggling with weak demand at home. A prolonged property slump has weighed on consumer spending, while cutthroat competition has triggered price wars. Domestic sales of passenger vehicles fell 28% in September from a year earlier.

That makes overseas markets increasingly important. With the U.S. shutting out Chinese imports, Europe remains one of the most lucrative markets still open to Chinese manufacturers.

Šefčovič gambled that Beijing would prefer to accept limits on exports rather than risk losing access to the European market altogether.

He set his sights on the automotive sector, where Chinese manufacturers have been making rapid inroads. Chinese carmakers accounted for just 2% of both the European hybrid and plug-in hybrid markets in 2024; by the first half of 2026, their respective shares had risen to 14% and 25%, industry figures show.

The Commission was preparing to restrict hybrid imports even without an agreement. But a negotiated settlement also offered Šefčovič something valuable politically: evidence that engagement with Beijing could deliver tangible results.

The negotiations were intense, according to a person familiar with the talks on the Chinese side.

“It was very, very tough,” the person said, speaking on condition of anonymity to discuss the closed-door negotiations. “Both sides hadn’t seen such intensity in a long time. No summer break, no holidays. They worked around the clock even one, two days prior to Šefčovič’s trip to Beijing.”

While pursuing dialogue, Brussels also wanted to convince Beijing that it was prepared to take tougher action if the negotiations failed.

Šefčovič had earlier flagged plans for a new “diversification instrument” that would require businesses in critical sectors to source essential inputs from at least three suppliers — a move to reduce China’s ability to exploit Europe’s dependence on its critical raw materials.

Then, just three days before Šefčovič’s trip to Beijing, France and Germany raised the stakes.

President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz called for a powerful new trade weapon that would allow Brussels to restrict — or even shut off — access to the European market within days for countries deemed to have severely distorted the bloc’s single market.

The proposal did not explicitly name China, but Beijing was its obvious target. 

Keeping it together

EU leaders are expected to welcome the agreement but also press the Commission to act quickly to strengthen the bloc’s trade defenses, according to several diplomats. The understanding reached in Beijing has bought time, but hasn’t settled how far Brussels should go if Chinese exports keep rising or negotiations stall.

“We’re losing thousands of jobs in industry; olive oil and ice cream won’t solve the core issue,” said one EU diplomat after Šefčovič briefed ambassadors on Sunday, referring to reported deliverables from the talks.

A senior German official welcomed the Beijing deal as a first step in the right direction. “It’s a positive sign — which, of course, doesn’t fully solve the problem of the trade deficit with China,” the official said.

But Berlin’s support for a tougher line might prove short-lived.

Alicia García-Herrero, a senior fellow at the Bruegel think tank, argued that Beijing’s concessions had been calculated to assuage Berlin, given the importance of the automotive industry to the German economy.

“I’m just hoping Merz doesn’t turn away from the letter he sent to the Commission,” she said. With the German chancellor politically weakened at home, García-Herrero fears he may be reluctant to risk a prolonged confrontation: “I worry Merz will take this quick win and run.”

That leaves Šefčovič facing a balancing act: keeping EU governments on board with continued engagement with China while maintaining a credible threat of tougher action if the talks break down. 

“I expect [leaders] to give the Commission a nod to move ahead with other trade defense measures. China may see this as a betrayal. If that is the case, we could return to conflict very quickly,” said Noah Barkin, a senior adviser at the Rhodium Group’s China practice.

The battle ahead

For Šefčovič, the challenge now is to turn a limited breakthrough on cars into a broader rebalancing of trade with China — while buying Europe time to strengthen its defenses should the negotiations fail.

“There is an argument for doing to China what China had done to Europe for years — bogging Beijing down in dialogue and process while Europe gets its tools in place. But the EU needs to make full use of the time that these talks provide,” said Rhodium’s Barkin. 

The trade chief is expected to hold a video call with Wang in January, before the two meet again next March. Those talks will test whether Beijing is prepared to make further concessions in sectors where European industry is increasingly on the defensive, including chemicals.

Another priority is critical raw materials, where China has agreed to continue issuing export licenses for rare earths. Beijing’s grip on their supply gives it considerable leverage over European manufacturers, underscoring the limits of Šefčovič’s negotiating position.

The Commission is also preparing two proposals for December: the diversification instrument, aimed at reducing dependence on Chinese supplies, and a mechanism to shield European industries and regions from retaliation.

The scale of the challenge is daunting. Chinese hybrid imports were worth €6.7 billion in the first half of 2026, against an EU-China trade deficit of €360 billion last year. The agreement offers some relief to European automakers but does little to address the underlying imbalance.

Brussels hopes the hybrid safeguard can serve as a blueprint for protecting other industries facing a surge in Chinese imports.

“We hear our industry. That includes the chemical industry, the wind industry, the furniture industry. We know where there’s a surge, and we know what hits the hardest in terms of our deindustrialization,” a senior Commission official said on Monday.

Šefčovič acknowledged the limits of dialogue in his August interview, warning that negotiations would become harder to sustain without tangible progress.

“What would be very important is to come back to say there is acknowledgment of the issue and there are already some pilot schemes which we want to test and to see if they are working,” he said.

“But if simply there will be no action, then of course it will be much more difficult for us just to talk about these issues.”

Jordyn Dahl in Brussels and Hans von der Burchard in Berlin contributed reporting. 

]]> en Philippe, Glucksmann, Retailleau : les temps forts du Sommet sur la compétitivité économique de POLITICO https://www.politico.eu/article/philippe-glucksmann-retailleau-les-temps-forts-du-sommet-sur-la-competitivite-economique-de-politico/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Tue, 13 Oct 2026 16:00:25 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9154085 PARIS — Un peu plus de deux semaines après le Playbook Paris Live, où Gabriel Attal, Marine Le Pen et Jean-Luc Mélenchon étaient reçus, trois autres candidats à la présidentielle étaient invités à s’exprimer ce mardi sur les enjeux économiques du moment lors du Sommet sur la compétitivité économique de POLITICO.

Voitures thermiques et droits de douane

Avec l’ouverture du Salon de l’Auto, c’est l’un des sujets d’actu du jour : l’interdiction de la vente des voitures à moteur thermique dans l’Union européenne à partir de 2035 — un accord pour assouplir cette mesure est sur le point d’être conclu entre la France et l’Allemagne. Sans surprise, Edouard Philippe, Raphaël Glucksmann et Bruno Retailleau ne partagent pas le même avis sur la question.

Le candidat Horizons considère que cette décision est une erreur. “Une stratégie, ça doit s’appuyer sur une analyse précise des moyens qu’on est capable de mettre en œuvre. Et de fait, on n’a pas été capable de mettre en œuvre ce qui aurait permis de rendre cette stratégie possible, pour autant qu’elle ait été adaptée”, a-t-il estimé lors de notre sommet. L’ancien Premier ministre plaide pour une meilleure protection du marché européen via la mise en place de droits de douane élevés sur l’importation de véhicules chinois. Une question de “réciprocité”, a-t-il martelé pendant l’entretien.

Une vision rejetée quelques instants plus tard par Raphaël Glucksmann. “Je ne vois pas du tout en quoi cet objectif [de 2035] était une erreur”, a rétorqué le tout nouveau candidat du PS et de Place publique. L’eurodéputé plaide pour que les constructeurs automobiles se concentrent sur le développement de l’électrique. “C’est ça l’avenir”, a-t-il insisté, jugeant que l’Europe a “un énorme sujet de naïveté vis-à-vis de la Chine”.

Deux positions renvoyées dos à dos par Bruno Retailleau, qui a rappelé que le groupe du Parti populaire européen, dans lequel siègent les eurodéputés LR, s’était opposé à l’instauration de cette règle lorsqu’elle a été votée au Parlement européen. “Ma position, elle est très nette, elle n’a pas changé, ça fait des années que je le demande, je dénonce cet accord”, a insisté le candidat des Républicains. Il aurait préféré voir “imposer le principe de la neutralité technologique”, via un “cadre très exigeant”, mais progressif pour les constructeurs.

Sur la question des échanges commerciaux avec Pékin, le Vendéen rejoint la position d’Edouard Philippe en s’affichant en faveur de “vrais droits de douane” sur les importations chinoises. “A partir du moment où les règles ne sont pas loyales, on doit pouvoir les compenser”, a défendu Bruno Retailleau.

Energies

Autre dissonance entre les candidats : l’énergie. Pronucléaire, Edouard Philippe a insisté sur la nécessité de “défendre” et “favoriser” l’atome, tout en ajoutant que le “risque associé à [son] exploitation” est “réel”. Si, par mesure de sécurité, il fallait interrompre la production des centrales nucléaires françaises, il faudrait que d’autres technologies puissent prendre le relai et produire de l’électricité, a-t-il exposé, mentionnant les énergies renouvelables. Sinon, la France pourrait se retrouver dans une “situation qui peut-être terrible”, a-t-il prévenu. Le candidat Horizons est par ailleurs favorable à la construction de tous les réacteurs EPR2 envisagés par l’exécutif.

Du côté de Bruno Retailleau, le discours est beaucoup plus mesuré sur les renouvelables. Le candidat LR a confirmé vouloir couper leurs subventions s’il était élu, tout comme il compte abandonner la programmation pluriannuelle de l’énergie (la PPE3), définie par le gouvernement Lecornu. Prudent, Bruno Retailleau l’est aussi sur le développement des EPR2. Alors que la construction de six nouveaux réacteurs a déjà été décidée, “on verra” pour les huit autres prévus, a-t-il temporisé.

Vision de l’Europe

Face aux menaces en matière de défense, sécurité ou IA, Raphaël Glucksmann a répondu qu’il fallait “sortir de l’intergouvernemental” et que l’Union européenne devait assumer sa puissance dans le rapport de force avec la Chine ou les Etats-Unis.

“Il faut un instrument pour les financements européens. Si vous avez des financements européens, oui, vous allez voir que subitement les projets européens fonctionnent”, a-t-il plaidé. Pour le candidat PS-Place publique, la France a tout intérêt à diversifier ses alliances en ne regardant pas seulement vers l’Allemagne, mais en se tournant vers la Pologne ou les pays baltes. “La puissance française, elle se construira dans sa capacité à construire une coalition en Europe”, a-t-il martelé.

Pour Edouard Philippe, la relation franco-allemande est “absolument déterminante dans l’ensemble européen”, même s’il ne faut “pas réduire la politique européenne” uniquement à ce duo. Selon le candidat Horizons, la France aurait tout intérêt à “être plus crédible” et à “régler [ses] sujets” (comprenez : ses sujets budgétaires et le redressement des comptes publics), si elle veut retrouver du poids politique en Europe. “Nous sommes les seuls à ne pas savoir respecter des règles communes qui ont été respectées par tous les autres. Et ça, ça nous plante”, a-t-il déploré.

La question budgétaire, c’est par cet angle que Bruno Retailleau a abordé le thème de l’UE. Selon lui, la France doit “absolument” réduire sa contribution au budget de l’Union européenne, a-t-il estimé. Le candidat des Républicains a par ailleurs apporté son soutien aux Etats membres dits “frugaux”, partisans d’un budget de l’UE réduit. “Si la France ne fait pas partie de ces pays frugaux, ça veut dire qu’on a totalement perdu contact avec la réalité”, a jugé l’ancien ministre de l’Intérieur.

Mouvement lycéen

Interrogé sur son soutien au mouvement lycéen, dont c’était “l’acte V” aujourd’hui, Raphaël Glucksmann considère que son rôle n’est pas de manifester, mais “de répondre aux revendications des lycéens et de répondre à une angoisse qui est une angoisse existentielle”. Favorable à la suppression de Parcoursup, il souhaite remplacer la plateforme par “un procédé qui est transparent, mais qui ne peut pas être le retour à ce qu’on faisait avant”, car “ce n’était pas non plus fonctionnel”, a-t-il jugé, sans donner plus de précisions.

Pour Bruno Retailleau, il ne faut pas considérer que les lycéens qui expriment des revendications dans les médias “représentent tous les lycéens”. S’il reconnaît que certaines préoccupations sont “justes”, comme “sur Parcoursup ou sur une angoisse pour l’avenir”, il oppose par exemple les revendications des lycéens ruraux aux citadins. Et note que la situation est moins bouillonnante dans une grande partie du pays.

Le candidat LR a aussi critiqué la présence de la militante écologiste suédoise Greta Thunberg devant un lycée de Seine-Saint-Denis ce matin, jugeant qu’elle incarne une “écologie dévoyée” se résumant souvent à “une forme de gauchisme”.

]]> fr France should seek rebate on EU contribution, says presidential candidate Retailleau https://www.politico.eu/article/france-bruno-retailleau-france-seeks-rebate-eu-budget-contribution/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Tue, 13 Oct 2026 15:26:04 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9153713 PARIS — Conservative presidential candidate Bruno Retailleau said France should seek a rebate on its contribution to the EU budget ahead of a key European summit in Brussels this week.

France pays more in to the EU budget than it gets out, but it is struggling to reduce a severe budget deficit.

“It’s crazy,” Retailleau, the leader of the conservative party Les Républicains, said at POLITICO’s Competitiveness Summit in Paris. “Why should we contribute more when we know how dire our public finances are?”

European leaders are meeting in Brussels on Thursday and Friday to discuss the bloc’s long-term budget, the Multiannual Financial Framework, which is pitting the so-called frugal countries against those who want a bigger EU budget. France sits in neither camp.

Retailleau singled out structural funds — money that is invested in poorer European regions — as an area where savings could be made.

“We’ve given billions to countries so they would catch up with us. Well they have, and in a couple of years they’ll probably have a higher standard of living. Sorry, but stop,” he said.

However, Retailleau, who is trailing center-right presidential candidate Edouard Philippe and far-right front-runner Marine Le Pen in the polls, did not put a figure on the rebate he would demand if he came to power. Le Pen, who is the front-runner ahead of next year’s presidential election, and her party have proposed slashing France’s yearly contribution by €11.1 billion as early as next year.

Retailleau said he would seek “a negotiation,” rather than unilaterally impose a lower contribution, as Le Pen says she would do.

“I’m not going to behave like Marine Le Pen, I’m pro-European,” said Retailleau.

Retailleau argued that France’s defense and nuclear deterrence investments should also be included in the country’s contribution calculation, because the concept of forward deterrence benefits France’s European neighbors.

“We formally call for the urgent deployment of all instruments at our disposal to protect the International Criminal Court from the consequences of these sanctions,” reads the letter, signed by 58 MEPs, led by ECON chair and S&D lawmaker Aurore Lalucq and EPP Dutch lawmaker Dirk Gotink.

They ask the Commission boss “to draw a clear line towards the US administration.”

The Trump administration has repeatedly threatened to demolish the ICC “brick by brick.” Washington has already sanctioned several judges, including judges from France, Italy and Slovenia, after the court issued an arrest warrant for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

U.S. sanctions announced on Friday risk to cut off the whole ICC from the financial system, which runs on the dollar, and from the majority of tech service providers.

Lawmakers said the sanctions are “an attack by a foreign power on an entity on EU territory, using our own financial system.” They want the Commission to activate a legislative shield known as Blocking Statute, that would prevent EU firms from complying with the U.S. sanctions as soon as a 180-day grace period ends.

After a meeting in Luxembourg, foreign affairs ministers agreed to seek pragmatic solutions to make it possible for EU firms to continue to work with the Court, according to two diplomats. MEPs called for a fiercer reaction.

“The survival of the values the European Union upholds is at stake, as is Europe’s autonomy and credibility in protecting its citizens and entities against foreign sanctions,” their letter reads. “This is about the survival of the Union itself.”

]]> en Poland arrests second man over threats to Prime Minister Tusk https://www.politico.eu/article/poland-arrests-second-man-over-threats-to-prime-minister-donald-tusk/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Tue, 13 Oct 2026 15:08:01 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9153629 Polish police arrested a man accused of calling for the murder of Prime Minister Donald Tusk and parliament speaker Włodzimierz Czarzasty, the government said Tuesday, marking the second arrest in connection to threats against senior politicians in three days.

Police detained the 46-year-old suspect Monday in Oborniki, western Poland, government spokesperson Adam Szłapka said on X.

Prosecutors charged him Tuesday with inciting murder and insulting Tusk, Czarzasty and an unnamed journalist at public broadcaster TVP Info, local prosecutor Katarzyna Sill-Szułczyńska said on RMF FM radio.

The man also faces charges of insulting Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, former President Lech Wałęsa and Krzysztof Paszyk, a lawmaker from Tusk’s governing coalition.

The suspect allegedly posted messages calling for the killings on Facebook and TikTok between Aug. 3 and Oct. 7, according to TVP Info.

The detention follows Sunday’s arrest of a man suspected of planning an attack on Tusk and Kosiniak-Kamysz.

That case began with a warning received by the State Protection Service and prompted an emergency meeting of police, government protection officers and the Internal Security Agency.

“In this case, we are talking about a strong probability that these threats could have been acted upon,” security services spokesperson Jacek Dobrzyński said Sunday.

Authorities have not established a link between the two suspects or suggested specific motives.

]]> en Lights, bells and liability: Europe’s privacy regulators crack down on smart glasses https://www.politico.eu/article/lights-bells-and-liability-europes-privacy-regulators-crack-down-on-smart-glasses/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Tue, 13 Oct 2026 14:34:37 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9152693 BRUSSELS — Privacy regulators want people wearing smart glasses in public to look and sound like a truck backing down a road.

Europe’s powerful data regulators have made stringent new recommendations on how smart glasses should alert people that the wearable devices are filming, including a combination of flashing lights, audio alerts and notifications sent to the phones of people nearby.

The European Data Protection Board (EDPB), made up of national privacy regulators across Europe, issued a statement about smart glasses on Tuesday, following a meeting in Brussels.

Privacy regulators are putting forward a united front on smart glasses, as privacy concerns about the wearable technology have multiplied since videos made with them have begun spreading online without the knowledge or consent of those being filmed.

The statement is not legally binding but will guide how privacy regulators in Europe assess whether smart glasses users and manufacturers are complying with EU privacy rules like the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR).

The regulators said smart glasses manufacturers should implement a combination of transparency measures to make other people aware that they are being recorded.

The measures may include lights or sounds when users are recording, requiring smart glasses users to activate them with an audible voice command, sending notifications to the smartphones of people nearby and other design “clues” to help people spot smart glasses.

The group of privacy regulators said that not only should users of smart glasses respect other people’s privacy but that the devices’ manufacturers and people providing connected apps or services may also be responsible for making sure they comply with privacy rules.

The GDPR applies to companies and organizations, and doesn’t apply when people process personal data in a household context. The regulators said this household exemption should be “narrowly interpreted” when it comes to smart glasses, and would not apply when someone shares photos or videos of others “to an indefinite number of persons on a public social media account.”

Tech firms like Meta have pitched their smart glasses to consumers on the basis that they are sleek and discreet. Meta has included an LED light in its smart glasses, which activates while recording, which it has said is a key privacy safeguard.

Samsung and Google have also recently announced that they’re collaborating on a new line of “intelligent eyewear” set to launch later this year, and Apple is reportedly aiming to hit the market with its own smart glasses by the end of 2027. 

The regulators’ statement could now force smart glasses manufacturers to reassess whether and how they sell smart glasses to European consumers. The EDPB called for industry-wide standards to be developed to make sure people are able to spot smart glasses and understand how they process data.

The European group of privacy regulators also commissioned a study into the social acceptability of smart glasses, published today.

EUobserver https://euobserver.com Independent EU journalism Tue, 13 Oct 2026 16:59:22 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.3 Could Islamophobia one day become EU law? https://euobserver.com/242540/could-islamophobia-one-day-become-eu-law/ Tue, 13 Oct 2026 18:00:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=242540 An Islamophobic EU Parliament motion has showed that Europe's Muslims have reached an impossible crossroads - to integrate and forget their roots, or stay true to their traditions and risk being treated as a fifth column. ]]> If the day should ever come where Islamophobia gets concrete legal backing in Europe, it could be soon.

The European Parliament (EP) just voted to “condemn the strategies of Islamist entryism” and to develop ways to disrupt Muslim political movements in a resolution on 8 October.

Some 381 out of 720 MEPs worry Muslims are seeking to infiltrate democratic institutions, weaken European rule of law, gender equality, and what they deemed “European values”. 

And almost every one of the centre-right and rightwing MEPs in the house voted to surveil EU funding for anti-racism organisations, so as to ensure none of it gets into the hands of the Muslim Brotherhood.

The brotherhood is a transnational Muslim group founded in 1928 in Egypt, involved in religious revival, social welfare, and political activism.

But according to a French government memo from May 2025, as well as the EP resolution, it is guilty of “entryism”, to sabotage French democracy.

The EP resolution and French memo were dubbed “a political witch-hunt targeting racialised people – particularly Muslim, migrant and refugee communities” by academics and civil society, like the European Network Against Racism (ENAR).

Read more

Centre-right’s Muslim Brotherhood witch-hunt in EU Parliament risks criminalising everyday activism

The group called the EP motion “a stain” on the EU Parliament, belonging “within the tradition of discredited far-right conspiracy theories.”

ENAR is among those the EU has sought to defund, due to rightwing views that its work aligns with Islamist threats.

The Forum of European Muslim Youth and Student Organisations (FEMYSO), a pan-European anti-Islamophobic group, which also risks EU defunding, said it had faced “relentless targeting and demonisation.”

Young Muslims in Europe were being forced “to choose between their identity and their right to belong,” FEMYSO president Hiba Latreche told EUobserver.

And the EP “witch-hunt” resolution, which was drafted by the centre-right European People’s Party (EPP) group and authored by its French MEP, Céline Imart, comes at a bad time for this demographic. 

Read more

Von der Leyen’s party backs mapping ‘Islamist networks’ and scrapping key EU asylum protection

Advocacy group Collective Against Islamophobia in Europe (CCIE) recently looked at 876 incidents of anti-Muslim hatred in Europe in 2025.

Four out of five incidents targeted Muslim women, 41 percent of which involved discrimination or violence linked to their headscarves.

Disturbingly, the documented episodes “occur predominantly in public or institutional spaces, highlighting the persistence of forms of institutional racism.”

But seeing as the EU Commission’s own anti-Muslim hatred group has been inactive since 2024, the prevailing view in Brussels appears to be that rampant Islamophobia in the EU is less of a problem than the imputed influence of a nebulous Islamic movement from Egypt, which is better known for providing social care to deprived communities, than aiming to overthrow French president Emmanuel Macron.

The EP motion did not legally bind the European Commission to propose new anti-Muslim Brotherhood measures.

But it did enforce a stereotype of Muslims “as acting in a nefarious, dangerous, anti-democratic manner, until proven otherwise,” said Omran Shroufi, a political science researcher at the Free University of Brussels.

Read more

Europe’s dangerous art of anti-Muslim doublespeak

Rightwing EU politics is pushing young European Muslims into a lose-lose, or Catch 22 situation.

The notion of “entryism holds Muslims to an impossible standard, where non-participation in public life is a sign of disinterestedness, a lack of civic duty and the growth of parallel societies, whilst active engagement in civic life is treated with suspicion,” Shroufi told EUobserver.

The centre-right EPP group used to represent a moderate EU mainstream.

But now it had joined with open racists on Europe’s far right to be “effectively calling for an institutionalised form of discrimination, where Muslim communities need to prove their European and democratic values – whatever these are supposed to mean – before being allowed a seat at a table,” Shroufi said. 

]]> Low pay and stress forcing Europe’s care workers to quit jobs, unions warn https://euobserver.com/242562/low-pay-and-stress-forcing-europes-care-workers-to-quit-jobs-unions-warn/ Tue, 13 Oct 2026 16:59:22 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=242562 Almost half of workers helping families care for children, older people, and people with disabilities in Europe have considered quitting due to low pay and bad working conditions.]]> Almost half of workers helping families care for children, older people, and people with disabilities, who provide vital domestic support in Europe, have considered quitting due to low pay and bad working conditions, a labour-union report found on Tuesday (13 October).

The 2026 personal and household services (PHS) employment monitor drew on more than 8,000 responses from workers, service users, and employers in 36 countries.

Around one in four respondents worked between 35 and 40 hours per week.

Meanwhile, six in 10 workers reported work-related musculoskeletal disorders, including back pain and tendon inflammation.

One in four also said they had experienced or witnessed verbal abuse, while nearly 15 percent had experienced either sexual harassment, physical, and/or sexual violence.

Care poviders’ mental health is impacted, with around six out of 10 reporting sleeping issues.

But these same workers play “an essential role in providing a dignified life for everybody in our ageing European societies,” Oliver Roethig, regional secretary of UNI Europa said in a statement.

]]> Ukraine killing record number of Russian troops, as Putin resorts to using gangs to boost enlistment (Ukraine Battlefield update, day 1,692) https://euobserver.com/242547/ukraine-killing-record-number-of-russian-troops-as-putin-resorts-to-using-gangs-to-boost-enlistment-ukraine-battlefield-update-day-1692/ Tue, 13 Oct 2026 15:47:16 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=242547 Soaring Russian casualty rates and shrinking recruitment mean frontline units risk running out of men to hold or advance in Donbas, even as Ukraine keeps blowing up their supply trucks and fuel tankers.]]>
  • Russia is estimated to be recruiting 10 percent fewer soldiers this year than last, despite regions raising signing bonuses.
  • There is growing talk that criminal gangs have begun to take part in recruiting “volunteers”.
  • According to the Ukrainians, Russia is losing large numbers of soldiers, and October could be a record month.
  • Attacks on the land route to Crimea continue, reportedly prompting Russia to transport fuel in jerry cans in smaller vehicles.
  • Map of the day: Where Russia is advancing and where Ukraine is advancing
  • Videos of the day: Ukrainians hit a Russian radar; a man surfed on a Russian drone near Odesa; speculation spreads that Iran is supplying Russia with fuel.

    • Many Russians have left Russia in recent months. They feared the mobilisation that had been so widely discussed. Ukrainians said Russian president Vladimir Putin might resort to it after the September parliamentary elections. Many Russians fled to Armenia and Georgia, affecting rental prices in the capitals of these Caucasus states.

    So far, no mobilisation has taken place. Russia continues to rely on its existing system of voluntary — and, in some places, involuntary — recruitment of new soldiers in Russian regions.

    German economist Janis Kluge, who tracks regional data, wrote last week that Russia recruits around 1,000 new soldiers a day (30,000 a month). That is less than last year — down six percent in September and 10 percent over the year as a whole.

    Nor did it help that, by his estimate, the sum paid by regions as a signing bonus had risen from $16,000 (€14,000) to $22,000.

    In some places, recruitment is also beginning to move into the illegal sphere. Kluge wrote that local criminal gangs were now becoming involved in the system.

    He mentioned the case of a prosecutor in Nizhny Tagil, a city of 400,000 in the Urals. In September, he appealed to the budget committee of the local duma.

    He complained that signing bonuses for Russian soldiers were leading to an increase in crime in the city. He called for payments to agents who find volunteers willing to sign an army contract to be stopped.

    According to Kluge, the prosecutor complained that criminal elements had become involved in recruitment in the city. He said an agent received $4,500 for finding one person to sign a contract.

    Many turned to gangs to help them, with the assistance of corrupt police officers or military recruiters who are part of the scheme. “And this ‘persuasion’ may also involve violence, as another case from Sverdlovsk region shows: two criminals forced their victims to sign contracts and then seized their bonus payments,” Kluge wrote.

    In Nizhny Tagil, 580 new soldiers were recruited last year, compared with 330 this year. It is not known how many of them criminal gangs helped to “persuade” in exchange for payment. In any case, the city does not want to change its system of rewards for agents because, in the words of the deputy mayor, it helps “fulfil our tasks”.

    Overall, it is becoming increasingly difficult for Russia to supply enough manpower to the front. Moreover, it is currently losing large numbers of soldiers there, and October’s losses could even be record-breaking.

    Ukraine publishes daily figures for killed and wounded Russian soldiers. These figures cannot be verified and may be inflated, but the trend suggests that the situation is worsening for Russia.

    The table below also shows this. According to it, Russia lost around 46,000 soldiers in September — more than 1,500 a day — making it, according to Ukrainian data, the second-worst month since the start of the war. The figure was higher only in December 2024.

    This October is on course to become Russia’s worst month in this respect. By the 12th day of the month, Russia had been losing an average of 1,620 soldiers per day. If Ukraine maintains this pace, it will be a record.

    Number of Russian military casualties per month, according to Ukraine. Source: minfin.com.ua

    Naturally, the question is how much these figures can be trusted. However, the Unmanned Systems Forces, a unit commanded by Robert Brovdi, known as Magyar, also publish figures for killed and wounded Russian soldiers.

    The Ukrainian units under its command compete with one another over which can strike more Russian targets. They receive points based on this, which they can then use to buy more drones. Individual strikes should therefore be confirmed by video.

    Given this, the data published by the Unmanned Systems Forces can be considered credible. They too indicate that October could be a record month, although their data cover only one-third of Russia’s total losses.

    Number of Russian soldiers killed and wounded by SBS drones

    Record-high losses and less substantial numbers of newly recruited soldiers suggest that Russia may have difficulties replenishing its units and, consequently, advancing further in Donbas or elsewhere.

    Attacks on the land route to Crimea continue. Last week, French OSINT analyst Clément Molin published a table according to which the number of Russian lorries and trucks struck had reached a record 770. Several videos show that the number of attacks on vehicles heading to Crimea or to the front in southern Ukraine remains high. They are simply not discussed as much because this is no longer new.

    Ukraine also destroyed the Chonhar bridge, which connects Ukraine with the Crimean peninsula. Russia has used a pontoon bridge there instead. This video shows Russian cargo vehicles crossing the pontoon bridge.

    The commander of Ukraine’s 41st Pilum Unmanned Systems Regiment, part of the 1st Azov Corps, recently provided interesting information on this issue. In an interview with Radio NV, he confirmed that the number of medium-range strikes was not declining and was increasing in some areas.

    He said that the operational zone overseen by Ukraine extended from 30 to 300 km.

    According to him, Russia is trying to bring as much fuel as possible to the front. Soldiers need generators to charge equipment, power radios and drones, and keep warm.

    However, Ukrainian attacks on fuel tankers are reducing Russia’s ability to bring fuel to the front. According to the commander, in the Dobropillia direction, where his unit operates, Russia began transporting fuel in convoys this summer and switched to distributing it in passenger cars or small trucks, carrying the fuel in jerry cans.

    This does not, of course, apply to all directions. However, an ongoing stream of new videos also confirms the destruction of fuel tankers.

    Map of the day

    Russian president Vladimir Putin’s latest — though certainly not final — deadline for capturing Donbas is by the end of this year. As on 14 previous occasions, it will not be met.

    Unlike in previous years, however, it appears entirely possible that by the end of the year the territory of the free part of Donetsk region could be even larger than it is now. This is suggested by a map published by French OSINT analyst Clément Molin. It highlights areas where Ukraine is advancing and areas where Russia is pushing forward.

    As can be seen, Russian forces largely hold the initiative in the north of Kharkiv region and at one location in the south of Zaporizhzhia region.

    In the crucial Donetsk region, however, the situation is balanced; indeed, it could be said that Ukraine holds the initiative in more places. More specifically, it is clearing the northern area above Lyman and pushing further south towards Velyka Novosilka.

    Source: Clément Molin

    Videos of the day

    Ukraine’s 15th Reconnaissance Artillery Brigade published a video showing it striking a Russian 96L6 radar. This is a key component of the S-300 and S-400 air-defence systems.

    The radar can be seen moving and hiding in a tree line. Nevertheless, a Ukrainian drone struck it. It is unclear whether it was actually destroyed, as the accompanying text claims.

    A man near Odesa decided to surf on a downed Russian drone floating on the water off the coast. It hardly needs to be said that this is a fairly risky pastime. However, it indicates how at least some residents of Odesa view the daily Russian attacks.

    This could be a potentially rather interesting plot twist. The United States is at war with Iran, which has raised petrol and diesel prices at US filling stations. Donald Trump therefore agreed with Putin to import diesel from Russia. Russia itself, however, does not have enough diesel and has to import it.

    This video shows a tanker truck with Iranian registration plates in Russia. Some infer from this that Iran is importing diesel — or other fuels — into Russia, which then sends diesel to America, despite America being at war with Iran.

    However, it is too early to draw conclusions: we do not know what is in the truck or how many such Iranian tankers are heading to Russia. In any case, Russia is helping Iran in other ways.

    A Western official told Bloomberg that Russia was supplying Iran with missiles that it uses in the war against the US and Israel. It was also previously reported that Russia was helping Iran target US bases in the region.

    What are the losses:

    • By Tuesday (13 October), Russia had verifiably lost 24,192 pieces of heavy equipment (24,170 on Monday, 5 October). Of these, 19,155 (19,133) were destroyed by Ukraine, 1,002 (1,003) damaged, 1,194 (1,194) abandoned by their crews, and 2,841 (2,840) captured by the Ukrainian army. The total includes 4,453 (4,452) tanks, of which 3,358 (3,357) were destroyed in combat.
    • Ukraine lost 12,259 (12,238) pieces of equipment, of which 9,652 (9,633) were destroyed, 713 (711) damaged, 695 (695) abandoned and 1,199 (1,199) captured. The total includes 1,471 (1,466) tanks, of which 1,131 (1,126) were destroyed in combat.

    Note: Neither side regularly reports its dead or destroyed equipment. Ukraine publishes daily figures for Russian casualties and destroyed equipment, which cannot be independently verified. This overview uses data from the Oryx project, which has compiled a list of equipment losses documented exclusively by photographs since the start of the war.

    ]]>         Von der Leyen pledges more cash for Egypt and Libya regimes to keep Sudanese genocide victims out of Europe https://euobserver.com/242504/von-der-leyen-pledges-more-cash-for-egypt-and-libya-regimes-to-keep-sudanese-genocide-victims-out-of-europe/ Tue, 13 Oct 2026 14:58:26 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=242504 They fled genocide in Sudan to find persecution in Egypt so they moved on to Libya, but von der Leyen aims to pay Cairo and Tripoli to keep Sudanese refugees out of Fortress EU. ]]> The European Commission is promising more support to Egypt, even as Egyptian warplanes reportedly bomb in Sudan and authorities carry out a campaign of violence against the refugees it hosts.

    The civil war in Sudan includes reports of genocide, chemical-weapons use, mass rape, and starvation, forcing some 1.2 million Sudanese people into Egypt, which was described as a priority migration-busting partner by commission president Ursula von der Leyen on Tuesday (13 October), who also promised continuing support for Cairo.

    In a letter sent to the 27 heads of state and government ahead of an EU summit on Thursday in Brussels, she spoke of “offering protection and durable solutions in … host countries”, as well as further aid for Sudanese people who had returned to parts of the country, now deemed relatively safe.

    Read more

    EU to offer Egypt more incentives at October summit

    But her warm words stand in sharp contrast to internal EU documents on Sudan, released by the London-based group Statewatch earlier this month, and which speak of an Egyptian-led campaign of violence against the Sudanese it is tasked to help.

    “The Egyptian authorities have continued arbitrary arrests, detention and deportation campaign against migrants, asylum seekers and refugees, with a sharp escalation of forced deportations being observed since January 2026,” said the Irish EU presidency, in an internal document written in September.

    Estimates suggest Egypt hosts over nine million migrants and refugees.

    Some 80 percent are Sudanese, Syrian, Yemeni, and Libyan nationals. Of those, just over 1 million are officially registered as refugees. Most come from Sudan.

    Read more

    The battle for equivalence — the EU’s role in Sudan’s civil war sanctions

    This article is paid for by JA Europe.

    On 15 September, the European Commission proposed a Skills Portability Act, a regulation designed to make qualifications digital, comparable, and easier to recognise across borders. It forms part of the Fair Labour Mobility Package and must still be adopted by the European Parliament and the Council before any of its measures can take effect. 

    It is a welcome step. But it leaves open a question that deserves more attention in Brussels: what happens to the skills young people develop every day but their diplomas and CVs do not capture? 

    Communication, teamwork, critical thinking, adaptability and resilience shape how people work with others and keep learning throughout their careers. Employers say they need these skills. According to the Commission’s 2023 Flash Eurobarometer, 74 percent of small and medium-sized enterprises reported shortages affecting at least one job role. Meanwhile, Eurostat found that in 2024 only 56.4 percent of people aged 15–34 in the EU with medium or high educational attainment reported a high or very high match between their field of education and the requirements of their current or last main job. 

    These figures measure different things and should not be read as pointing to a single cause. Together, though, they show that having qualified people and having the right capabilities in the right place are not the same thing. Young people build those capabilities in classrooms, vocational training, volunteering, creative projects and first jobs. Yet they struggle to show them in a form that an employer, particularly one in another country, understands and trusts. 

    The stakes are not abstract. In 2025, 11 percent of Europeans aged 15–29 were neither in employment nor in education or training. Skills recognition cannot resolve that on its own, but stronger links between learning and work are part of the answer. 

    In effect, we are asking young Europeans to cross borders with incomplete passports. 

    This is where micro-credentials can make a difference if they are built with credibility in mind. JA Europe coordinates EMPASS (Employment Skills Pass), an Erasmus+ Forward-Looking Project co-funded by the European Union. It brings together education providers, industry partners and Junior Achievement organisations to develop and validate an employability micro-credential covering 11 employability skills, from communication and teamwork to resilience and critical thinking. 

    The micro-credential was designed to be piloted with 1,500 students in Greece, Romania and Spain. According to the project’s latest monitoring figures, 2,700 young people now hold an EmPass certificate. 

    Beyond the pilot, the EMPASS approach is already demonstrating potential for wider uptake. The methodology has informed implementation and exploration activities in other countries, including Ukraine and Lithuania, and has been incorporated into wider youth employability initiatives such as the Global Alliance for Youth mentoring programme. This suggests that employability micro-credentials can be integrated into different learning and workforce-development contexts while maintaining a common framework for skills recognition. 

    A micro-credential does not replace a diploma, and no single certificate can capture everything a person brings to a job. Its value lies in complementing formal qualifications with clearer, validated evidence of what someone can do. The aim should not be another certificate that employers overlook. 

    Europe does not need more initiatives that show promise but struggle to reach scale. It needs bridges: between education and employment, between national systems, and policy ambition and lived experience. That means asking practical questions. Can a young person show the same verified capabilities to employers in different countries? Can employers see what microcredential assesses and how it was validated? Can schools and universities build it into existing pathways without adding administrative burden? 

    The answers will decide whether skills portability becomes opportunity or remains a policy ambition. They are also the focus of From Skills to Opportunity, a JA Europe forum in Brussels on 14 October, bringing together policymakers, employers, educators and youth organisations, including speakers from the European Commission, the World Employment Confederation and the European Vocational Training Association. 

    As the Skills Portability Act moves through parliament and council, Europe has a chance to put employability skills into the conversation from the start: not only how qualifications are recognised, but how capabilities developed through formal, non-formal and experiential learning can carry meaning across borders. 

    Employability skills are not an abstract policy debate. They are part of the foundation for participation, mobility, and opportunity in Europe’s labour market. The task now is to ensure that every young person carries a passport that employers recognise, wherever their learning and career take them.

    That said, a colder or longer winter than expected, or disruptions to supplies in other parts of the world, could put additional pressure on the market. Especially at a time when the EU is preparing to phase out Russian gas imports in 2027.

    In Europe, a grand scheme, a so-called “One Europe, One Market”, aims to spike European fortunes by saving an estimated €37.5bn for EU businesses by 2029.

    The drive is part of a larger initiative to cut red tape and remove internal market barriers, including the eventual launch of a so-called EU Inc.

    Ireland, which is currently steering the EU’s rotating presidency, had already announced that the summit would start with the competitiveness theme. And leaked draft conclusions, seen by EUobserver, lead with a sales pitch to step up ambitions over the ‘One Europe, One Market’ proposal.

    It also gives a nod to the German car industry, by citing efforts needed to stop China from making too much money off Europeans. The goal is to get Europeans to spend more on European products, even if they are more expensive and less innovative.

    The ‘more money’ talks dovetail into how to spend it (or not) in the EU’s next long-term budget, spanning 2028 to 2034.

    António Costa, the president of the European Council, is hoping for an agreement of the nearly €2 trillion budget before the end of the year. People need predictability and stability, he said, in a invitation letter sent to the 27 EU states.

      <title>Threat of AI share crash puts world financial stability at risk, says IMF</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/13/ai-share-crash-risk-global-imf-debt-corrowing-cyber-attacks</link>
      <description><p>High valuations and debt put sector in danger, while fund also warns on government borrowing and cyber-attacks</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/13/imf-global-economy-world-economic-outlook-uk-gdp-forecast-2026">IMF warns global economy ‘could soon test the limits of resilience’</a></p></li></ul><p>The threat of an AI share price crash rippling out across global markets is putting world financial stability at risk, the International Monetary fund has warned.</p><p>In its twice-yearly Global Financial Stability Report, the IMF highlighted the sky-high valuations for AI companies along with their increasing debt pile as one reason that risks in the system are “elevated”.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/13/ai-share-crash-risk-global-imf-debt-corrowing-cyber-attacks">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>BBC asks US federal judge to compel Trump’s lawyers to schedule deposition after his team canceled initial session</p><p>The BBC is asking a federal judge in <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/florida">Florida</a> to force <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/donaldtrump">Donald Trump</a> to sit for a deposition as part of the president’s $10bn defamation lawsuit against the British broadcaster.</p><p>According to a Tuesday filing, the BBC and Trump’s legal team had agreed for him to be deposed on Friday.       <description><p>US economists developed models that help central bankers and finance ministers to stabilise their economies</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/live/2026/oct/12/uk-growth-inflation-pressures-oil-price-sveriges-riksbank-nobel-prize-economic-sciences-awarded-latest-news-updates">Business live – latest updates</a></p></li></ul><p>Two US economists have won the 2026 Nobel economics prize for their work developing models that help central bankers and finance ministers to stabilise their countries, avoiding long recessions and runaway inflation.</p><p>Robert Hall of Stanford University, California, and Michael Woodford of Columbia University, New York, were recognised for <a href="https://www.nobelprize.org/uploads/2026/10/advanced-economicsciencesprize2026.pdf">developing the “microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation”</a>, giving policymakers better tools to smooth out the peaks and troughs of their economies.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/12/nobel-prize-for-economics-hall-woodford-new-keynesian-models">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>Analysts say fuel will take weeks to ship and quantity is too small to affect prices, while full deal is unlikely to be met given damage to Russian refineries</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/11/zelenskyy-trump-ukraine-russia-energy-ceasefire">Trump announces partial ceasefire but Zelenskyy says deal is ‘news to me’</a></p></li></ul><p>Donald Trump’s deal with Vladimir Putin to temporarily lift sanctions on US imports of Russian diesel will have little “meaningful” effect on motorists and businesses in the US and overseas, energy and foreign policy analysts have predicted.</p><p>The US president <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/09/trump-putin-russian-diesel-ukraine">infuriated Volodymyr Zelenskyy</a> when he announced the deal on Friday, writing on Truth Social that the agreement with his Russia counterpart to supply millions of tonnes of diesel was essential to reduce fuel prices in the US, which have soared after his decision to go to war against Iran.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/11/trump-russia-diesel-deal-putin-little-impact-prices">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>Is punishing the poor Trump’s last hand to play?</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/13/trump-aca-healthcare-politics-midterms</link>
      <description><p>The pre-midterm defenestration of ACA enrollees looks like political madness – but the president appears to believe hitting poor people might work for him</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/08/economy-midterm-elections-tell-us">Send us your questions on how the US economy is shaping the midterm elections</a></p></li></ul><p>There is a manic quality to <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/donaldtrump">Donald Trump</a>’s desperate dash to do something, anything, ahead of November’s <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/us-midterm-elections-2026">midterm elections</a> to convince beleaguered Americans that he can make the pressures his policies have imposed on their livelihoods go away.</p><p>The US president <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/aug/28/trump-cattle-ranchers-beef-imports-backlash">offered</a> to lower barriers against beef imports to limit surging meat prices, only to consider <a href="https://www.politico.com/news/2026/09/23/trump-beef-imports-midterms-gop-panic-01090261">backtracking</a> under <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/aug/25/trump-republican-backlash-beef-tariff-import">pressure</a> from the cow lobby. He <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/sep/22/trump-diesel-export-ban">offered</a> to stop diesel exports, only to find oil companies <a href="https://finance.yahoo.com/energy/articles/market-chatter-us-oil-executives-112235250.html">were</a> <a href="https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/07/chevron-ceo-diesel-export-ban-trump-supply.html">not interested</a>. He weakened fuel efficiency standards, claiming this would trim the price of a new car (and forgetting to point out it will also raise spending on gas). In early October he started mailing <a href="https://www.cnn.com/2026/10/01/economy/trump-obamacare-500-check">$500 checks</a> to nearly a million people touting his healthcare “wins”. Oh, and he promised adult Americans a <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/sep/10/trump-5000-midterm-cash-dividend-response">$5,000 check</a> if Republicans maintain control of Congress. That, too, will <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/sep/10/trump-dividend-republican-midterm-convention">go nowhere</a>.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/13/trump-aca-healthcare-politics-midterms">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>John Steinbeck’s hometown of Salinas is the least affordable city in the US for the middle class, a recent Brookings Institution analysis found </p><p>Nestled between two mountain ranges at the crook of central California’s coastline sits a valley known as the “salad bowl of the world”.</p><p>Farm workers stoop over neatly lined rows of crops off Highway 101 to harvest more than half of the nation’s supply of lettuce and nearly a third of its strawberries. <![CDATA[Irish Times Feeds]]>https://www.irishtimes.comWed, 14 Oct 2026 00:50:11 +0000en1hourly1<![CDATA[Why we must have this performative strike by public sector workers ]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/10/13/why-we-must-have-this-performative-strike-by-public-sector-workers/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/10/13/why-we-must-have-this-performative-strike-by-public-sector-workers/Tue, 13 Oct 2026 13:49:29 +0000Years ago – in the days of social partnership – I remember an industrial correspondent of this newspaper telling me that on one occasion after an amicable arrangement had been reached in the early evening on the latest national pay agreement, all sides sat around Government buildings until the early hours of the following morning before announcing it. They needed to convey the impression to their respective constituencies – the public and private sector workers, their bosses and the rest of us – just how tough the negotiations had been and how close they came to failure.

Apocryphal as this story probably was, it highlights a truth about the public sector strike on Wednesday. Everybody knows that the Government will eventually agree to a public sector pay increase in line with inflation and get some concessions from the public sector to offset the bill. There is no other possible, sustainable outcome.

So why all the theatrics? Both sides have their reasons. Some are about optics; others are more substantial.

The union representatives obviously need to be seen to be earning their dues. From that simple perspective, arriving at predictable agreement after some ritualistic bloodletting in the form of strike – or a couple of strikes – makes sense.

As well as letting public sector workers blow off some understandable steam, it also makes the eventual and ultimately disappointing outcome in some way more valuable because it has been fought for.

The Government also needs to be seen to fight for the taxpayer – although what seems to get lost in these fights is that public sector workers pay tax. Some of them pay quite a lot of tax.

In much the same way as the unions need to be seen to have fought for every fraction of a percentage point of an increase, the Minister for Public Expenditure and Reform Jack Chambers needs to be seen to have shown a willingness to die in the ditch for the exchequer.

But if it was just about optics, you would expect this biennial process to evolve into some sort of ritualised combat akin to the World Wrestling Federation’s WrestleMania. We know it’s pretence but enjoy it anyway. To a certain extent, this is what happened between 1987 and 2010 under eight successive social partnership agreements, including the one referred to above.

The model broke down in the aftermath of the 2008 financial crash when the cuts sought by the government were too big for the unions to wear and ended up being imposed unilaterally.

An interesting question is why the unions have not tried to put social partnership back together again and have instead adopted a much more antagonistic approach that has brought us to this strike. Rather than enter negotiations without precondition – social partnership style- they have demanded the Government first agree the pay element before then moving on to terms and conditions.

This is where the game theory wonks come in. There is plenty of research to suggest unions can have the upper hand in antagonistic negotiations of this sort in certain circumstances.

These include a tight labour market where the Government finds it hard to recruit and retain employees. There also has to be a credible threat of industrial action and significant consequences for the Government from the resulting disruption, such as damage to its fiscal credibility with electoral consequences.

The final ingredient is significant public support for public sector workers, such as nurses, teachers etc.

It all sounds very familiar. It also explains why the unions are trying to split the talks into two. They want to use their pretty significant leverage where it matters most – pay increases – rather than fritter it away fighting over tea breaks and the like.

The Government can of course see them coming and will not fall into the trap. Not yet at least.

It has given an indirect indication of what is on the table by including a figure for the impact of public pay increases next year in the budget that has just been passed. It can be seen as a reasonable opening bid and has already been upped with the indication that more is available from a €1.6 billion contingency fund.

This reflects the interest of the Government to avoid the strike. But the unions seem confident enough in the strength of their hand to stick to their maximalist position.

Much will now hinge on the blame game that will follow the 24-hour strike and any subsequent ones should they materialise.

Eventually public support or sympathy for the strikers will run out. The disruption of 150,000 medical appointments will erode it. As will the headaches involved in organising someone to look after your children. Both sides know this. They just don’t know when it will happen.

At some point the deal will be done and it will not be very different from the one that could be hammered out this morning. Social partnership for slow learners.

]]><![CDATA[Retirement crisis looms for those in mortgage arrears, new analysis shows]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/13/retirement-crisis-looms-for-those-in-mortgage-arrears-report/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/13/retirement-crisis-looms-for-those-in-mortgage-arrears-report/Tue, 13 Oct 2026 18:52:42 +0000One in two of those in mortgage arrears are unlikely to clear even half their outstanding loan balance by the time they retire, according to a fresh Central Bank of Ireland analysis.

While the number of mortgages linked to family homes that are in arrears of more than 90 days has fallen from a peak of 12.9 per cent of all principal dwelling home mortgages back in September 2013 to just 3.1 per cent at the end of last year, that still amounts to more than 21,000 home loans.

And three-quarters of those in arrears now have their loans managed by loan servicing firms rather than the banks.

The Solution Waterfall: Insights from Irish Mortgage Distress Cases examines the arrangements put in place for close to 5,400 people in 2024 by banks and loan servicing firms.

Based on what they are paying and the time to retirement, the report’s authors suggest that 31 per cent of those in arrears will not be able to make any headway in clearing their mortgage balance.

A further 19 per cent will clear less than 50 per cent of the amount outstanding.

Pepper rate hike to heap more misery on distressed borrowers

The figures are worse for those whose loans are held by loan servicing firms than by banks. More than two-thirds of those at loan servicing firms will clear less than half of what they owe by the time they retire, the authors project, compared to just over a third of bank customers.

In the 2024 sample used in the report, loan servicing firms’ customers are older – 56 on at the median – compared to 51 at banks and have been in arrears for longer with larger outstanding loan balances.

Customers of loan servicing firms are more likely to be on higher variable interest rates – a premium of about 1.4 percentage points in 2024, according to the report – and less likely to be meeting the terms of the restructured repayment arrangements, write Patrik Gorše, Thomas Joyce and Paul Lyons.

“The ability to repay mortgage obligations by borrowers in long-term arrears who are now approaching or at retirement age remains a concern,” the authors say. “Finding sustainable restructures within the financial system for engaged borrowers in long-term mortgage arrears may not be possible.

“Many of those in long-term mortgage arrears today are now in their 50s or 60s, are mentally exhausted and need a permanent viable solution,” said Stephen Curtis, chief executive of mortgage-to-rent specialist Irish Homes.

“These people have had mortgage arrears hanging over them for decades and, in turn, the worry that they could lose their home.”

Curtis noted that central bank mortgage arrears data for the second quarter of this year showed that the number of accounts in arrears that are being brought before the courts had jumped by 6.6 per cent over the previous 12 months.
