]]>Bloomberg<![CDATA[LNG critical to energy security, conference told]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/13/lng-critical-to-energy-security-conference-told/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/13/lng-critical-to-energy-security-conference-told/Tue, 13 Oct 2026 18:00:02 +0000Liquefied natural gas (LNG) is critical to the State’s energy security, a member of the Government’s infrastructure taskforce warned on Tuesday.

The Oireachtas passed legislation this year giving Minister for Energy Darragh O’Brien power to bypass planning laws to approve a proposed State LNG storage project.

Businessman Seán O’Driscoll, a member of the Government’s Accelerating Infrastructure Task Force, told the Institute of Directors annual conference that he had heard arguments in the media that the Republic does not need LNG.

“Thirty per cent of our primary energy is gas,” he said, adding that it came through a pipeline from Scotland.

“If anything happens those pipelines, our economy shuts down in three or four hours. For people to peddle the line, and get away with it, that we don’t need LNG facilities, is complacency,” O’Driscoll argued.

He remarked that the State took a lot of risks with its energy system. While it depends on imported oil for 50 per cent of its energy, its strategic reserve amounts to just 90 days’ supply, O’Driscoll added.

Speaking afterwards, he said the enactment of the Critical Infrastructure Act and new planning laws showed the Government’s commitment to overhauling the State’s system for planning and building infrastructure.

The infrastructure legislation means that key projects move to the top of the planning system’s queue. Government has since earmarked nine projects in transport, energy and water as critical infrastructure.

Those projects include the MetroLink, Shannon-Dublin water scheme, and North-South Interconnector, a high-capacity electricity line between the Republic and Northern Ireland.

That project was announced 20 years ago and has made it through the planning systems on both sides of the Border, but is not expected to be completed until 2031.

O’Driscoll said it was up to local and national politicians to win public acceptance for the project, which has met strong opposition from locals and landowners along the proposed route.

“These things have to be built; political leaders will have to step up,” he insisted.

The absence of the long-delayed project costs electricity users North and South €100 million extra a year, he said.

O’Driscoll is a former chairman of industrial group Glen Dimplex and of the Economic and Social Research Institute.

The infrastructure taskforce identified four key areas that Government needed to tackle to speed up the construction of projects vital to the State: legal reform, regulatory reform, co-ordination and public acceptance.

O’Driscoll said he concurred “100 per cent” with Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers’ remark last week that Government was working on unprecedented levels of change on the State’s systems for planning and building infrastructure.

Actual building of the MetroLink, tying Dublin’s city centre with its airport, could begin in February 2027, while State utility Uisce Éireann hopes to begin construction of the €1.3 billion wastewater project, the Greater Dublin Drainage scheme, shortly. That should be completed in 2030.

]]><![CDATA[Workers have no ‘collective responsibility’ for business losses, WRC tells catering firm]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/13/workers-have-no-collective-responsibility-for-business-losses-wrc-tells-catering-firm/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/13/workers-have-no-collective-responsibility-for-business-losses-wrc-tells-catering-firm/Tue, 13 Oct 2026 17:20:53 +0000A worker left unpaid for over a year after her ex-boss claimed she had “collective responsibility” for poor catering trade at a music festival last year has secured an order for €2,300 in unpaid wages.

“This may come as news to the respondent, but where a business loses money, there is no ‘collective responsibility’ for these losses,” an adjudication officer wrote in a decision published on Tuesday.

Belfast-based Nord Events Ltd has been directed to pay the sum to the worker Martina Tierney after being found in breach of the Payment of Wages Act 1991 by the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC).

Tierney, a secondary schoolteacher, told the WRC that she took up short-term temporary work doing administration for the firm before and during Forest Fest 2025, a three-day music and arts event in Co Laois.

At the time she was hired by company co-owner Aaron Cleary, she was told it was one of a number of festivals for which Nord Events was the catering contractor, she said.

Her duties were in preparation and administration for the catering operation, and she performed “many days” of work between July 18th and 28th, 2025, she said.

Tierney wrote to her employer seeking payment for 119.5 hours on August 8th, 2025, with Cleary having undertaken to pay her no later than 28 days after doing so, she said.

She filed a WRC complaint under the Payment of Wages Act five weeks later on September 15th, 2025 and confirmed at a hearing in September 2026 that she had still yet to be paid – over a year later.

Adjudication officer Pat Brady noted that Tierney wrote to her employer setting out the hours she worked and seeking payment.

In reply, the employer set out a list of issues stated to have arisen at the festival, including reduced turnover and complaints about food.

They blamed these alleged trading difficulties on “a failure of the team put together by [Tierney] to run the operation” Brady wrote.

“He stated that there was what he described as ‘a collective responsibility’ for these poor commercial outcomes. This may come as news to the respondent, but where a business loses money, there is no ‘collective responsibility’ for these losses,” Brady added.

He wrote that businesses had no right to present trading losses as a justification for failing in their legal duty to give staff their properly payable wages.

He upheld Tierney’s complaint and directed the firm to pay her the €2,321.75 in outstanding wages.

]]><![CDATA[Supreme Court to hear appeal in LinkedIn challenge to €310m DPC fine]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/crime-law/courts/2026/10/13/supreme-court-to-hear-appeal-on-preliminary-issues-arising-in-linkedin-challenge-to-310m-dpc-fine/https://www.irishtimes.com/crime-law/courts/2026/10/13/supreme-court-to-hear-appeal-on-preliminary-issues-arising-in-linkedin-challenge-to-310m-dpc-fine/Tue, 13 Oct 2026 15:40:35 +0000The Supreme Court will hear an appeal by the Data Protection Commission (DPC) relating to certain preliminary matters arising in LinkedIn’s challenge to the imposition of a €310 million fine by the commission.

In October 2024, the DPC fined LinkedIn €310 million for breaches of European data protection legislation.

Microsoft-owned LinkedIn claims that the fine was a sanction that is “criminal or penal in nature” due to its magnitude. The company subsequently initiated High Court proceedings challenging this decision.

LinkedIn asked the High Court to quash the DPC’s decision of October 2023, which came on foot of a 2018 complaint originally made to the French data watchdog by a French non-profit organisation called La Quadrature du Net.

In a statement at the time of its decision, the DPC said LinkedIn had obtained the consent of its users for their personal data to be sent to third parties for generating targeted advertising. However, it found the consent was not “freely given, sufficiently informed or specific, or unambiguous”, as is required under the GDPR.

LinkedIn Ireland said the DPC initially proposed imposing administrative fines of between €430 million and €490 million. That figure was reduced following submissions from the company.

The social media group focused on professional networking claims the severity of the fine entitled it to a fair and public hearing before an independent and impartial tribunal and to the presumption of innocence, as provided for in the Charter of Fundamental Rights.

In a judgment handed down in April, the High Court determined several preliminary issues in the proceedings. The DPC has appealed to the Supreme Court on three of the issues decided on by the High Court. LinkedIn is also looking to bring a cross-appeal on another preliminary issue.

Granting permission for the appeal, a three-judge Supreme Court panel noted that parties to the dispute agree that the issues raised in the High Court determination are matters of general public importance, a prerequisite for any case heard by the Supreme Court.

“[The case] will likely affect the approach to other statutory appeals. The DPC is the lead supervisory authority for GDPR [General Data Protection Regulation] purposes in this respect. The complaint in this case was initiated by a French non-profit organisation,” the court said.

“The number of subscribers to LinkedIn runs to hundreds of millions and the number of persons affected by the GDPR infringement found by the DPC was very significant indeed. And, finally, the State had been permitted to participate in the hearing in the High Court precisely because of the significance of the issues involved.”

The panel also decided that the issues raised warranted a leapfrog appeal from the High Court.

In those High Court proceedings, LinkedIn alleges the DPC, in inflicting such a severe fine and other reprimand, was not exercising limited functions and powers of a judicial nature within the meaning of the Constitution.

The company claims various sections of the 2018 Data Protection Act related to the commission’s powers are contrary to the Constitution, the Charter of Fundamental Rights and the State’s obligations under the European Convention on Human Rights.

]]>Daniel Sambraus<![CDATA[McDonald’s uses Ireland to test hand-breaded chicken in Europe]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/13/mcdonalds-uses-ireland-to-test-hand-breaded-chicken-in-europe/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/13/mcdonalds-uses-ireland-to-test-hand-breaded-chicken-in-europe/Tue, 13 Oct 2026 16:34:26 +0000McDonald’s has launched a four-month “operational pilot” for hand-breaded chicken products in Ireland, the fast-food giant has announced.

“Ireland’s strength in chicken makes it the ideal market to help us understand what it takes to deliver this at scale and support our ambition to become the first choice for more customers, more often.

McDonald’s operates 96 restaurants across the State and employs more than 7,000 people as of April 2026.

]]>Zhang Peng<![CDATA[Surge in stud fees help Godolphin cut losses sharply at Irish operation]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/13/surge-in-stud-fees-help-godolphin-cut-losses-sharply-at-irish-operation/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/13/surge-in-stud-fees-help-godolphin-cut-losses-sharply-at-irish-operation/Tue, 13 Oct 2026 16:09:57 +0000Revenues at Godolphin’s Irish thoroughbred stud operation surged by 42 per cent to €44.29 million last year on the back of a sharp rise in nomination fee income.

That helps Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum’s Godolphin Ireland Ltd dramatically cutting pretax losses to €1.93 million from €11.34 million previously, a fall of 83 per cent.

Godolphin’s operation in Ireland comprises five farms in Kildare, one in Meath and two in Tipperary.

The Godolphin displayed its financial muscle in recent weeks when it outbid Coolmore to pay €1.3 million for Churchtown House Stud’s Modern Games filly at Goffs’ Orby Sale on September 29th.

The rise in revenues coincided with a strong year on the track by Godolphin-trained horses globally.

In May last year, Godolphin created history with four Classic winners in three days, including the Kentucky Derby victory in the US for Sovereignty.

The headquarters of the Irish operation, which embraces stud, arable and livestock farming, is Kildangan Stud, just outside Kildare town.

Ruler of Dubai and vice-president of the United Arab Emirates (UAE), Al-Maktoum is one of the world’s richest leaders and one of the most famous names in the world of horse racing, pouring billions of euro into the industry over the past 40 years.

Nomination fee income – the stud fee that owners of mares pay to have their horses covered by a Goldophin horse – last year surged 55 per cent to €36.99 million as accommodation, or “keep fee” income remained flat at €5.8 million.

Accumulated losses at Godolphin Ireland rose to €212.38 million at the end of last year with a shareholders’ deficit of €184.52 million.

The firm’s cash funds increased from €5.46 million to €12.77 million.

On the company’s going concern status, the directors state that Godolphin Ireland had received written confirmation of continued support from a group company, Reliance Holdings Ltd and that it will settle all third party liabilities.

At the end of December, Godolphin Ireland owed €269.7 million to Reliance Holdings Ltd.

]]>Vince Caligiuri<![CDATA[Google to spend $5m to improve forecasting of extreme weather events in Ireland]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/technology/2026/10/13/google-to-spend-5m-to-improve-forecasting-of-extreme-weather-events-in-ireland/https://www.irishtimes.com/technology/2026/10/13/google-to-spend-5m-to-improve-forecasting-of-extreme-weather-events-in-ireland/Tue, 13 Oct 2026 08:29:40 +0000Google’s philanthropic arm will spend up $5 million (€4.46 million) on high-tech weather forecasting and climate research in Ireland, aiming to improve local forecasting of severe storms, flash flooding and other weather events.

The commitment from Google.org includes €2.5 million in funding for the Aimsir Centre and the Climate + Co-Centre – the organisation’s largest funded initiative in Ireland – and will also see the creation of a new schools-based network of weather stations.

The investment will fund a four-year research initiative that combines Google Earth AI, satellite imagery and real-time weather observations from 560 solar-powered weather stations deployed at schools across the State, known as the Climate+ School Weather AI Network (Swan).

Overseen by UCD’s Aimsir Centre in partnership with Met Éireann and the Climate+ Co-Centre, the stations will measure temperature, atmospheric pressure, rainfall, humidity, wind speed and wind direction at one-minute intervals.

The project will combine that data with historical weather patterns to build “nowcasting” models that can detect severe weather events earlier.

“This combination of central research and the distributed gathering of information, working with the network of 560 schools, is not something we’ve done anywhere else in the world,” said Kent Walker, president of global affairs at Google and Alphabet.

“It is a shift in the way the Irish weather forecasting services are doing it. They are used to having a small number of very high end data points. This is a distributed model we have, and lots of very localised data points. In the aggregate, it may lead to better forecasting for the whole country.”

The data will also be freely available online. Teachers will be provided with training and lesson plans to help students get the most out of the data. The initiative is also being supported by the Irish Schools Sustainability Network, the Irish Science Teachers’ Association, and education portal Scoilnet.

The project will roll out a pilot phase to 20 schools initially, to test the equipment’s function and longevity over the winter months. It then plans to install around 200 weather stations a year in secondary schools around the State.

The stations will connect via wifi, meaning they need to be close enough to a building to pick up the connection, but far enough away that they pick up good wind and rain data.

Aimsir’s Prof Andrew Parnell said the programme was prioritising Deis schools. The stations can also be adapted for different school needs, such as adding air quality sensors for schools in urban areas.

Head of Google Ireland, Vanessa Hartley said the initiative showed how AI could be used to address a real-world challenge.

“What makes this initiative particularly impactful is that communities across the country will play an integral role,” she said. “With weather stations located in schools across Ireland, students and teachers will have the opportunity not just to learn about weather and AI, but to contribute directly to a nationwide – and potentially global – scientific initiative.”

The project was welcomed by Taoiseach Micheál Martin.

“Ireland has built a strong international reputation for innovation, research and technology and initiatives such as this demonstrate how those strengths can be applied to challenges facing communities across the country,” he said.

]]>Tom Honan<![CDATA[Mark Zuckerberg says Meta has reached AI ‘frontier’]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/13/mark-zuckerberg-says-meta-has-reached-ai-frontier/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/13/mark-zuckerberg-says-meta-has-reached-ai-frontier/Tue, 13 Oct 2026 13:45:00 +0000Mark Zuckerberg says Meta has caught up with rivals at the “frontier” of artificial intelligence (AI), committing to further vast spending to challenge Anthropic and OpenAI and downplaying warnings about the risks of the technology running out of control.

Speaking as Meta released its Muse Wonder AI model on Monday, the billionaire chief executive claimed the new system was “going to allow much more sophisticated behaviours that are at the frontier of what is being done in the AI field”.

The Silicon Valley group claims Muse Wonder performs better than comparable models released by Anthropic and OpenAI in some tasks, according to technical benchmarks.

The release marks a big milestone for Zuckerberg, who since last year has committed billions of dollars to shake up Meta’s AI leadership, build vast data centres and hire star AI researchers on multimillion-dollar salaries – all in a bid to keep pace with OpenAI, Anthropic and Google.

“Getting to this point both required a large amount of compute and investment, and a lot of very rigorous scientific work by the group working on it over an extended period of time,” said Zuckerberg.

The AI push initially unnerved investors, but the company’s share price has risen almost 10 per cent since early September when Meta launched the Muse personal AI assistant, which uses autonomous bots to carry out everyday tasks such as ordering groceries and booking travel.

The Muse app quickly became – and remains – the most downloaded on both the Apple and Android app stores in the US. The $1.8 trillion (€1.6 trillion) company intends to integrate its new model into Muse. We forget the role of emotions in markets at our peril, because the “mood” plays a huge part in the way people see prices and bargains. Sometimes, my profession, the economists, don’t get this. When economists see a price, we see a number; when ordinary people see a price, they get a feeling. It is this feeling that makes them confident, or anxious, as the case may be. Confidence pushes people to pay the extra bit over the asking price; anxiety has the opposite effect.

We are seeing a sharp reversal of behaviour. For example, in Dublin, according to the latest Daft report (Daft Q3 2026), sale prices fell 5.2 per cent year-on-year, the largest annual fall since 2014, and this fall has accelerated over the summer, with prices dropping 2 per cent in the three months to September. The easing we’re seeing is not driven by new supply. We are still building three-bed semidetached homes in commuter towns, in a country that wants urban apartments, because the size and nature of the Irish household has changed. We are having fewer children, and more people are single and want to live alone or in a couple without necessarily wanting two extra bedrooms.

Let’s look at the first development. Prices are simply too high, and potential buyers have hit the price ceiling. The expression “the cure for high prices is high prices” is one of the oldest in economics. Eventually, very high prices fix themselves by depressing demand, because people run out of money and can’t afford to pay the higher prices. In addition, the high prices usually imply higher profits for builders and the higher prices prompt higher supply, which brings down prices in time. However, in Ireland right now, it is a simple fact that buyers are “maxed out” and can’t afford relentless rises in house prices – so they cannot play the game any longer.

Since Covid, although wages have been more or less rising in line with inflation or a small bit more, house prices across the country are up massively. In Munster, outside the cities, prices are up 72 per cent since the pandemic. If Irish property is overvalued, will house prices fall?

Dublin lags behind, with prices up by 32 per cent in the same period. The current asking price for a three-bed semi is €635,000 in Dublin, €431,000 in Cork city, €424,000 in Galway city; €376,000 in Limerick City and €313,000 in Waterford city.

The font of all borrowing is income, so let’s look at these prices relative to wages and the ability to borrow, and then let’s see where prices should be. At a cost of €502,000 it is about €18,000 over the couple’s maximum threshold, and it would require €66,500 in cash.

The Irish Times view on the ESRI housing report: house prices alarmingly overvalued

Long may this last.

The surprise seemed to be shared by the Taoiseach and Tánaiste, whose intervention reportedly led to an emergency meeting between the Minister and RTÉ’s chair and director general on Thursday.

While all concerned were tight-lipped afterwards, it has been clearly signalled that the Government will stump up the €20 million, subject to RTÉ satisfying the Minister on the progress of its reform and redundancy programme. Given that these were always the terms on which the multiannual payments were based, there is as yet no clear explanation as to why the money was withheld in the first place.

None of this is good for O’Donovan’s political reputation, and there were mutterings from various unnamed Government figures over the weekend that he might not keep his Cabinet seat when the midterm reshuffle takes place at the end of next year.

The Limerick TD seems to have an unfortunate knack for losing friends and alienating people, but last week’s embarrassments and the subsequent clean-up may have forced the question of how RTÉ is funded back on to the agenda, and that would not be a bad thing.

The current arrangement was agreed by the previous government in the summer of 2024. It guaranteed RTÉ €725 million in public money over three years, rising from €225 million in 2025 to €240 million this year and €260 million in 2027. The licence fee was retained, and the Exchequer committed to making up the difference between what it brought in and the agreed total. The lower amount raised from licence revenue, the bigger the cheque from the State.

That difference is growing quickly. Licence sales have fallen every year since the 2023 payments scandal. Figures released by O’Donovan last week show sales down 6 per cent in the first nine months of this year, putting full-year income on course for about €114 million, compared with more than €150 million in 2022.

Less widely understood is how much of the licence fee the State already pays. The Department of Social Protection funds free licences for everyone over 70 and others who qualify for the household benefits package, a bill in excess of €80 million a year. That is more than 500,000 licences, set against roughly 715,000 bought by households this year.

Free licences grow by up to 20,000 a year as the population ages, while paid ones keep falling. Remarkably, if current trends hold, licences paid for by social protection will outnumber those paid for by households as early as 2029. This seems untenable.

Does Patrick O’Donovan’s explanation for €20m RTÉ funding cut add up?

Add the direct top-up and the picture is starker still. In 2025, about 54 per cent of RTÉ’s public funding came from the Exchequer in one form or another. By 2027, that share is likely to be above 60 per cent. The licence fee survives in name, but the money increasingly comes directly from Government.

European law now has something to say about this. The European Media Freedom Act requires member states to fund public broadcasters through transparent procedures based on objective criteria set in advance, and to ensure they have “adequate, sustainable and predictable” resources. The point is to protect editorial independence by making sure money cannot be used as a political lever. The Broadcasting (Amendment) Bill now before the Oireachtas is meant to give effect to those rules here.

Last week’s episode looks much more like political incompetence than a deliberate act of interference. But cutting an agreed sum at a few hours’ notice, without explanation, is clearly not in keeping with the spirit of the EU rules. Whatever its cause, it has shown how easily the money can be turned on and off.

Nor should the role of ill-will be underestimated. Members of the Oireachtas media committee have indicated they intend to question RTÉ director general Kevin Bakhurst about a newspaper column by radio presenter Oliver Callan, which questioned Simon Harris’s credentials as Minister for Finance. One source described Callan’s piece as “antigovernment”. Whether a presenter’s newspaper column should be a matter for a committee examining RTÉ’s finances is debatable. That the two are being raised alongside each other is telling.

The new legislation will strengthen the role of Coimisiún na Meán, which will assess RTÉ’s needs and recommend a level of funding for each three-year period. But the regulator’s role will be advisory. There will be no legal obligation on the minister of the day to follow its recommendations, nor, as far as can be seen, any requirement to explain a decision not to. The final call will remain where it was last week, with a politician putting together a budget.

The licence fee has many faults, including the fact that it is now collapsing before our eyes. But it was based on a sound principle. Money paid directly by citizens to a public service broadcaster, at arm’s length from the government of the day, gave that broadcaster a degree of independence that an annual grant cannot.

If public service broadcasting is to retain public trust and integrity, it must be insulated from political pressure, whether born of malice or just haplessness. If nothing else, we can thank O’Donovan for reminding us of that.

The net cost to you is determined by two things: fee per band and the personal subsidy to which each child is entitled, depending on your income.

Under the budget measures, the fee for Band F will fall from €336 a week to €300. And, for those on the universal subsidy (anyone with family income of more than €73,000), the subsidy for children up to senior infants will rise to €2.50 from €2.15 per hour up to a maximum of 45 hours.

]]>AP<![CDATA[Ireland’s new personal investment accounts: Here’s how the scheme will work]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/06/consumers-can-save-up-to-50000-tax-free-in-new-personal-investment-accounts/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/06/consumers-can-save-up-to-50000-tax-free-in-new-personal-investment-accounts/Tue, 06 Oct 2026 15:44:46 +0000People will be able to put €12,000 a year tax-free into the Government new personal investment accounts, Minister for Finance Simon Harris announced in his Budget 2027 speech.

The accounts will feature a low tax rate of just 1 per cent. However, this tax will be levied on any amount in the account over a tax-free threshold of €50,000, not just the profit the account made over that year.

This holds out the prospect of people paying tax on their savings in years when they lost money simply because the balance of their account was above the €50,000 tax-free threshold.

Harris said the new accounts will be available from July 1st next year. About €170 billion is currently on deposit in Irish bank accounts, with the Minister having previously described that money as “sitting idle”.

Alongside the new accounts, the Minister announced a financial literacy campaign. The Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (CCPC) has set up a webpage that will allow people to read up about issues around investing, and the choices available.

It also offers a quick multiple choice self-assessment quiz that allows consumers to assess their investment readiness.

Irish households hold just 2.3 per cent of their financial assets in direct investments such as listed shares and debt securities, compared with an EU average of approximately 7.5 per cent.

Budget Q&A: Submit your questions to our expert panel on budget day

The new scheme has been designed to encourage people to move their savings into market investments.

“The long-mooted investment account is an important step towards making long-term investment more accessible,” said Cróna Clohisey, director of members and advocacy at Chartered Accountants Ireland. “Now that the broad design has been announced, Government should move quickly to finalise the legislation, systems and guidance so that financial service providers can establish these accounts and people can begin using them.

“It is critical that there is no delay to the introduction timeline of mid-2027,” she said.

Michael Healy, chief executive of IG Consumer, said the Government had missed the chance to get Irish people investing.

“While the decision to set the tax-free threshold at €50,000 is better than we expected, it is a small victory within a fundamentally flawed model. The €12,000 annual contribution limit is far too low if the ambition is to get people investing seriously and building meaningful long-term wealth.

“But the bigger problem is the proposed 1 per cent annual tax on investments above the threshold,” said Healy. “Taxing the value of an investment rather than the return it generates means someone could face a tax bill even when their investments have fallen in value – effectively paying tax on losses. That is the wrong principle for an account designed to encourage people to invest.”

Budget Calculator 2027: Here’s how this year’s budget will affect your income

Robert Dever, head of tax at Eversheds Sutherland, agreed. The Government he said had adopted a cautious approach to the new scheme. “For a lot of taxpayers, in the long term, it will probably be more tax efficient to maximise tax relief arising on pension contributions before contributing to an investment account.”

However, Rory O’Brien, head of wealth management, Dublin, at Baker Tilly Ireland Wealth was more upbeat.

“On the whole, the new Irish Investment Account looks like a fantastic opportunity for those looking for better returns from the investment markets over the medium to long term to do so without being harshly punished when their investments do well. The opportunity for younger investors to start small and build up to the 50k without CGT is very positive and l would expect those looking to build deposits, to consider this as a viable option.”

The Government also announced a lowering of the rate of tax under the “deemed disposal” or exit tax regime that applies to investors in products currently available in the market.

Budget 2027 main points: Minimum wage to rise 79 cent; €12,000 per year limit for investment scheme

Last year, as part of Budget 2026, the deemed disposal tax rate was reduced from 41 per cent to 38 per cent. In 2024, a report by the Department of Finance into the funds sector advised the deemed disposal rule should be ended for exchange-traded funds (ETFs) and investment funds.

Exit tax is levied on profits when an investment is cashed in. Deemed disposal sees that tax levied every eight years after an investment is taken out, even if the investment is not cashed in.

Chartered Accountants Ireland’s Cróna Clohisey said it was “extremely disheartening that the eight-year deemed disposal rule remains. It has no place in a modern Irish investment landscape.

Irish Funds chairwoman, Andrea Kelly welcome dthe three point cut in the rate of tax but said the lack of any clear path to phasing out deemed disposal was “deeply disappointing”.

“The Government should now use the Finance Bill to provide the certainty that was missing from the Budget,” she said.

New accounts

Anyone over the age of 18 who is resident in the State and holds a PPS number can invest in the new personal investment scheme, but they can only have one account.

Eligible investments will include listed shares, listed bonds, financial instruments traded on a regulated market and a range of investment funds suitable for retail investors, including ETFs.

Investors will not be permitted to invest in what are deemed highly complex and risky products, including derivatives and crypto assets.

There will be no minimum holding or lock-in period, and moving investment accounts between providers will be allowed, where possible, on a tax-neutral basis.

Any tax due will be calculated and paid at source by the companies providing the investment funds available under the scheme.

This sends all the wrong signals, and it also means there will be significantly fewer resources to protect those who are energy poor and to fund important climate investment, including flood protection.

The number of children in poverty is increasing, despite our run of economic success. Research by the ESRI has shown that the best way to tackle this problem would be to introduce targeted income supports for children living in low-income families. An opportunity to do this was missed last week.

Dealing with the effects of higher inflation on living standards is best done in a number of ways. The income tax system should be indexed so that the tax take does not increase by stealth. In contrast to last year, this budget does this.

The exceptionally high energy prices pose particular problems for those on low incomes, with higher expenditure on heating. This clearly needed to be addressed, and the best way of doing it would have been to increase welfare payments and introduce targeted support for the energy needs of the most vulnerable.

The Government won’t raise carbon tax again but promises to decarbonise the economy – how?

Instead, Government expenditure on social payments will rise by only 2.7 per cent next year, less than inflation, and there is no significant targeted support for those who need it most.

More of the reduction in excise tax on fuel goes to those on high incomes, reducing the incentive to cut our emissions of greenhouse gases. None of it goes to those who cannot afford a car. An unsatisfactory outcome for the climate, and for those on low incomes who will suffer from the cold this winter.

If the Government sticks to the numbers in the budget it looks likely that it will be neutral, neither stimulating nor deflating the economy. While some tightening would have been better, the stimulus largely arises from the very desirable increase in public investment.

The budgetary numbers published last week also show the share of public expenditure in national income next year will remain roughly unchanged compared to this year. If this proves to be the outcome, it would be satisfactory. However, as with recent budgets, this one carries the seeds of another overrun.

It is no surprise that Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers did not put a precise number on the provision for public service pay next year. He is beginning a negotiating process, and anything he provided would be taken just as the starting point by trade unions. Thus, there is likely to be some overrun to provide for the final outturn of the pay talks.

The provision for social payments looks like an underestimate of what will be spent. Also, once again in some departmental budgets, it looks as if the estimates do not provide for expenditure that will prove unavoidable, for example in health.

While on paper the budget numbers look moderately prudent, as in previous years, they may prove a poor guide to the eventual outturn.

]]>Paul Faith<![CDATA[More needs to be done to help home-grown companies scale and offset reliance on FDI]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/12/more-needs-to-be-done-to-help-home-grown-companies-scale-and-offset-reliance-on-fdi/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/12/more-needs-to-be-done-to-help-home-grown-companies-scale-and-offset-reliance-on-fdi/Mon, 12 Oct 2026 04:31:00 +0000Ireland’s economic model has been one of the great success stories of modern Europe. Our multinational sector has transformed employment and public finances. But we have come to a point now when what made us stand apart feels a little less different and we need to look at future-proofing our economy.

At the same time, Ireland’s private sector continues to underperform when it comes to scaling indigenous companies into globally competitive multinationals. Ireland needs to enhance its offering to FDI as well as putting measures in place to help its home-grown businesses scale into global companies.

Ireland’s corporation tax receipts rose from €4.7 billion in 2014 to €32.9 billion in 2025, now accounting for about 31 per cent of total exchequer tax revenue, compared with just 8.3 per cent in 2014.

This concentration is more than 2.5 times the OECD average (12 per cent). Revenue analysis shows that foreign-owned multinationals generate almost 90 per cent of these receipts, while the three largest companies accounted for 46 per cent of all corporation tax paid in 2024.

While it is unlikely that there will be a significant reduction in corporation tax receipts over the next few years, the picture is far less certain over a 10- to 15-year horizon. The challenge for policymakers is that decisions about future investment are being made today. If Ireland waits until corporation tax receipts begin to decline before responding, it may be too late to attract the next wave of investment required to sustain our spending commitments and economic success. The Government needs to act now.

There are several ways Ireland can enhance its offering to international companies as well as doing more for home-grown private businesses.

Firstly, Ireland needs to invest now for the future. This is not simply about protecting existing industries; it is about identifying the sectors that will drive economic growth in the decades ahead and putting the policies, infrastructure and incentives in place now to attract them.

Ireland should be reinvesting part of today’s corporation tax revenues to develop domestic businesses, support innovation and secure the next generation of FDI. The objective should be clear: act while the tide is still coming in, not after it has turned.

Secondly, Ireland needs to become a more compelling location for high-value research, development and innovation activities. The current R&D tax credit, despite small enhancements in Budget 2027, would benefit from expanding the range of activities covered.

State’s tax take boosted by €3bn as multinationals ‘front-load’ payments

The relief should be expanded to increase the benefit for advanced manufacturing investment opportunities. Budget 2027 missed an opportunity to introduce a separate innovation incentive for broader innovation activities, supporting investment in areas such as digitalisation and decarbonisation. These reforms would strengthen Ireland’s attractiveness as a global innovation hub while further supporting private companies.

Thirdly, too many promising private businesses are acquired before they reach scale. Irish firms face systemic barriers that limit their ability to grow and scale. Three things are needed to help – capital, capabilities and culture.

The Government has begun to recognise the capital challenge through its proposed €1 billion Scaling Fund announced in Budget 2027. This is a welcome start, but much will depend on the accessibility of funds. Scaling an Irish business towards a public listing should be more attractive and achievable – Euronext Dublin has only about two dozen actively traded equities, compared with nearly 2,000 listed companies across European markets.

The introduction of the State investment account is also a welcome step towards mobilising pools of capital in Ireland, with the potential to channel significant household savings towards active investment and broaden participation in capital markets. The next challenge is ensuring that a meaningful proportion of those funds is channelled into promising Irish companies, helping to create the next generation of indigenous businesses.

While the budget announcement to reduce Capital Gains Tax to 31 per cent is positive, a larger reduction to 20 per cent would have gone a lot further towards encouraging further investment. Furthermore, revised entrepreneur relief should be enhanced and retirement relief expanded.

Irish businesses need the talent, leadership and expertise to help them scale from successful start-ups into global enterprises. The announcement of funding to the National Training Fund to build skills and resilience fit for an AI-enabled workforce was a practical step and a sign that the State can provide supports to nurture these capabilities. But more of this is needed. Finally, Ireland must create a culture that rewards ambition, celebrates success and makes scaling indigenous businesses a national priority.

Budget 2027: Measures put public finances on worse trajectory, State watchdog warns

Not every competitiveness issue requires money. Often, smaller businesses face administration burdens that consume valuable time and resources without delivering meaningful economic benefits. Simplification has minimal cost to the exchequer but can have a significant impact.

For example, in our pre-budget submission, we suggested pre-populated simplified tax returns for small businesses. The budget move to allow enhanced reporting requirements to be submitted monthly rather than on a real-time basis is a welcome step. However, there remains a strong case for moving to an annual reporting requirement.

The announcement of a holistic assessment of the various grant schemes, enterprise tax incentives and business development programmes now on offer will hopefully lead to meaningful simplification. However, this will only truly deliver impact if a cross-departmental approach is taken, as success is measured by a reduction in form-filling and hours saved processing applications.

Ireland does not need a completely new economic model. The foundations of our success remain strong. However, maintaining success in a changing world requires enhancing our offering to FDI and the private sector – reinvesting for competitiveness. The real question is whether we are prepared to invest today in what will make us attractive tomorrow.

Paraic Burke is head of tax at PwC Ireland

]]><![CDATA[‘Politeness premium’ costing Irish consumers €600m each year, research suggests]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/12/politeness-premium-costing-irish-consumers-600m-each-year-research-suggests/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/12/politeness-premium-costing-irish-consumers-600m-each-year-research-suggests/Mon, 12 Oct 2026 04:00:00 +0000Irish consumers lose an average of €150 each year as a result of a “politeness premium” which sees them overpay on shared bills and fail to collect personal debts, according to research published by AIB on Monday morning.

The study suggests that fewer than one in 20 Irish adults will always ask for money they are owed back, with as many as 90 per cent saying they would let as much as €50 slide rather than have a conversation they consider difficult.

All told, about €600 million gets lost to social awkwardness every year, AIB said.

And as if to prove the Shakespearean wisdom about never being either a borrower or a lender, the unspoken debt has “soured a relationship” among almost 50 per cent of those surveyed.

The research also highlights how consumers handle peer-to-peer debts varies dramatically depending on county, age and gender.

The geographical divide in financial assertiveness indicates that people from Galway have Ireland’s highest ‘threshold of asking’ and willingly absorb up to €32.50 in unpaid amounts before speaking up.

By contrast, people living in Wexford draw the line much earlier by refusing to let more than €12.50 slide.

Adults from Limerick are the most likely to insist on itemising group bills line by line, while those living in Dublin prefer splitting bills evenly among the group.

When asked why they hesitate to chase small debts, Irish adults often frame their silence as kindness and say things such as “they’d do the same for me”, “it evens out over time”, or “I’d rather be generous than keep score”.

Ireland’s new personal investment accounts: How does it work if I have €1 or €12,000 to put in?

However, behavioural data reveals the underlying tension when payments arise, with 40 per cent saying owed money left unspoken has soured how they feel about a relationship and two thirds admitting to a level of discomfort when someone suggests itemising a group bill.

Nearly half said they regularly overpay on shared bills or rounds to keep the peace, with 25- to 34-year-olds feeling the greatest pressure and 74 per cent overpaying regularly, according to the survey of 1,009 adults conducted by Bounce Insights on behalf of AIB and Ogilvy.

Close friends and colleagues were deemed to be the hardest groups to ask for money back from, with women saying they found it particularly difficult to reclaim money from close friends.

“People rarely describe their silence around money as awkwardness,” said Dan Bennett, global head of behavioural science with Ogilvy Consulting. “They describe it as generosity. But the cost of that politeness is real, showing up both in people’s bank accounts and in their relationships. In Ireland, the fear of appearing impolite leads many of us to pay a ‘politeness premium’.”

“The behavioural science research that AIB’s new Everyday Banking campaign is rooted in highlights how social dynamics impact our daily finances, create social friction and can even cost people money,” said the bank’s chief customer officer Orlaith Ryan.

]]>MilosStankovic<![CDATA[Ireland goes Swedish on investment, but deemed disposal remains a problem]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/12/ireland-goes-swedish-on-investment-but-deemed-disposal-remains-a-problem/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/12/ireland-goes-swedish-on-investment-but-deemed-disposal-remains-a-problem/Mon, 12 Oct 2026 03:01:00 +0000Earlier this year, Stocktake suggested Minister for Finance Simon Harris might be tempted to borrow Sweden’s model for encouraging people to invest.

It turns out he was. The Savings and Investment Account (SIA) announced in Budget 2027 is not a carbon copy of Sweden’s ISK, but the resemblance is clear.

Investors can put up to €12,000 a year into the account, with the first €50,000 of investments exempt from tax, while amounts above that will face an annual 1 per cent charge.

Some will be irked by that charge, especially in years where stock markets have fallen. However, a UK-style tax-free wrapper, allowing savers to invest up to £20,000 a year completely free of tax, always appeared excessively generous and politically indefensible.

For the Government, a Swedish-type approach offers a predictable tax stream while encouraging people to put their savings into shares and funds (and a €50,000 tax-free limit is more generous than many expected) rather than leaving them in cash.

However, the new account also highlights the problem with the system outside it. Investments held in the SIA will escape deemed disposal, while investors buying ordinary ETFs will continue to face an eight-year tax charge on unrealised gains, albeit at the reduced rate of 35 per cent.

The Government says it intends to move beyond deemed disposal during the lifetime of this administration, but substantive reform has again been deferred.

And there is a second, less discussed problem. The Funds Sector 2030 review recommended limited loss relief, but the Government’s roadmap says it will not be introduced. As Stocktake previously noted, an investor who makes €5,000 on one ETF and loses €5,000 on another can therefore have no overall gain but still face tax on the €5,000 profit.

Is the State’s new investment account going to be a good deal?

That is less of an issue for someone holding one broad global ETF, but it matters for a portfolio of separate funds.

Some will have issues with the SIA, but it’s arguably a welcome attempt to make investing simpler. The harder task is making the wider investing tax system equally sensible.

]]>Nick Bradshaw / The Irish Times

   <description>Papst Leo XIV. ist nach Angaben seiner behandelnden Ärzte an Lungenkrebs erkrankt. Das teilte das Ärzteteam der Gemelli-Klinik in Rom nach einer Operation des 71-Jährigen mit. <item rdf:about="https://orf.at/stories/3444929/">
   <title>Unis und ÖH warnen vor Kürzungen</title>
   <description>Bis Ende Oktober muss laut Gesetz feststehen, wie viel Geld die öffentlichen Unis für ihr nächstes Dreijahresbudget ab 2028 erhalten. Am Wochenende will die Regierung die Summe fixieren. Die Universitätenkonferenz (uniko) befürchtet wegen der Einsparungen im aktuellen Doppelbudget Einschnitte von rund einer Mrd. Euro bis 2030 und warnt vor einem großen Stellenabbau. Die Österreichische Hochschülerinnen- und Hochschülerschaft (ÖH) rief erneut zum Protest auf, die Unis unterstützten die Aktion.</description>

A 66-year-old Polish man has been charged with planning an attack on Prime Minister Donald Tusk as part of an attempt to overthrow the government. A search of his home revealed improvised explosive devices that he allegedly planned to use in the plot.

The suspect, who can be named only as Krzysztof N. under Polish privacy law, has also been charged with a number of other offences, including promoting a war of aggression in Ukraine and inciting hate crimes. Media reports have identified the man as a radical-right extremist.

Do Prokuratury Okręgowej w Warszawie został doprowadzony 66-letni Krzysztof N., zatrzymany w związku z planowaniem zamachu na @donaldtusk i @KosiniakKamysz ⤵️ pic.twitter.com/rjcR3rNvyW

— tvp.info 🇵🇱 (@tvp_info) October 13, 2026

On Sunday, Poland’s security services announced that they had received what they described as “credible” information indicating a “high probability” of an assassination attempt against Tusk and his defence minister, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz.

Later that day, a 66-year-old suspect was detained in the city of Wrocław, southwest Poland, and his property was searched. Interior minister Marcin Kierwiński told broadcaster TVP that the man was “very active in groups promoting extreme views”.

On Tuesday, the district prosecutor’s office in Warsaw, where Krzysztof N. has been transported, announced that he had been charged with nine offences.

“The most serious charge is for planning to forcibly overthrow state authorities, including the prime minister and cabinet, using explosives,” said spokesman Piotr Antoni Skiba. That crime carries a potential prison sentence of up to 15 years.

 

Skiba revealed that “a dozen or so” improvised explosive devices, which appeared to be similar to fragmentation grenades, had been found in the man’s home. There was also a crossbow, sharp-tipped metal bolts, and what are believed to be blank-firing or pneumatic guns.

Skiba said that Krzysztof N.’s plans had been discovered after an anonymous person sent a message to the State Protection Service (SOP), which is responsible for the security of high-ranking officials, that included a recording of a conversation purportedly with the suspect.

Krzysztof N. could be heard claiming that he had gathered “sevel hundred people” who shared his ideological beliefs and would help him overthrown the Polish government by force.

At the moment, there is no indication that Krzysztof N. or the group around him were inspired in any way by foreign intelligence agencies, but the issue is still being investigated, added Skiba, quoted by the Polish Press Agency (PAP).

Poland’s security services say they have received “credible” information indicating a “high probability” of an assassination attempt against Prime Minister Donald Tusk and defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz https://t.co/zl3vt6mah3

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 11, 2026

Among the other charges Krzysztof N. has heard are “promoting a war of aggression, including in Ukraine, as well as incitement to commit crimes based on nationality, ethnicity, race and political views”, added Skiba. The suspect has so far pleaded not guilty on all counts.

On Monday, Gazeta Wyborcza, a leading daily, reported that Krzysztof N. had for months been posting videos online calling on fellow right-wing extremists to fight against the authorities. He also expressed antisemitic and anti-Ukrainian sentiment.

Another newspaper, Rzeczpospolita, found that he runs a Facebook page called Radical Polish Resistance Movement that has almost 8,000 followers and claims Poland’s two main political parties – Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) and the national-conservative opposition Law and Justice (PiS) – are “in the hands of globalists and Judeo-communists”.

"Patriota do przesady". Kim jest Krzysztof N., Wrocławianin podejrzewany przez służby o planowanie zamachu na premiera Tuska

Mężczyzna, który miał planować zamach na premiera Donalda Tuska Od kilku miesięcy nagrywał w mediach społecznościowych filmiki i skrzykiwał prawicowych…

— Bartosz T. Wieliński 🇵🇱🇪🇺🇺🇦🇬🇱 (@Bart_Wielinski) October 12, 2026

In a separate case, government spokesman Adam Szłapka announced on Tuesday that a 46-year-old man in the town of Oborniki in western Poland had been detained on suspicion of publicly calling for the murder of Tusk and the speaker of parliament, Włodzimierz Czarzasty.

A spokeswoman for the district prosecutor’s office in Oborniki told PAP that the man had been charged with inciting murder, for which he could face up to three years in prison.

“He admitted to publishing content insulting various government officials, but denied the charge of inciting their murder,” she revealed. “He expressed regret and remorse.”

Poland and Norway have signed a declaration on deepening security cooperation, including joint defence production, strengthening NATO’s northern and eastern flanks, and continuing to support Ukraine.

Data harvested from mobile phones by the Polish authorities using Pegasus spyware were transmitted outside Poland and were accessible to the tool’s Israeli producer, Polish prosecutors have revealed as part of an investigation into the use of Pegasus under the former government.

Prime Minister Donald Tusk says that the case is “one of the biggest scandals in Polish history since the fall of communism”, and that it is “beyond any doubt” that the Israeli firm behind Pegasus, NSO Group, cooperates with Israeli intelligence.

Pegasus is a powerful and controversial tool that allows the extraction of large amounts of data from mobile phones without users’ knowledge. A number of countries have been found to have used it to spy on opposition figures.

In 2017, Poland, under the government of the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party, purchased Pegasus from NSO. The spyware was subsequently used against hundreds of targets, including a number of PiS’s political opponents.

Among them was the head of the 2019 election campaign of Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party (which was then known as Civic Platform, PO). Last year, Tusk revealed that his own wife and daughter had been among those caught up in the surveillance.

PiS, however, has insisted that Pegasus was a necessary tool to fight crime and ensure national security. It says the spyware was only used with court approval against targets legitimately suspected of wrongdoing.

 

After a coalition led by Tusk took power from PiS in December 2023, it launched investigations into the use of Pegasus under the former government.

Today, the National Prosecutor’s Office released its latest findings, based on analysis by experts at the forensic research office of Poland’s Internal Security Agency (ABW).

The experts confirmed that Pegasus allowed the harvesting of emails, instant messaging and text messages; the content of telephone conversations, both via mobile networks and internet calls; browsing histories, calendars and contact lists; photos, videos and other files; and location data.

“Additionally, Pegasus allowed the use of the device’s built-in microphone and cameras to record audio and video in real time and take screenshots,” reports the National Prosecutor’s Office.

The ABW experts also highlighted serious concerns over management and security of the harvested data, noting that Poland’s Central Anti-Corruption Bureau (CBA), which was responsible for using the spyware, “did not have full control over the Pegasus system”.

“The CBA did not have passwords to access some accounts with administrative privileges and some system components remained under the control of the manufacturer [NSO],” wrote the prosecutor’s office. “The server module responsible for infecting mobile devices remained under the manufacturer’s exclusive control.”

Data transmitted through the Pegasus system travelled outside Polish territory, through “servers located in various parts of the world”, in a network managed by NSO and “beyond the CBA’s control”, found the experts.

Meanwhile, NSO “had technical access to materials from operational surveillance”, although prosecutors say that the experts “did not determine whether the manufacturer actually obtained access to materials from specific operations”.

Before today’s election, both Miszalski and Majchowski had called on Cracovians to vote for Piątkowska. After his victory had become clear, Gibała declared that “11 October 2026 will be remembered as the day when, after 24 years, the inhabitants of Krakow regained their city”.

The vote had been particularly closely watched as it came just a year before the parliamentary elections. Gibała’s victory has been celebrated by figures from the right-wing opposition, though the new mayor is not politically aligned with them (and indeed previously served as an MP in Tusk’s party).

Polish prosecutors have asked a court to discontinue a case against three South Asian men who were caught illegally slaughtering a goat at the back of a kebab bar.

They say that the men did not realise they were breaking the law, that such practices are normal in their home countries, and that that the meat was for their own consumption. Prosecutors therefore believe the crime was of low social harm and not worth the court’s time.

🔴Ubili kozę na zapleczu. Wkrótce decyzja sądu, zastanawia ruch prokuratury

Sąd Rejonowy w Wałbrzychu w najbliższym czasie zdecyduje o losie trójki obcokrajowców, którzy pod koniec zeszłego roku niezgodnie z polskim prawem ubili kozę. Oskarżająca Hindusa i dwójkę Bengalczyków…

— Wirtualna Polska (@wirtualnapolska) October 7, 2026

The case involves two Bangladeshi nationals and one Indian, all legal residents in Poland. The incident came to light in December 2025, after witnesses reported seeing the trio leading a goat through the centre of the city of Wałbrzych, before taking it to the back of a kebab bar.

After killing the animal, the men began butchering it for meat, which they were still portioning out when the police arrived. They told officers that the meat was intended for their own consumption. The kebab bar was closed for renovations at the time.

The men also said that such slaughter was customary in their home countries and they were unaware that, with limited exceptions, animals in Poland may generally be slaughtered only at authorised slaughterhouses, reports broadcaster RMF

 

A spokesman for prosecutors, Mariusz Pindera, told the Wirtualna Polska news website that the men’s unfamiliarity with Polish law did not “absolve them of the obligation to comply with the regulations”.

However, “the harmfulness of the act is relatively low, although I know that what these people did shocks many people”, he continued. “We must be realistic about the fact that the court proceedings will take some time, thus blocking the docket for other cases. A trial also entails costs for the state.”

Prosecutors have therefore asked the court for a so-called conditional discontinuation of the case, a very common procedure under Polish law. Almost 25,000 such motions were submitted last year by prosecutors, citing the low social harm of the offences involved, reports Wirtualna Polska.

The court must now decide whether to accept or reject the prosecution’s motion. In the latter case, prosecutors would be required to proceed with an indictment against the suspects and seek a conviction. No hearing date on the motion has yet been set.

An overwhelming majority of MPs in the Sejm, the lower house of Poland’s parliament, have voted in favour of a bill that would introduce tough new anti-alcohol measures, including a ban on all forms of advertising and on sales in shops during nighttime hours.

The legislation must still pass through the upper-house Senate and will then require the signature of President Karol Nawrocki. However, given the level of support – with only two small far-right groups voting against the bill – it appears likely the measures will be approved.

#PILNE | Sejm uchwalił ustawę wprowadzającą na terenie całego kraju nocną prohibicję, zakazującą reklamy alkoholu i podnoszącą opłatę za sprzedaż alkoholu. https://t.co/OawNUdtqM6

— tvn24 (@tvn24) October 8, 2026

The new restrictions were initially proposed in separate bills submitted by two junior members of Poland’s ruling coalition, The Left (Lewica) and the centrist Poland 2050 (Polska 2050), which were combined into a single package.

The measures include a ban on the sale of alcohol for off-premises consumption between 10 p.m. and 6 a.m., with local authorities able to extend those hours up to 9 p.m. to 9 a.m. if they wish. Bars, clubs and restaurants would still be allowed to sell alcohol for on-premises consumption as presently.

Almost 200 Polish municipalities, including large cities such as Warsaw and Kraków, have already introduced their own local bans on nighttime alcohol sales.

In the first six months following the implementation of its restrictions in 2023, Kraków saw a nearly 50% decrease in nighttime police interventions, with other cities reporting similar improvements.

 

The newly approved bill also includes a complete ban on advertising and promoting alcoholic drinks. Those who violate the prohibition can be fined up to 1 million zloty (€228,400).

Packaging for alcoholic drinks will be required to include warnings about their harmful effect on pregnant women and minors. The legislation also toughens requirements for shop staff to check the age of buyers if they suspect they may be underage.

The cost of licences to sell alcohol will be increased from 525 to 1,050 zloty for drinks with up to 18% alcohol content and from 2,100 to 4,200 zloty for stronger drinks.

Warsaw has announced a ban on nighttime sales of alcohol in shops.

In a vote on Thursday night, the bill won support from 400 of the 433 MPs present in the Sejm, the more powerful lower house of parliament. The only groups that did not vote in favour were the far-right Confederation (Konfederacja) and Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP).

The legislation now passes to the upper-house Senate, which can suggest amendments but only delay, not block, a bill’s passage. Once finally approved by parliament, it will reach the desk of President Karol Nawrocki, who can sign the bill, veto it, or send it to the constitutional court for assessment.

Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition, has vetoed a record number of bills. However, given the level of support for the alcohol bill in the Sejm, including from the largest opposition groups, Law and Justice (PiS) and Development Plus (Rozwój Plus), it appears likely he will sign it.

Recent data released by Statistics Poland (GUS), a state agency, showed that alcohol consumption among Poles is continuing its recent decline.

City AM https://www.cityam.com/ London's Business Newspaper Tue, 13 Oct 2026 16:51:43 +0000 en-GB hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.0.7 https://www.cityam.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/app_launcher_icon_final_rounded.png?w=32 City AM https://www.cityam.com/ 32 32 213406410 ‘Expect to be spied on’: MI5 chief warns UK tech startups over foreign threats https://www.cityam.com/expect-to-be-spied-on-mi5-chief-warns-uk-tech-startups-over-foreign-threats/ Tue, 13 Oct 2026 16:06:36 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2465467

British tech startups should expect to be targeted by foreign spies, the head of MI5 has warned, as the security service ramps up efforts to tackle cyberattacks and the growing national security risks posed by AI. Sir Ken McCallum, director general of MI5, has urged British businesses to strengthen their cyber defences, warning that hostile [...]]]>

British tech startups should expect to be targeted by foreign spies, the head of MI5 has warned, as the security service ramps up efforts to tackle cyberattacks and the growing national security risks posed by AI.

Sir Ken McCallum, director general of MI5, has urged British businesses to strengthen their cyber defences, warning that hostile states were increasingly targeting the UK’s tech sector and critical infrastructure.

“If you’re a tech start up, expect to be spied on by foreign actors and sort your cybersecurity”, he said in his annual threat update at Thames House.

McCallum warned that Britain’s financial systems and supply chains were increasingly vulnerable to attacks designed to cause maximum disruption.

“Our interconnected financial systems, energy grids, supply chains and manufacturing bases, designed during simpler times for maximum efficiency, are vulnerable to malicious disruption and coercion”, he said.

He pointed to a destructive cyberattack on a UK energy generator, warning that the consequences of such incidents could extend directly to consumers.

“A hack of your banking app could lock you out of your accounts”, he said. “A cyber attack on your local hospital could delay your treatment”.

MI5 launches new AI threat unit

The MI5 chief also revealed that the agency had launched a new AI Threat Assessment Centre (AITAC), bringing together expertise from the AI Security Institute, National Crime Agency and National Cyber Security Centre.

The unit, housed within MI5, will assess emerging threats from AI as intelligence agencies race to keep pace with increasingly sophisticated technology.

“Today AI is already supercharging the cybersecurity contast between attackers and defenders”, McCallum said.

He warned that terrorists were already attempting to exploit AI to improve their reconnaissance and attack methods, while the technology could also generate personalised propaganda and radicalising material.

“We’ve caught terrorists seeking to exploit AI to improve their reconnaissance and attack methodologies, with AI-enabled drones adding a new twist”, he said.

McCallum identified the potential development of biological weapons ass one of his greatest concerns, although he stressed that the threat had not yet materialised”.

“Not yet realised – but the misuse case to which I’d attached greatest weight – is AI’s potential to change the stakes on existing or even new bioweapons”, he said.

His intervention comes amid mounting concerns over foreign attempts to obtain sensitive British tech and research.

Last month, MI5 warned that over 100 UK-linked academics had contributed to projects funded by a Chinese institute allegedly connected to Beijing’s intelligence services.

The agency said the China General Technology Research Institute had funded research into AI and cybersecurity designed to strengthen China’s espionage capabilities.

McCallum referenced the warning on Tuesday, saying Chinese intelligence had been using research partnerships to target British expertise.

The MI5 chief also revealed that the agency’s state-threat caseload had quadrupled over the past decade, with more resources now devoted to countering hostile states than during the Cold War.

He warned that Britain had entered a new era of national security in which businesses and individuals could no longer assume they were insulated from geopolitical threats.

“In this new world, we should expect to be tested”, he said.

ASCOT’s British Champions Day this Saturday provides a final chance for some of the stars of the Flat season to strut their stuff before the campaign winds down.

On a star-studded card, the aim is to hunt out a bit of ante-post value and take on the many short-priced favourites set to line up.

There are races where you can’t follow that policy, however, and I do think CALANDAGAN can win the Group One Champion Stakes (4.00pm) for a second year running.

Francis Henri-Graffard’s five-year-old was so impressive in this contest 12 months ago, when he powered clear of Ombudsman to win by over two lengths.

Arriving here fresh last year saw him produce one of his best performances and, given a similar preparation this time, I can see this French raider repeating the feat.

The ground at Ascot might not be as soft as it can be at this time of year, but I expect it to be on the slow side of good come Saturday.

Autumnal good ground can still be hard work, but Calandagan proved he can get through it last year, and I’m not so sure it suits his main market rival Ombudsman as much.

Hotazhell and Almaqam make some each-way appeal, but I expect Calandagan to once again stamp his class on this contest and the 5/2 around is fair.

William Haggas’ Almeraq will be a banker for many in the Group One British Champions Sprint Stakes (2.05pm), and that would be especially true if more rain arrives.

This is a race that can produce a shock, as was the case 12 months ago when Powerful Glory returned a 200/1 winner, and there have also been winners at 40/1, 33/1 and 28/1 in the last 10 years.

With that in mind, I’m happy to take a chance on two at each-way prices.

The first is another Haggas horse in DIVISION, who is probably a bigger price at 10/1 than he would be if his trainer didn’t also saddle the market leader.

This horse has some excellent form to his name, including when beaten less than a length into third in the Commonwealth Cup over this course and distance.

It didn’t look as though he was ready for his most recent run at Ascot earlier this month, having been given a break since August.

He still finished his race off well to be fourth though, and, with that run behind him, he should do better on Saturday.

Given the form he has shown, GREAT WISH looks a big price at 14/1.

This son of Night Of Thunder has won his last two races, including when destroying his rivals by over four lengths in a French Group Three last time.

It’s also worth remembering he was only just over two lengths behind Almeraq when they met at Royal Ascot this summer.

He’s likely such a big price as he’s trained by Danish handler Bent Olsen, and I’m happy to take the inflated odds.

Kalpana looks likely to cap a brilliant season for trainer Andrew Balding as she bids to defend her Group One British Champions Fillies & Mares Stakes (2.40pm) crown.

While it takes a bit of imagination to see past her, I do think Johnny Murtagh’s BELIEVED is interesting at 20/1.

She ran a fine race to be a close third behind Enceladus in the King George V Stakes at Royal Ascot, and last time out won a Group Three at Cork.

She’s clearly improving and, being owned by the day’s sponsors Qatar Racing, she should be primed to go well.

THERE looks to be ante-post value to be had in two other British Champions Day contests, the QEII and the Balmoral Handicap.

Starting with the competitive Group One mile contest (3.20pm), current favourite TALK OF NEW YORK looks the bet at this stage.

As is often the case at this point in the season, some runners may be feeling the effects of a long campaign.

Charlie Appleby’s colt has enjoyed a quieter season, progressing through the grades, and he now looks every inch a Group One miler.

He’s clearly talented and, while he can be keen, a strong pace looks guaranteed from the Coolmore contingent as they look to make it a test for Constitution River, who drops back to a mile.

That should bring out the best in Talk Of New York and, if he reproduces the late acceleration shown in his recent Newmarket performance, he’ll be hard to beat.

The ever-reliable EBT’S GUARD must be considered at 16/1.

He may lack the attractive profile of others, but he’s consistent in these races and returns on the same mark as when finishing second in this contest last year.

His record over Ascot’s straight mile is admirable, making an each-way bet look good value.

TRIBAL CHIEF is of interest after getting back on track at Goodwood.

He won when finally breaking on terms last time and, if he can do so here, he looks a threat under a penalty.

A price of 16/1 could look big if he exits the stalls on terms.

Football regulator boss David Kogan has vowed to quit if prevented from punishing Manchester City’s owners — and is ready to ask government for extra cash to fight any legal challenge from Abu Dhabi. The Independent Football Regulator has the power to disqualify City’s owners and force Sheikh Mansour to sell up following the club’s [...]]]>

Football regulator boss David Kogan has vowed to quit if prevented from punishing Manchester City’s owners — and is ready to ask government for extra cash to fight any legal challenge from Abu Dhabi.

The Independent Football Regulator has the power to disqualify City’s owners and force Sheikh Mansour to sell up following the club’s conviction for systematically breaking Premier League rules.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has raised concerns about that outcome, prompting fears of government interference, but Kogan has made it clear he won’t stand for ministerial meddling. 

“Our independence is absolute, and my independence personally is absolute,” said Kogan, who previously donated to the Labour leadership campaigns of Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy and Burnham’s predecessor Keir Starmer. 

“I made it very clear last year that any form of political interference in the way we operate is going to result in my resigning from this role, and I stand by that completely. 

“To be crystal clear, we’ve come under absolutely no political pressure whatsoever on this or any other topic, and I don’t expect to in the future. I think ministers and indeed opposition parties know full well that we’re going to act entirely independently.”

The IFR will wait for City’s appeal against more than 100 convictions of financial rule-breaking before taking any action, which Kogan said would be based on legal advice.

IFR will demand more funding if sued by Man City, says Kogan

If disqualified, Sheikh Mansour would be given a deadline to sell which, if not met, would trigger a third party taking over the sale at a price City would have no control over.

“We are not a black and white, tick-box regulator,” said IFR CEO Richard Monks. “It allows us to take a broad view of the suitability of a particular owner.”

Kogan dismissed concerns that the IFR did not have deep enough pockets to sustain long-running legal action from super-wealthy owners such as City’s, saying it would demand more money from the government in order to fight its case.

“If we’re facing a long-running legal challenge, we will clearly go back to government and get financial support from government. That’s nothing to do with our current budget. That’s going to be an exceptional circumstance,” he added. 

“I don’t expect a problem with the Treasury or with DCMS if we’re suddenly facing a substantive legal challenge, assuming that legal challenge is one that we’re prepared to fight and prepared to win. But as I say, we have yet to face that situation.”

State of the Game report and New Deal close

Kogan and Monks were speaking in Manchester at the launch of the draft State of the Game report, which will inform its policy and, they said, highlighted the dichotomy between English football’s great success and growing financial risks.

A major step towards resolving that – a new deal that will see more money flow more evenly from the Premier League to the divisions below – now appears close after years of wrangling. “I think the leagues are pretty much agreed on most of the detail,” Kogan said.

The IFR will take a more proactive approach to clubs seeking to exploit loopholes in financial rules by, in the case of Chelsea, selling their women’s team to a related party or, in several others, selling their stadium or other assets to their ultimate owner.

“If a club tried to do something like that under our regime, we would just say no,” said Monks. “We wouldn’t just say no in terms of pointing to a specific rule, but because we have this much broader assessment of risk.” Monks added the regulator could instead allow it but insist on other measures, such as clubs trebling their cash balance.

The IFR will next week reveal its plans for the levy on clubs which will fund its costs and those incurred by government in establishing the watchdog. Any extraordinary legal action it is required to fight would not come from its levy-derived budget, Kogan said.
