Artificial film review and star rating as OpenAI movie premieres at the London Film Festival: ★★★★★

It isn’t typically a film’s duty to push a political agenda, but with Artificial, the biopic of OpenAI co-founder Sam Altman, there is a clear call to action. It is inevitable that people will ask: ‘What can this film do?’ 

Luca Guadagnino’s eleventh film is a particularly disturbing portrait of AI, following the tech entrepreneur Sam Altman, who launched AI chatbot Chat GPT in 2022, instigating an arms race involving Grok, Gemini, and Claude. Some leading scientists have claimed that the power and potential of these programmes means they could destroy humanity by the end of the 2020s.

A decade ago that would have been the stuff of science fiction movies, but in autumn 2026, Artificial feels terrifyingly prescient.

Artificial: film conveys how Sam Altman is loved in Messianic way

It is also very good. Most unnerving is Andrew Garfield’s psychopathically cocksure impression of Altman. The Spider-Man actor nails the businessman’s frenetic energy; he’s forever gyrating his hips, casting strange Cheshire cat grins, and glancing his eyes toward the sky in a way that you can never quite interpret. Is he performatively cocksure, or is that humanity? Garfield conveys how Atlman is impossible to decipher. 

Luca Guadagnino conveys his emotional distance through dreamlike sequences involving Altman and Ilya Sutskever, OpenAI’s chief scientific officer and co-founder, who pioneered the technology but later warned of its unethical effects. In one trippy scene, the duo depart on a hike through the San Francisco hills, the camera blurring out of focus during Altman’s ramblings. 

Altman is presented as emotionally complex, unable to properly express his love for his partner Oliver but adored in a messianic way by OpenAI staffers, who at one point chant “feel the AI” as they carry him up a flight of stairs.

Campy Elon Musk

Ike Barinholtz’s campy Elon Musk will surely infuriate the Grok founder, who worked with Altman during the early days of Chat GPT. His farcical impression – all peace signs and pouty faces – is just about close enough to the real man to work, while bringing some light relief. Writer Simon Rich, who based much of Artificial on conversations with a friend who works at OpenAI, writes clearly in the voices of these giants, although the physical impressions are so effective that the words play second fiddle.

Yura Borisov is magnetic as eastern European science whizz Ilya, who is at emotional boiling point as he argues endlessly with Altman that OpenAI must maintain its not-for-profit status. OpenAI insists on sprinting forward despite the scientist’s warnings the technology could have devastating effects. Their friendship might be platonic, but Atlman and Sutskever’s love affair is no less compelling than the heartbreak at the centre of Call Me By Your Name, the director’s most famous work.

Rylance is magnificent

Mark Rylance is quietly magnificent as Ilya’s moral compass, the principled academic Geoffrey Hinton. You hang on the every word of this grounded professor, particularly as employees learn that AI gaining sentience doesn’t necessarily mean it’ll be better than humans, rather it will be flawed like us.

“Rogue” AI agents from OpenAI are already threatening online security with the latest example being a flood of requests from their AI robots causing Wikipedia to temporarily go down. At the same time, the UK’s AI minister is warning of an “inevitable” AI attack on the country. In what will surely be the talking point film of 2027 – its UK cinematic release is end of January – Artificial is the closest look we’ve had at the charismatic, terrifying men at the heart of the AI revolution.

Artificial played at the London Film Festival. The film is released in UK cinemas on 22 January

]]> 2465090Adam Bloodworth Adam Bloodworth iPhone 18 Pro review: Like a fine burgundy https://www.cityam.com/iphone-18-pro-review-like-a-fine-burgundy/ Tue, 13 Oct 2026 15:20:42 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2465465

Explore the burgundy iPhone 18 Pro, with longer battery life, a brighter screen, upgraded cameras and formidable A20 Pro performance.]]>

iPhone 18 Pro | ★★★★☆ | From £1,199

Every year a new iPhone comes out and every year my peers at CNET and TechRadar and Wired begin to foam at the mouth over the number of cores on the CPU – how many milliseconds might that shave off the time it takes to open an app? And every year my first thought is OMG, this comes in gold now? Or holy s**t, check out that orange! Or, this year, wow, burgundy!

The way an iPhone looks and feels – the way it sits in your hand, the smoothness of the aluminium, the curve of the bezel, its hue and vibrancy – is every bit as important as the gubbins whirring beneath the screen. An iPhone is – for better or worse – an irreplaceable part of your life, an extension of your very being. It needs to look the part.

The burgundy iPhone 18 Pro

So I am pleased to report that the burgundy iPhone 18 Pro looks lovely, its deep, rich colour bringing to mind the Tom Ford nail polish Plum Noir. The sheet of coloured glass inlaid into the back is now tone-matched with the rest of the body, which you’ll only ever notice if you’re the kind of cowboy who uses their £1,199 iPhone without a cover. It is slightly heavier than its predecessor (five grams) but if you notice that without using scales, you’re more attuned to the universe than I. 

Apart from the colour, this is very much an iterative upgrade: it’s faster and has more battery life, which Apple reckons will get you about 34 hours of video playback. In that time you could watch the extended editions of the Lord of the Rings trilogy three times and still have enough battery left to get through the director’s cut of Blade Runner. I just spent 90 minutes playing the puzzle game Machinika: Atlas, which is relatively graphics intensive, and my battery is still at 86 per cent. We’re creeping closer to the day when you’ll be able to go two sleeps before plugging your phone in, although by that time the AI apocalypse will be well under way and we’ll be back to telling the time using a sun dial and playing games with sticks and bits of string.

Speaking of playing Machinika: Atlas: I was sitting in the sun and could still make out what was happening thanks to the incredibly bright screen (3,000 Nits!). Putting the brightness up to full when you’re in bed feels like you’re being interrogated by a 1940s policeman.

You will notice that the “dynamic island” that houses the front-facing camera is now smaller, giving you more screen space when it’s not in use and allowing you to display three “Live Activities”. In theory you could watch a timer, track an incoming Uber and see the current song playing on Spotify.

All you need to know about the camera

And then there is the camera, which is a genuinely impressive upgrade. The 18 Pro introduces a variable aperture for the main camera, which gives you more control than ever over your photographs. Most people will never leave “automatic” mode but if you crave faster shots in low light with less blurring, you’re in luck.

The photography suite now includes a 48MP main camera, 48MP ultra-wide camera and 48MP 4x telephoto lens, in addition to the 18MP selfie camera. Shooting out and about in the City shows off just how good this set-up is. Image stabilisation that borders on witchcraft coupled with that telephoto lens means you can snap a picture from atop a skyscraper and see what kind of trainers someone at street level is wearing.

There’s also a new AI-assisted focus tracking feature that’s great for taking pictures of your pets, which, let’s face it, is about 90 per cent of the world’s photography output. Google’s Pixel has made huge strides in photography in recent years but these improvements keep Apple’s flagship ahead of the competition.

And finally, for anyone who has accidentally ended up here instead of TechRadar, let me tell you about the new A20 Pro chip, which replaces the A19 Pro chip in the iPhone 17 Pro: it’s 20 per cent faster, with 40 per cent faster graphics performance. You won’t get close to testing its limits through normal use. Make of that what you will.

• The iPhone 18 Pro is available now priced from £1,199

]]> 2465465Steve Dinneen Steve Dinneen AI firms taking ‘catastrophically high’ risks, ex-OpenAI researcher warns MPs https://www.cityam.com/ai-firms-taking-catastrophically-high-risks-ex-openai-researcher-warns-mps/ Tue, 13 Oct 2026 14:49:23 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2465391

The world’s biggest AI companies are taking “catastrophically high” risks in their race to develop superintelligent systems, a former OpenAI researcher has warned MPs, as Parliament examines whether tech giants can be trusted to regulate themselves. Daniel Kokotajlo, who quit the ChatGPT maker over safety concerns, told the Business, Innovation, Science and Trade (BIST) Committee [...]]]>

The world’s biggest AI companies are taking “catastrophically high” risks in their race to develop superintelligent systems, a former OpenAI researcher has warned MPs, as Parliament examines whether tech giants can be trusted to regulate themselves.

Daniel Kokotajlo, who quit the ChatGPT maker over safety concerns, told the Business, Innovation, Science and Trade (BIST) Committee on Tuesday that the industry was developing increasingly powerful AI models without knowing how to control them.

“I would say that the risk tolerance across the industry is catastrophically high”, he told MPs.

The warning came as former researchers from OpenAI and Anthropic faced questions over whether the development of advanced AI was outpacing the safeguards designed to prevent the technology from behaving unpredictably.

Kokotajlo said he had resigned after losing confidence in OpenAI’s willingness to act responsibly as it pursued superintelligence, referring to systems capable of outperforming humans across virtually all tasks.

“I came to believe that OpenAI, in fact, would not behave responsibly around the creation of this technology”, he said.

He also alleged that staff had faced pressure to play down concerns about the technology.

“I did feel pressure to mince my words a bit in my public communications”, he said, adding that some internal research and forecasts was stopped from being published.

Steven Adler, another former OpenAI researcher, told MPs there had been resistance within the company to describing its technology as “dangerous”.

“Unfortunately, the reality of the technology – whether it is dangerous – does not depend on whether you call it dangerous”, he said.

Adler, who left OpenAI in late 2024, acknowledged that its internal culture may have changed since his departure.

OpenAI and Anthropic have been contacted for comment. Both firms have recently called for a slowdown in the development of the most advanced AI models to enable safety measures to keep pace.

AI safety fears mount as MPs scrutinise tech giants

Geoffrey Irving, a former researcher at OpenAI, Anthropic and Britain’s AI Security Institute, warned MPs that progress in AI capabilities was far outstripping advances in safety research.

“We are still undergoing very, very rapid capability advances without corresponding advances in safety”, he said.

Asked whether he stood by his assessment that advanced AI could have a 50 per cent chance of destroying humanity, Irving said a “coin flip is roughly the right model to have”.

The figure reflects his personal assessment of a hypothetical future risk, rather than an established scientific probability.

Adler urged governments to impose clearer limits on AI developers, warning that competition was encouraging companies to justify increasingly dangerous decisions based on what their rivals were doing.

“What I hope governments will do is they will help set the ceiling essentially on how much risk these companies can impose”, he said.

The hearing follows AI minister Kanishka Narayan’s warning on Monday that a major breach of Britain’s cyber defences was likely to be inevitable.

It also comes after Washington restored the UK’s access to advanced American AI models for pre-release safety testing, following a temporary restriction that raised questions about Britain’s ability to scrutinise the technology independently.

Anthropic itself warned on Monday that its models may soon be able to self-replicate and takeover devices like ovens and TVs. In filings for its upcoming IPO, the company reportedly said its technology could pose “existential risks to humanity”.

The number of ISA millionaires in the UK hit a record high, as more Brits chose to plough their cash into the tax-shielded account.

The total number of stocks and shares ISA millionaires increased by more than 50 per cent in the 2023/24 tax year, reaching a record 7,730 according to an FOI request from financial app Plum to HMRC.

This marked a further 2,660 Brits holding £1m or more in their ISA accounts, up from 5,070 in the 2022/23 tax year, and represented the largest year-on-year increase since 2016.

According to HMRC data, the average ISA millionaire was holding a pot worth roughly £1.3m in April 2024.

Patient investors

“These aren’t people who suddenly saved their way to £1m. It’s the result of years of patient investing, where the growth on your growth starts doing the heavy lifting. That’s the bit people underestimate,” said Will Bryant, director of wealth strategy at Plum.

“These figures underline the value of investing and the importance of taking a long-term approach. Despite the geopolitical volatility of recent years, global markets powered by the U.S. stock market have continued to climb.”

Tax system upheaval

Bryant also pointed towards the benefit of allocating capital into an ISA as families brace for pensions to be pulled into the scope of inheritance tax (IHT) from April 2027.

ISA pots remain exempt from IHT if passed onto a spouse or civil partner.

The cash ISA ceiling is also set to be slashed from £20,000 to £12,000 from the next financial year, while the stocks and shares ceiling is set to remain at £20,000 in a bid to get more people to opt to save into the product.

Bryant said: “The ISA reforms may lead people to use more of their stocks & shares ISA to make full use of their tax-free allowance.”

Meta has challenged the UK regulator in court over how it calculates fees and fines under the UK’s online safety law, as it argued the methods are disproportionate and unlawful.

The tech giant has questioned the media regulator, Ofcom, over its definition of ‘qualifying worldwide revenue’, which it uses to calculate financial penalties and fees for tech companies which earn over £250m a year.

The parties are at a judicial review hearing in the English High Court on Tuesday and Wednesday.

The regulator created and drafted the Qualifying Worldwide Revenue (QWR) provisions in September last year under the Online Safety Act, which introduced new protections against harmful online content. Under the rules, firms found to have breached safety rules can face fines of up to 10 per cent of qualifying worldwide revenue or £18m, whichever is the higher amount.

Under the new rules, if Ofcom enforces against a single entity owned by a tech firm, such as a social media platform, it will calculate financial penalties based only on that entity’s revenue.

However, if the regulator enforces against multiple entities, including a firm’s parent company and subsidiaries, it can instead calculate the amount based on the group’s total revenue generated from everything, including non-regulated activities such as enterprise software.

According to court filings seen by City AM, Meta has alleged the Online Safety Act does not give the regulator powers to include revenue for non-regulated services when pursuing multiple entities, and so Ofcom is breaching its own statutory powers and “acting irrationally” by creating a “double counting” approach to calculating fines and fees.

The US tech firm is claiming Ofcom deliberately adopted the “broadest possible approach” of those rules to grant itself power to impose financial penalties on providers “at an unprecedented level of magnitude.”

Ofcom, however, argued that Meta “is incorrect” and that it “struck a careful balance” in adopting its approach to calculating financial penalties.

“A fundamental flaw with this argument is that it was no part of the purpose of the QWR Regulations to set the ‘level’ of any penalty. The QWR Regulations determine the methodology for calculating the maximum penalty in a particular case, but Ofcom will determine the appropriate and proportionate level of penalty on the facts of the case at hand,” Ofcom said in court filings seen by City AM.

In a statement, a Meta spokesperson said the tech giant is “committed to cooperating constructively with Ofcom as it enforces the Online Safety Act.”

“However, we and others in the tech industry believe its decisions on the methodology to calculate fees and potential fines are disproportionate. We believe fees and penalties should be based on the services being regulated in the countries where they’re being regulated. This would still allow Ofcom to impose the largest fines in UK corporate history,” the spokesperson said.

An Ofcom spokesperson said in a statement: “Parliament has charged us with the job of regulating an industry that has been unregulated and unaccountable for more than 20 years.”

“Effective regulation relies on our ability to gather information, levy appropriate fees, issue fines and apply the law as intended. While legal challenges are an important part of any regulatory regime, we will defend them robustly as part of our mission of making life safer online for people in the UK.”

Regulator ‘operating in a highly litigious environment’

During a meeting for the House of Lords Communications and Digital Committee on 15 September, Ofcom’s group director for online safety, Oliver Griffiths, said the regulator is “operating in a highly litigious environment” as it is facing two lots of legal proceedings brought by Meta over its fee calculation, amongst other online service providers bringing similar claims.

Griffiths added the regulator has “a raft of services that are bringing judicial reviews against us for trying to collect data so that we can monitor and evaluate what is happening” with the online safety regime.

The Midday Market report is a new newsletter from City AM, giving you fresh analysis on the biggest stories in the City straight into your inbox every lunchtime. Today, Ali Lyon weighs up what Tuesday’s IMF report says about the state of the UK economy. Sign up to the City AM News Updates newsletter here.

To read this morning’s World Economic Outlook from the IMF is to be left confused about the state of the UK economy.

The dollops of good news – and there certainly were a few – were without fail accompanied by caveats and qualifications. Where we were singled out for praise, economists from the pre-eminent monetary authority quickly brought us back down to earth with a thud.

We are – if you’ll allow me to lean on a rather tortured analogy – in the top quartile of our class. Our academic performance – 1.3 per cent GDP growth this year and 1.2 per cent next – is solid if by no means remarkable. And our behaviour – a promise to balance the books (excluding investment) by the end of the parliament – is positively gold-star worthy.

But that good end of term report is made a lot less impressive when one considers that almost everyone else in the class is, by the IMF’s reckoning, on the brink of being put in special measures. And that the teachers’ comments for us left quite a bit of room for improvement.

It was a paper teeming with interesting and politically dicey contradictions. One long do-you-want-the-good-news-or-the-bad-news assessment. But there were three big paradoxes that are worth singling out.

The Great British Paradox in the UK economy

Growth – but make it hot:

Let’s tackle the two big-ticket items up top. We are on course to have the second-fastest growth of any major European economy both this year and in 2027. Given that the IMF’s last global economic temperature check warned we were especially exposed to the then-nascent Iran war, those real GDP numbers can be chalked up as a success. We have proven to be much more resilient than many expected.

But while we’re all enjoying the spoils of our economic unexceptionality, we will also be fighting to contain the second-highest inflation of any developed economy, the IMF warned.

Prices will rise by an average of 3.3 per cent this year, and are on track to jump by a further 2.8 per cent in 2027, assuming the Middle East war dies down by around March, as the report’s authors have.

In short, the UK is looking relatively growth-y. But our exposure to external events – be that via our poor food security, our ideological energy system or our embarrassment of hyper-regulated industries – means we’ll have to get used to higher prices for longer than our counterparts.

Our fiscal position is better than most – but vulnerable to slippage:

Authors singled the UK out for its ambitious deficit reduction targets, which are the most ambitious and impressive of any G7 economy. Speaking at a press conference, IMF chief economist Silvana Tenreyro praised our “consolidation path”, which official targets say will see us bring tax revenue back in line with day-to-day spending by 2029/30. That is considerably lower than the yawning deficits on show in countries like France and the US, which were both placed firmly on the IMF’s naughty step.

But she also raised a gentle eyebrow as to just how realistic our goals are given the rather expensive-sounding mood music coming out of 10 (if not 11) Downing Street. “The message for the UK is simply: stay the course,” Tenreyro said. “And continue on that trajectory.”

Bifurc-AI-tion in the UK economy

As one would expect, AI, and how it will uproot the global economy, was a theme throughout the IMF’s big barometer. The technology’s rapid development helps explain much of why the Middle East conflict has not taken an even larger chunk out of countries’ GDP figures. That is particularly the case in the UK economy, where our abundance of white-collar, professional industries allows us to adopt AI – and its economic uplift – faster than many others.

The kicker (there was always going to be one, wasn’t there) is that once that initial adoption is over, we are among the most exposed of any developed country to its disruptive impact. Our high energy costs preclude us from developing frontier models here almost entirely. We can’t point to any meaningful cottage industries – be they chipmakers, designers and the like – to boost our enormous trade deficit. And, most disconcertingly, there is the small issue of what happens if all those white-collar workers who are currently leaning on the tech for their productivity are suddenly not needed at all.

That worrying notion notwithstanding, there are plenty of positives to take from our bi-annual MOT from the world’s monetary authority. If it really were a report card, it would likely read, “Some good work done this term by the UK economy – but come 28 October, it can’t afford to let itself down at its first big exam.”

Investec recently chaired a panel discussion with its charitable partner, the Black Young Professionals Network (BYP), exploring the relationship between belonging and performance in the workplace. Jason Spivey, Investec’s Head of People and Organisation, reflects on why belonging is about more than inclusion. It’s about having the opportunities and backing to succeed.

Black History Month gives organisations a moment to celebrate Black history, culture and achievement. But the harder question is what happens when the month ends? Once black and ethnically diverse colleagues are through the door, are they given the same chance to build a career, be stretched, be heard and be backed?

Belonging is felt in the everyday moments when someone notices what you can do, gives you space to prove it and backs you when it matters. It is being listened to properly, trusted with work that matters and spoken for when decisions are being made elsewhere.

Ambition exists, the blockage is often access, to the people, opportunities and backing that turn potential into progression. Business in the Community’s 2025 Breaking Barriers to Progression report put the gap plainly: ethnically diverse people made up one in 10 of Britain’s population, but only one in 15 of those are in management positions.

Recruitment figures only tell us who came through the door. They do not tell us who was trusted with an important piece of work, who received useful feedback or whose name came up when the next opportunity was discussed. 

Carl Konadu, co-founder and chief executive of youth social enterprise 2-3 Degrees, puts it well: “If you walk into a room and feel out of place, find someone else who might feel the same, and help them belong.”

There is something practical in that. Belonging is not created by a statement on a website. It happens when someone makes space at the table, explains what others assume everybody knows or gives a colleague a chance before they feel completely ready.

At Investec, some of this work happens through our partnerships.  Our work with the BYP Network brings us closer to Black professionals at different stages of their careers. 

Kike Agoro, founder and chief executive of the BYP Network, says Black professionals are looking closely at what employers offer. “Black talent has their eyes wide open when it comes to opportunities,” she says. “They won’t just jump ship without truly assessing the culture, pay and promises.”

They are right to look closely. Trust is not something an employer can switch on when there is a vacancy to fill.

I heard versions of this at a recent panel I hosted at the BYP Leadership Conference. The stories were different, but each person could remember a moment when somebody’s response helped them see themselves differently.

World-ranked boxer and social entrepreneur Valerian Spicer (and past winner of Investec’s Beyond Business programme) described walking into a boxing gym for the first time in her thirties. The coaches watched her work, saw that she was committed and gave her their time. “No one gave me a big speech of welcoming me in,” she said. “I just started and they could see the commitment.”

Her phrase “start before you’re ready” stayed with me. We often talk as if confidence is something a person should arrive with. In reality, it can be the result of being given an opportunity and finding that people take you seriously once you begin.

Black professionals may have every qualification needed for a role yet still find the unwritten parts of career progression harder to reach. Who explains how decisions are really made? Who offers candid feedback early enough for it to be useful? Who introduces you to the person who can open the next door ?

Sponsorship can make a real difference here. A mentor can help someone think through a choice. A sponsor goes further; they mention that person when an opportunity comes up and put their own credibility behind the recommendation.

The further people move through their careers, the more opportunities are shaped by conversations they may never hear. If black colleagues are missing from the networks around those conversations, strong recruitment at junior levels will not be enough to change who reaches leadership.

This is not only about fairness, important though it is. Work is better when people can ask a question without fearing it will be held against them, offer an idea without having to judge whether it is safe to speak and learn from a mistake without feeling that they have confirmed somebody else’s assumption.

So I would encourage employers to look past the headline number. Notice who gets the stretching work. Pay attention to whose career has slowed down and ask why. And when somebody has ability, do not wait for them to arrive fully formed before offering your support.

Belonging often comes down to small choices made by people with influence. Invite someone into the conversation. Say their name when they are not there. Give them the context, the honest feedback or the first chance that somebody once gave you. Being welcomed matters. Being able to shape what happens next matters even more.

The turnover of FTSE 100 chief executives has tumbled to a five year low as companies choose to hold onto top leadership amid ongoing economic volatility.

Executive churn this year is on track to fall to the second lowest level seen since 2012, according to data from AJ Bell, as boards opt for stability. Nine chief executive changes have occurred since January, below the typical average of 13 annually since 2000. 

Babcock, Diageo, GSK and Rentokil are among the firms who replaced the person in the top job, while British Land has also announced it will welcome a new chief executive set to start in 2027.

Don’t rock the boat

Finance director turnover has also cooled, falling from 25 changes last year to just 15 so far in 2026. 

Diageo and Barrett Redrow were the two firms who replaced their finance chief as well as their chief executive, while BT and Vodafone also switched out their top financial officers.

The downfall in turnover has been credited to a desire to “not to rock the boat” amid widespread market volatility caused by the conflict in the Middle East.

Swelling cost pressures off the back of energy market shocks has left firms unable to justify overhauls to leadership, as replacing executives triggers lengthy strategy resets, including portfolio restructuring, supply chain overhauls and assessing headcount, which many firms cannot afford.

“For some companies, it might be the wrong time to rock the boat with new leadership, maintaining…continuity may be viewed as the lower-risk option,” said Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell.

Halting at the top

The index has also managed to avoid the growing influence of activist investors, which “often act as a catalyst for leadership change”.

Activists, which are typically US and European hedge funds, are known to exert their influence over the running of UK listed companies amid turmoil. Earlier this year, Domino’s faced calls from its activist investor Browning West to return more capital to shareholders.

Greggs also battled pressure from Singapore-based Lauro asset management to cut costs to avoid a takeover bid earlier this year.

Despite the pushes to change company dealings, minimal firms have faced pressure to make changes at the top.

Coatsworth identified distribution group Bunzl and Premier Inn owner Whitbread as groups who are in the most hot water with activist investors. 

Bunzl’s chief executive Frank van Zanten has been in the role since April 2016 and has brought in a 61 per cent total return for the group’s shareholders, which is less than half the 146 per cent from the FTSE 100. 

Meanwhile, Whitbread boss Dominic Paul, has caused shareholders to lose 6.6 per cent of their investment, even after accounting for dividends since taking over in 2023. 

Activist shareholder Corvex recently called for one of its representatives to join the board.

Coatsworth said:“Activists typically push for new management… Bunzl and Whitbread have encountered their fair share of challenges of late, meaning disgruntled investors might welcome an activist shake-up.”

    Did you know the Rugby League World Cup starts this week?

    If you’re reading this in the north of England then the answer is probably yes. If down south then I suspect the answer is much more likely to be no. This is a huge problem.

    Rugby league has one of the most watchable products in British sport. It is fast, physical, easy to understand and packed with elite athletes. Yet once again, as its biggest international tournament approaches, it’s trapped inside its own bubble.

    The issue is not the quality of the sport. It’s the distribution and storytelling.

    Four years ago, the 2022 Rugby League World Cup was everywhere. Every match was available through the BBC. England’s opening game against Samoa reached a substantial audience and, importantly, the tournament brought people into the sport who had not previously watched rugby league.

    This time, every match sits exclusively on Premier Sports in Britain and Ireland. That might make commercial sense in a rights negotiation, but it raises other questions.

    Such as: what is the purpose of a Rugby League World Cup?

    It’s the shop window the sport has. The moment when people who do not watch Super League every weekend are introduced to the players, the international rivalries and intensity of the sport. Putting that shop window behind a paywall reduces the chances of people discovering it.

    Rugby league needs personalities, narrative and cultural relevance

    The wider problem is that rugby league too often markets itself to people who already love rugby league.

    George Williams, Mikey Lewis, Herbie Farnworth and Jack Welsby are brilliant players. But how many casual sports fans could pick them out of a line-up? 

    The sport should be creating personalities, rivalries and storylines that mean something beyond its traditional heartlands. That’s the job for the marketing department.

    Team-wise, Australia remain the benchmark, but they are no longer untouchable. New Zealand regularly beat them, while Samoa reached the last World Cup final. Tonga have also become a genuine force and England have players performing at the highest level in both Super League and Down Under in the NRL.

    There is always jeopardy, brilliant athletes and off-field drama. We just don’t have any noise around the World Cup. 

    Where are the players on mainstream podcasts, breakfast TV and being serenaded by politicians? Where are the documentaries, creator collaborations and crossover campaigns? Where are Premier League clubs in rugby league heartlands pushing England’s World Cup campaign to their own enormous audiences?

    Sport today competes in the attention economy. Rugby league needs to build personalities, narratives and cultural relevance.

    Rugby league has spent years wondering why it does not receive the attention it deserves, but no sport deserves any attention. You must compete for it.

    With the World Cup about to begin, rugby league’s biggest challenge is not convincing its existing supporters that it matters but connecting with and convincing everyone else.

    Simon Dent is an entrepreneur and brand builder with more than 20 years’ experience. He is currently chairman of Counteruck.

    Andy Burnham earned his spurs as a great communicator on the back of a few summer TikToks, but is the shine coming off just a couple of months into the new job? While some people still appreciate the supposedly down to earth ‘tell it like it is’ approach, there can be no denying that the PM’s loose lips have got him into hot water in recent weeks. Labour sources concede that Burnham’s tendency to “shoot from the hip” is becoming a problem.

    Consider his comments on Heathrow expansion, when he said the third runway “is a matter for London” before suggesting he shouldn’t offer a view, given the proposal is currently subject to a consultation. The apparent lack of support for the multi-billion pound national infrastructure project sent panic through the sector, and saw a concerted effort from Whitehall to reassure industry figures that the government remains supportive.

    Most recently the PM seemed to share the details of a high-level intelligence briefing he’d asked for on Russian interference in the 2016 Brexit vote, to the delight of podcast hosts Alastair Campbell and Rory Stewart. Having offered much more heat than light, his own ministers and, ultimately, the Downing Street spokesperson, spent all of Monday rowing back from the comments and clarifying that there was no evidence of such activity affecting the result of the vote.

    He seems to revel in a ‘just saying’ attitude

    Do you see the pattern here? Burnham speaks with all the confidence of a regional mayor but without the gravitas of a Prime Minister. He seems to revel in a “just saying” attitude, without recognising the consequences of his words. Time and again he lets slip a comment or a point of view that has to be clarified, rectified or disowned by his aides or ministers. Thu, 08 Oct 2026 13:15:32 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.9.10 Researchers tracked the passwords 154 people used online for an average of 147 days and found them logging into 26 websites with fewer than 10 unique passwords — roughly 60 percent were reused outright or built from pieces of passwords they were already using elsewhere https://siliconcanals.com/d-researchers-tracked-the-passwords-154-people-used-online-for-an-average-of-147-days-and-found-them-logging-into-26-websites-with-fewer-than-10-unique-passwords-roughly-60-percent-were-reused/ Tue, 22 Sep 2026 14:30:40 +0000 https://siliconcanals.com/?p=109740

Most people protect their digital lives with a handful of passwords they've memorized—a security practice so common it's become catastrophic.]]>

For about five months, a browser extension sat quietly on the home computers of 154 people and watched them log in.

The researchers never saw a password. Everything was hashed on the machine before it went anywhere, leaving them with the shape of each one: its length, its mix of characters, the site it was typed into, and whether the same string had appeared before.

Very often, it had.

What 154 people actually typed

Sarah Pearman and her co-authors at Carnegie Mellon University presented the results at a 2017 computer security conference, having followed each participant for an average of 147 days. Those people logged in across 26 web domains apiece and covered the lot with fewer than 10 distinct passwords.

Roughly 60 per cent of those distinct passwords were recycled, either typed identically on another site or built around a chunk of four or more characters lifted from one the same person used elsewhere.

Banking got no special treatment. Around 85 per cent of the passwords on financial sites appeared elsewhere too, and nearly all of that crossover ran into unrelated categories, so the login for a savings account was also the login for a shoe shop.

What partial reuse looks like up close

Mostly it looks like adding a character.

Among passwords that shared a substring with another, the most common gap between the two was a single character. Digits were the strongest predictor in the Carnegie Mellon model, multiplying the odds of reuse by more than twelve. The authors’ own explanation is that a password with a number in it satisfies more websites’ fussy signup rules, so it travels further.

The tidy minority had barely any accounts

Ten participants mostly built something new for each site, which sounds like a win for good habits until you look at what they were doing online. With one exception, every one of them entered passwords on eight domains or fewer, and they were active on their computers on only 17 per cent of the days they spent enrolled.

The heavy users went the other way. Ninety-four participants, the largest cluster by far, both copied passwords outright and modified them, and they averaged 32 online accounts each. Discipline held up fine at eight accounts and collapsed at thirty.

The password manager result, with a handbrake

Only 19 of the 154 participants had a password manager installed, and the study found no measurable effect on either reuse or strength.

That result deserves caution. One paper is one paper, the subgroup is tiny, and the software could not tell whether people were generating random strings or merely parking passwords they had invented themselves. Rick Wash and colleagues at Michigan State University, who watched 134 participants over six weeks, found each password being reused on 1.7 to 3.4 websites. Their study did not measure partial reuse at all, so the higher figure out of Pittsburgh partly reflects counting a habit nobody had counted before.

Why a recycled password is worth money

Somewhere there is a text file with an old forum password in it, sitting in a folder alongside a few hundred million others. Troy Hunt, the Australian security researcher behind the breach notification service Have I Been Pwned, has documented the trade in combo lists, which are exactly that: vast dumps of email and password pairs scraped out of past breaches. Cheap automated tools fire them at unrelated websites until one opens. Defending against it is awkward, because a successful run looks identical to a customer logging in correctly.

One shared string, and the breach at a defunct hobby forum becomes a problem at an email provider.

The rules that encouraged this have been withdrawn

In 2025, the US National Institute of Standards and Technology finalised revision 4 of its digital identity guidelines, and the password section reads like a quiet apology. Websites must stop demanding mixtures of character types, and they must stop forcing periodic changes unless there is evidence of compromise. Password managers and autofill have to be allowed, and every new password gets checked against blocklists of strings already known to have leaked.

Each of those requirements targets the behaviour the extension recorded: a handful of memorable strings, nudged sideways by a digit, stretched across an entire online life.

The standard now assumes a machine is doing the remembering. Anyone who ever stuck a “1” on the end to get past a signup form was just covering the shift until it arrived.

]]> A telemarketer refused to keep his webcam on for nine hours a day while working from home and was fired the next day — a Dutch court ruled the demand invaded his privacy and ordered his employer to pay him roughly €75,000 https://siliconcanals.com/d-a-telemarketer-refused-to-keep-his-webcam-on-for-nine-hours-a-day-while-working-from-home-and-was-fired-the-next-day-a-dutch-court-ruled-the-demand-invaded-his-privacy-and-ordered-his-employ/ Tue, 22 Sep 2026 14:15:27 +0000 https://siliconcanals.com/?p=109737

A Dutch court sided with a worker who refused constant video surveillance, forcing his employer to pay damages—a warning shot across the evolving battle over remote work monitoring.]]>

A camera that stayed switched off cost a Florida software company about 75,000 euros.

It belonged to a telemarketer working from the small Dutch town of Diessen, employed since January 2019 by Chetu, an American software firm that at the time ran a Dutch office in Rijswijk. On 23 August 2022 he was told to join something called the Corrective Action Program, which meant staying logged in for his whole shift, sharing his screen and leaving his laptop camera on. He shared the screen. The camera stayed dark.

His objection was brief and entirely unlegalistic. Court filings quoted by The Register record him saying he was not comfortable being monitored for nine hours a day, calling it “an invasion of my privacy” and noting that his laptop activity was already visible to management.

Two more instructions followed, each firmer than the last. On 26 August he was dismissed on the spot, the stated reasons being refusal to work and insubordination.

Three days from the first instruction to the sack.

What the company argued

Chetu’s case, set out in the published judgment of the Court of Zeeland-West-Brabant, was that watching a remote worker through a webcam is no different from a manager walking past a desk. Performance software already sat on the man’s laptop, and that was not considered enough. Chetu wanted to see him working.

Nobody from the company turned up to make the argument in person, as TechCrunch noted, so it went undefended.

What the judge decided

Ruling on 28 September 2022, the subdistrict judge in Tilburg found that ordering an employee to keep a camera running for a full shift conflicted with his right to respect for private life, and that nothing had been offered to justify it. An unreasonable instruction cannot be unreasonably refused, so there had been no refusal to work and no grounds for summary dismissal.

Data protection law dropped out early. On the understanding that no footage would be recorded, stored or used for anything, the judge treated the monitoring as falling outside data processing altogether, and tested it directly against Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, alongside Strasbourg case law holding that filming staff at work, covert or not, is a serious intrusion into private life. Had the images been kept, the analysis would have looked quite different.

One much-quoted line deserves care. Coverage including a report in Fortune presented the claim that all-day camera tracking is disproportionate and not allowed in the Netherlands as a finding of the court. In the Dutch record it sits among the employee’s own submissions. What the judge actually held was narrower, and sufficient: this instruction, to this man, in his own home, breached Article 8 with no justification advanced.

Why the sum was so large

Almost none of the money was a penalty for the privacy breach. The largest slice, 50,000 euros, was a billijke vergoeding, an equitable award Dutch judges reserve for employers whose conduct in ending a job has been seriously culpable, with a wrongful summary dismissal among the standard triggers, as the Amsterdam employment firm Workx Advocaten explains. Privacy is why the sacking failed. The sacking is what got billed.

Around that sat roughly 8,375 euros for ignoring the notice period, close to 9,500 euros in statutory transition payment, more than 2,700 euros in unpaid wages, 23 days of untaken leave, the 8 per cent holiday allowance and some 585 euros in costs, all itemised by NL Times. His non-compete clause was lifted as well, leaving him free to walk to a competitor.

How common all-day camera rules are

Is this a bizarre one-off or a policy plenty of people are quietly living with? A survey of 1,000 business leaders at mostly remote companies, commissioned by ResumeBuilder in March 2023, found 37 per cent required staff to sit on a live video feed, and that 93 per cent of those firms had somebody monitoring it, usually for four hours or more a day.

The same survey found 73 per cent had dismissed workers on the strength of monitoring data, and 69 per cent had lost staff who would not accept it.

One survey is one survey. It polled American executives, it relied on self-reporting, and executives describing their own management habits are not a neutral instrument. Treat it as a temperature reading rather than a census.

Where the line actually falls

Whatever this settles, it settles in one jurisdiction, on one set of facts, at the lowest rung of the court system. Article 8 offers nothing in Florida, where employment is generally at will and can end without a stated reason, subject to the usual exceptions for discrimination, retaliation and whatever a contract says.

What the case supplies is a price tag on a boundary that remote-work policy has been drifting across without much thought: supervising the work is one thing, keeping a lens open in somebody’s house for the length of a shift is another. A Dutch judge has now looked at that question once, and the employer left lighter.

]]> Agility’s 284-pound Digit 5 runs for 90 minutes and recharges in nine, a 10-to-1 work-to-charge ratio the company says can deliver more than 20 productive hours a day, with early customer access planned for the first half of 2027 https://siliconcanals.com/n-agilitys-284-pound-digit-5-runs-for-90-minutes-and-recharges-in-nine-a-10-to-1-work-to-charge-ratio-the-company-says-can-deliver-more-than-20-productive-hours-a-day-with-early-customer-access/ Mon, 21 Sep 2026 19:00:38 +0000 https://siliconcanals.com/?p=109721

Agility says Digit 5 is engineered for unfenced work near people; its runtime, charging and daily-productivity figures remain manufacturer specifications ahead of planned 2027 customer access.]]>

Correction, 1 October 2026: An earlier version miscounted the number of charge cycles in a 24-hour day and said early access was more than a year away. The idealised 90-to-9-minute ratio implies about 21.8 hours of runtime and 2.2 hours of charging; early access is planned for the first half of 2027.

Agility Robotics has unveiled Digit 5, the fifth generation of its bipedal warehouse robot, and the headline change is the safety cage — specifically, its absence. Earlier Digit models, like most industrial robots, operated inside fenced cells to keep people out of reach. Digit 5 is designed to work in the open, using sensors and a separate safety controller that can make it stop, back away or drop into a seated position when a person gets close, according to the company’s hardware rundown from The Robot Report.

The robot stands 5 feet 11 inches tall and weighs 284 pounds, roughly the mass of two adult humans packed into a torso, legs and a pair of articulated arms. That weight matters less as a curiosity than as context for what follows: a machine that heavy needs a battery system that can be recharged fast enough to stay useful across a full shift, and Agility has built its pitch to investors and warehouse customers around exactly that number.

The 90-minute run, nine-minute charge math

Digit 5 runs for about 90 minutes on a charge and returns to full power in roughly 9 minutes, a figure Agility frames as a 10-to-1 run-to-charge ratio, up from the 2-to-1 ratio it says the previous Digit 4 managed, per the company’s own announcement. In practical terms, that means a robot could in theory swap onto a charger for the length of a coffee break and be back on the floor before a human coworker finishes one.

The idealised arithmetic gives each 99-minute cycle 90 minutes of runtime and nine minutes of charging. Repeating that ratio across 24 hours yields about 21.8 hours of runtime and 2.2 hours of charging before allowing for maintenance, handoffs or faults. That is the basis for the company’s more conservative claim that Digit 5 can deliver more than 20 productive hours in a 24-hour day.

What a 20-hour day actually means

Agility is measuring two things and projecting a third. The 90-minute runtime and 9-minute recharge are specifications the company attaches to Digit 5’s battery hardware. The “more than 20 productive hours” figure is a company calculation built from those two hardware numbers, assuming charging cycles that fit cleanly around a robot’s task queue — no downtime, faults or maintenance stops of the kind that show up in real operations. Agility has not published an independent customer-floor validation of a Digit 5 working day yet.

Independent reporting on the launch has generally repeated the 20-hour figure as Agility’s claim rather than as a verified outcome. IEEE Spectrum’s Evan Ackerman, reviewing Digit 5, raised a broader doubt about Agility’s underlying assumption that the robot can function as what he called “a more or less effortless drop-in replacement for human labor,” noting he was not sure that had happened yet with any robot, anywhere. The one field metric that has been independently reported involves the previous generation, not Digit 5: at a GXO logistics facility, Digit 4 reportedly 98% accuracy sorting totes over more than 100,000 units, a real operational number — though it speaks to picking accuracy, a separate metric from hours worked per day.

Heavier lifts, taller reach than the last generation

Alongside the battery changes, Agility increased what Digit 5 can physically do. The robot can repeatedly lift loads of up to 50 pounds, which the company describes as a 40 percent jump over Digit 4’s payload, and it can reach items up to 7.2 feet high, up from about 5.5 feet on the previous version, according to Forbes’ coverage of the launch. Both changes target the same use case Agility has pursued since the original Digit: moving totes, boxes and cases between conveyors, shelving and pallets in warehouses and distribution centers, work currently done by human “pickers” and “stockers.”

How Digit 5 compares with Boston Dynamics’ Atlas

Agility is not the only company chasing this category, and the comparison is not entirely favorable to Digit 5 on paper. Boston Dynamics’ electric Atlas, per the same Forbes report, is rated to carry up to 66 pounds, reach 7.5 feet and run for about four hours on a hot-swappable battery pack that can be physically pulled and replaced rather than recharged in place. On payload and reach, Atlas currently claims an edge. Digit 5’s advantage is charging speed and, by extension, uptime: a fixed nine-minute recharge cycle is a different operational model than swapping battery packs, and it is the piece Agility is betting its productivity math on.

Orders, a SPAC, and a company still losing money

The timing of the announcement lines up with a corporate transition. Agility disclosed more than $300 million in multi-year customer orders for Digit 5, a figure the company itself qualifies as subject to unspecified contractual milestones being met, and it disclosed the number days after filing paperwork for a SPAC merger with Churchill Capital Corp XI, a deal valued at roughly $2.5 billion. Regulatory filings tied to that merger show a company still far from commercial scale: Agility net sales and losses came to $1.78 million in 2025, up from $310,000 in 2024, against an operating loss of $140.2 million that roughly doubled year over year, and an auditor’s note flagging “substantial doubt” about its ability to continue as a going concern absent further financing.

That financial picture is the backdrop against which the hardware claims should be read; it doesn’t make them false. A company preparing to go public via SPAC has a direct financial incentive to publish its most favorable operating math right before that listing, and the $300 million order figure and 20-hour productivity claim are doing real work in that narrative, alongside more grounded facts, like Amazon’s $1.05 million purchase of five Digit units — a completed transaction, not a pipeline projection.

What 2027 actually promises customers

Agility says early customer access to Digit 5 is expected to begin in the first half of 2027, with general availability, aimed at manufacturing, warehouse and distribution operators, following by the end of that year. The company also plans to extend sales into the European Union and United Kingdom alongside its existing North American base, pending regulatory approval in those markets. Those dates put Digit 5’s actual commercial debut several months out from this week’s unveiling, and every performance figure attached to the robot right now, from its 90-minute runtime to its 20-hour workday, is a specification and a projection. Still, this has not yet been measured on a customer floor.

]]> At 19, an Estonian borrowed €5,000 from his family and recruited Tallinn taxi drivers face-to-face for an app he had built because the city’s taxis were unreliable; twelve years later the company took €2.27 billion in revenue in more than 50 countries and posted its first annual profit — €920,000, a margin of four hundredths of one percent https://siliconcanals.com/n-at-19-an-estonian-borrowed-e5000-from-his-family-and-recruited-tallinn-taxi-drivers-face-to-face-for-an-app-he-had-built-because-the-citys-taxis-were-unreliable-twelve-years-later-the-company-took/ Mon, 21 Sep 2026 14:00:26 +0000 https://siliconcanals.com/?p=109712

An Estonian founder’s company posted its first annual net profit in 2025: €920,000 on €2.27 billion in revenue.]]>

Markus Villig was 19 in 2013, fresh out of high school in Tallinn, and frustrated with how hard it was to get a reliable taxi in his own city. He borrowed €5,000 from his family to build a first version of an app, then did the unglamorous part himself: walking up to taxi drivers on the street in Tallinn and persuading them, one at a time, to sign up. The company launched as Taxify and rebranded as Bolt in March 2019, taking the name from the electric scooter service it had just launched, a signal, as the company put it at the time, that it saw the future of urban transport as electric and intended to be far more than a taxi app. Existing users didn’t have to do anything; the new name and logo simply appeared the next time they opened the app.

From a taxi app to a five-line business

What Bolt actually is today looks very different from what Villig built in 2013. Ride-hailing still accounts for the large majority of its revenue, 82 percent in 2024, according to figures reported in public company profiles of Bolt, but the company has spent the years since methodically bolting on new verticals, largely by copying its own playbook of arriving in a category cheaper and faster than the incumbent. Bolt Food launched in Tallinn in August 2019 and now operates in more than 80 cities across 20 countries with over 30,000 partner restaurants. Micromobility came earlier, e-scooters in Paris from September 2018 and e-bikes from mid-2020, and by early 2023 had grown into roughly 250,000 shared vehicles across 260 cities in 25 countries. Bolt Drive, a car-sharing service, launched in Tallinn in May 2021 and has since spread to Latvia, Lithuania, Germany, Poland, Czechia and Portugal. Bolt Market, a grocery-delivery arm launched the same year, has partnered with the robotics company Starship Technologies on autonomous sidewalk delivery in parts of the Baltics.

A decade of growth without a profit

None of that expansion was cheap, and for most of Bolt’s history it wasn’t profitable either. The company pushed early and aggressively into markets Uber had mostly ignored or arrived in late, establishing itself in South Africa, Kenya and Nigeria as early as 2016, and it now operates in more than 850 cities across over 50 countries spanning Europe, Africa, Asia and Latin America, with more recent entries into Dubai (December 2024) and the Toronto area (February 2025).

Investors funded that land grab at increasing valuations: Bolt crossed $1 billion, and unicorn status, in May 2018 after a $175 million round led by Daimler, according to TechCrunch’s coverage, then climbed to $2 billion by March 2021, $4.75 billion five months later, and $8.4 billion by January 2022.

Revenue kept climbing through all of it. Profit didn’t.

As recently as 2024, the company’s operating loss was €87.7 million even as revenue grew, a pattern common among ride-hailing and delivery platforms still spending to win market share rather than to defend one already won.

Who was willing to fund a decade of losses

Villig’s own €5,000 loan covered exactly one prototype. Everything after that came from investors willing to bet that Bolt’s low-cost, fast-mover approach would eventually outlast better-funded rivals in the markets it entered. The largest of those rounds closed in January 2022: $709 million, co-led by Sequoia Capital and Fidelity Management and Research, with Whale Rock, D1, G Squared and several other funds also participating, valuing the company at $8.4 billion, according to TechCrunch’s coverage of the round.

Bolt said at the time the money would go toward opening more of the small, city-centre “dark stores” that supply its 15-minute grocery delivery service, and toward pushing further into new geographic markets, the same expansion strategy that had defined the company since Villig first stood on a Tallinn street corner recruiting drivers by hand. That January 2022 round is the most recent outside capital the company has raised at scale; the 2025 results suggest it hasn’t needed another one since.

The first profit, and how thin it was

That changed with the 2025 financial year. According to Bolt’s own results, reported in coverage from Trade with Estonia, the company took €2.27 billion in revenue across more than 50 countries, a 14 percent increase on the year before, and posted its first-ever annual net profit: €920,000. Set against €2.27 billion in revenue, that works out to a margin of roughly four hundredths of one percent, the kind of number that is technically profitable and not much more. This density didn’t happen by accident, and it didn’t start with a startup. In 1996, five years after regaining independence from the Soviet Union, Estonia launched a state programme called Tiigrihüpe, or Tiger Leap, championed by future president Toomas Hendrik Ilves and education minister Jaak Aaviksoo. The rollout was rapid but not instantaneous. Education Estonia says all schools had computers by 2000 and all were connected to the internet by 2001. It wasn’t only talent that recirculated. Toivo Annus, one of Skype’s founding engineers who led its engineering team until the eBay sale, went on to co-found Ambient Sound Investments with three other early Skype engineers in 2003, a private investment firm that has since backed more than 50 early-stage ventures, according to documented accounts of his career. The ecosystem underneath those ten companies is larger and more active than the unicorn count alone suggests. For a country with fewer people than a mid-sized American county, that is the more durable claim.

An hour disappears into the phone and the honest inventory afterwards runs to three items: a man cutting marble, somebody’s strong opinion about interest rates, a dog on a skateboard.

None of it is retained in any way worth having. The hour still lands like work.

That mismatch, between the feeling of effort and the absence of anything learned, has a reasonable research explanation behind it, and willpower barely features in it.

A feed is a run of cold starts

Reading a book is one long continuous job. The brain loads a setting, a cast, an argument, and then keeps using that same setup for as long as the reading lasts.

A feed offers nothing of the kind.

Each post arrives with its own subject, tone, format and rules, which means the machinery of attention has to reconfigure itself before any of the content can be processed.

A feed adds another recurring job: a verdict. Each item has to be sized up for whether it is true, whether it is funny, whether it is aimed at anyone in particular. That call gets made before the thing can be dismissed, and then made again at the next one, and the one after that.

Psychologists have taken that reconfiguration apart. In a paper published in the Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance, Joshua Rubinstein, David Meyer and Jeffrey Evans described two stages: goal shifting, meaning the decision to do this now instead of that, and rule activation, meaning the swap of mental instructions from the old job to the new one. Both stages take time. A single switch might cost only a few tenths of a second. That sounds trivial until you count the switches inside an hour of scrolling.

Their experiments used arithmetic and shape-sorting rather than phones, so applying the finding to a feed is an inference, not a measurement.

The part that stays behind

Switching also leaves something on the floor. Sophie Leroy, now a professor at the University of Washington Bothell, coined the term attention residue in a 2009 paper in Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, after experiments in which people were pulled off one task and pushed onto another. Performance on the second task dropped, because a slice of their attention was still parked on the first, and the effect was sharpest when the first task had been left unfinished.

Scrolling has the shape of that setup. Post after post is dropped mid-thought and replaced by the next one, which looks a great deal like the unfinished condition Leroy identified as the costly one. Her participants were working through lab tasks, though. The parallel to a phone is drawn by analogy, and nobody has run the experiment there.

Forty-seven seconds

Gloria Mark, a professor of informatics at the University of California, Irvine, has been logging how long people stay on a single screen since 2004. Back then the average was about two and a half minutes. In an interview with the University of California, she put the recent figure at roughly 47 seconds, with a median of 40, meaning half of all observed stretches were shorter than that.

That number needs handling with care. It is assembled from separate studies across two decades, not one group of people followed the whole way, and what it measures is screen behaviour. People still read long books. They just do it somewhere other than a browser tab.

Why a book behaves differently

Does the medium itself change how much gets understood? Pablo Delgado of the University of Valencia and three co-authors pooled 54 studies covering more than 171,000 participants in a meta-analysis for Educational Research Review, and found a consistent, modest advantage for paper. The gap widened when reading was timed instead of self-paced, held for informational texts but not narrative ones, and grew across the years studied, an unhelpful trend for anyone expecting digital natives to close it.

Pooling dozens of experiments makes that result sturdier than any single study, though the effect itself stays small.

Maryanne Wolf, who studies the reading brain at UCLA, argues in an op-ed for the Guardian that skimming squeezes out the slower processes that make reading useful: drawing inferences, making analogies, testing whether a claim is true, stepping into another person’s point of view. Move the eye fast enough and there is no room left for any of it.

Fatigue needs its own explanation, and it comes from a separate strand of Mark’s research.

In a study presented at the 2008 CHI conference, Mark, working with Daniela Gudith and Ulrich Klocke, interrupted people mid-task and measured what happened. The interrupted group finished faster, with no drop in quality, which was the surprise. They also reported more stress, more frustration, more time pressure and more effort.

Compensation, in other words.

The brain appears to cover the cost of fragmentation by spending harder. Mark’s participants were working rather than scrolling, and the equivalent test has not been run on a feed, so the link is suggestive rather than established. Even so, the flatness and irritability at the end of a long scroll, the vague sense of having been mugged, match what those participants described.

Which puts the whole exercise in a different light. An hour on a feed involves several hundred small decisions made at speed, each one demanding a quick ruling on what the thing is and whether it matters. The content was the least of it. The deciding was the job.

Nobody sends an invoice for that. The tiredness is the receipt.

A pair of speakers, two years old, is up for sale online. When no music is playing, they give off an annoying static noise, and the listing does not say so.

A buyer’s message ends with a pointed question: “The speakers don’t have any problems, do they?” In one of the experiments built around that exact question, 85 percent of sellers mentioned the noise, and fewer buyers than that expected their seller to mention a problem.

Buyers, they found, often underestimated how honest sellers would be. Sellers also reported more concern with being honest, fair and kind, and less concern with the money, than buyers credited them with.

How often did sellers come clean?

In each of the five main studies, some participants played sellers of a secondhand device with a defect they had been told about: an iPod whose battery drained fast, an electric scooter with a faulty battery, the speakers with the static. The rest played buyers, who could earn bonuses for accurately predicting how honest sellers would be.

In the first four studies, a seller counted as honest only if a reply named the defect. Staying quiet counted as dishonest, and so did a dodge like a battery that “isn’t brand new.”

The first pilot set the pattern. Of 76 online workers playing sellers, 63.2 percent picked a truthful opening message over one describing the iPod as being in excellent condition. Of 85 observers given the same information, 43.5 percent predicted the truthful one.

In Study 1, the 176 sellers wrote their own replies to “What can you tell me about it?” and “Anything else?” Of those sellers, 51.7 percent disclosed the battery problem, while the 270 buyers guessed, on average, that 43.2 percent would. With the scooter and a direct question in Study 2, three quarters of sellers disclosed the fault.

The rate swung with the setup. One cause, a direct question, got its own test; other swings the researchers could not fully explain. Until the last study, the exchanges were also largely scripted, with sellers answering pre-written buyer messages rather than a live counterpart.

Study 3, with 483 participants, gave half the sellers the pointed “The speakers don’t have any problems, do they?” and half the open “What can you tell me about them?” Buyers here were not told about the static, which is closer to how a real listing works.

The direct question made sellers more likely to mention the noise. Buyers’ predictions did not move with it.

The gap between expected and actual honesty was statistically significant under the direct question and not under the open one, so even inside this paper it did not show up everywhere. Of several possible reasons Study 1 still found a gap with open questions, the authors single out one: sellers there had two chances to come clean, and concealing twice may weigh more on a seller’s conscience than concealing once.

Study 5 was the only one that paired people live. It matched 422 participants into 211 buyer-seller pairs on an online platform, and some pairs first spent three minutes chatting about something they had enjoyed recently or how they unwind after a busy day.

The sellers still cared about the money. They cared about it less, and about their own decency more, than the buyers pictured.

A seller holds the object and the information, so, the authors argue, a buyer casts them as a doer, and the competitive setting makes that doer look like someone chasing an advantage rather than guarding a clean conscience. Ongoing work relationships and repeat customers sit outside what was measured.

A buyer facing a salesperson expected to use persuasion tactics, or shopping where one side knows far more than the other, as with used cars, has good reason for care. This paper did not measure what the gap costs. The authors’ illustration is a used car that looks too good to be true, and a buyer who distrusts the seller, walks away, and settles for something worse. Every restaurant service contains a half-second that gives the whole game away. A plate lands. The customer looks up at whoever carried it and says thanks, or looks straight through them and carries on talking.

Nobody is scoring it. Nobody remembers it an hour later. And yet the reflex tends to have a long history behind it, much of it laid down years earlier by an adult asking one small, maddening question at exactly the wrong moment.

The magic word was never magic

Spend an afternoon near a toddler and the routine is unmissable. Someone offers a biscuit, the kid grabs it and turns to leave, and a parent says: what do you say?

Linguists have sat down and measured this. A 1980 study in the journal Language in Society watched 22 children and their parents at play, then sent an assistant in with a gift. Unprompted, the children rarely produced these little courtesies, and thank you was the scarcest of the three. What did happen was prompting. Parents nudged, the children almost always complied, and they parroted the adult’s phrasing exactly.

One detail is easy to skip past. Parents used the routines themselves, in front of the child. Mothers more than fathers. The study measured that behaviour without testing its effects, but it is hard to watch a parent thank a stranger a thousand times and come away with nothing.

So that reflexive thanks nobody thinks about? This is one place it can begin. Hundreds of tiny repetitions, every one long forgotten, are the sort of thing that builds a habit able to fire before conscious thought does.

This is where the usual class assumptions wobble. A 1986 study of 250 preschoolers tested what children did with no parent in the room. Around 37 per cent said thank you spontaneously when handed a reward. Children from low-income families did so more often than those from middle-income families.
