Amazon Web Services (AWS) today launched an open-source Physical AI Toolchain designed to help roboticists move from collecting data to training, simulating, validating and deploying AI models on their robots.

The toolchain brings together AWS services and NVIDIA’s Physical AI software stack into a single development workflow. The goal is to address one of the biggest challenges facing companies developing AI-powered robots: connecting the many pieces required to turn a trained model into a system that can reliably operate in the real world.

“We’re trying to make this easy button, if you will, so that people can actually focus on the problem that they’re trying to solve rather than having to worry about all of the infrastructure,” Sri Elaprolu, director of Frontier AI Science and Engineering at AWS, told The Robot Report.

The Physical AI Toolchain is not a direct replacement for RoboMaker, a  cloud-based robotics simulation platform that was shut down in 2025. Elaprolu described RoboMaker as one of the components of AWS’s robotics stack, while the new toolchain brings together a broader set of development technologies.

From data to deployment

The toolchain combines five pieces of the AI development process: synthetic data generation, model training, simulation and validation, edge deployment, and continuous improvement. A robotics company could collect demonstrations of a robot performing a task, generate additional training scenarios synthetically, train or fine-tune a model, and test that model in simulation before deploying it to a physical robot.

AWS uses Amazon SageMaker for model training and AWS IoT Greengrass for distributing models to edge devices. NVIDIA’s contributions include Isaac Sim, Isaac Lab, Isaac GR00T and Cosmos. Companies can use the components individually or combine them into an end-to-end workflow.

“The amount of data that you need to train these models is significant, and there’s not a lot of data that’s available, unlike LLMs where there’s a ton of data on the internet,” Elaprolu said. “So how do you generate that data? How do you generate synthetic data that is representative of the real world? That’s one of the things that we’re trying to solve.”

Synthetic data can help companies generate additional scenarios, while simulation lets developers test models before deploying them to physical hardware. The toolchain supports a feedback loop in which data collected by robots in the field is returned to the cloud and used to improve models.

“As you start scaling out these robotic deployments, the learnings that get captured locally need to be flown back into the cloud,” Elaprolu said. “So you continually iterate the brain.”

Register now and help us celebrate 20 years of RoboBusiness!

Lessons from Amazon’s robots

Elaprolu said the toolchain includes lessons from Amazon’s own robotics operations, which now include more than 1 million robots. But Amazon’s controlled fulfillment centers don’t represent every environment where Physical AI will operate.

Elaprolu pointed to Japanese robotics company Telexistence, which is deploying humanoids in convenience stores. More than 300 have been deployed, he said, with more expected. Unlike a controlled factory, a convenience store introduces more variables and requires robots to respond quickly to changing conditions.

“The fault tolerance levels tend to be much lower, but at the same time, the response rates have to be much higher,” Elaprolu said.

AWS is keeping the toolchain hardware-neutral. Rather than prescribing a particular robot, it provides infrastructure for training and deploying models across different machines.

“There’s going to be a wide range of hardware designs and components that are being built and will be built in the future,” Elaprolu said. “The toolchain is intentionally staying neutral to that final step.”

Vulcan is Amazon’s first robot with a sense of touch, using sensors to pick and stow items at a fulfillment center. | Credit: Amazon

Tactile sensing and construction

Elaprolu also pointed to tactile sensing as an example of the specialized capabilities Physical AI may require. AWS has worked with RLWRLD, a South Korean company developing tactile capabilities for humanoid hands. Elaprolu said existing models weren’t sufficiently capable for certain five-finger dexterity tasks, leading AWS and the company to develop a specialized model.

Amazon’s Vulcan robot provides another example. The system uses tactile sensing to help manipulate and stow items in Amazon’s fulfillment centers. The Robot Report recently named Amazon’s Vulcan Robot the 2026 Robot of the Year.

The Toolchain isn’t a tactile-sensing platform, but its support for different data sources, model training, simulation and edge deployment could allow developers to incorporate specialized sensing into their systems.

AWS also sees applications beyond warehouses and factories. Elaprolu pointed to Bedrock Robotics, which has developed hardware and AI models for autonomous construction robots. The models are trained in the cloud on AWS and then used to operate equipment in real construction zones.

An open-source approach

The Physical AI Toolchain is open source, allowing startups and larger companies to use and modify it.

Elaprolu said the individual AWS and NVIDIA components have already been used by customers, including companies participating in AWS’s Physical AI Fellowship with MassRobotics and NVIDIA. The new offering packages those components into a more cohesive workflow.

“It’s the packaging them up and making that seamless for a company that’s going to take forward,” he said.

Global energy company Schneider Electric this week said it will acquire industrial design, engineering, and data management firm PTC Inc. for about $22.6 billion. The Boston-based companies claimed that the combination will bridge the “digital and physical worlds across the lifecycle, from design and build to operate and maintain.”

Schneider Electric said it will be better able to serve industry with digitalization and AI, combining its operational expertise with PTC’s design and data intelligence. The company said a “digital thread” will provide CAD-to-shop floor continuity, accelerate robot testing in simulation, enhance regulatory compliance, and facilitate maintenance.

“By connecting and contextualizing data across the lifecycle of products and assets, we will create a unique digital thread for the next generation of industrial AI, helping customers to optimize their systems with greater intelligence, from design and build to operate and maintain,” stated Olivier Blum, CEO of Schneider Electric.

“We gain substantial scale and resources to accelerate innovation, advance our Intelligent Product Lifecycle vision, and expand our business into more geographies and end markets to serve more customers,” added Neil Barua, president and CEO of PTC.

Acquisitions could help Schneider compete with Siemens

The PTC deal could help Schneider Electric compete with Siemens and other global leaders in industrial automation and software in sectors such as aerospace and defense, noted Matthieu Kulezak, a senior analyst at Interact Analysis.

“PTC would extend Schneider’s reach from factory operations and energy management into product design and lifecycle management,” he told The Robot Report. “Together with AVEVA and the proposed Cognite acquisition, it could connect engineering decisions with how products are manufactured, operated and maintained.”

PTC Onshape gives Schneider access to robotics developers and machine-building teams, while PTC‘s Codebeamer supports requirements, testing, and traceability for increasingly complex software-driven products, Kulezak added. “The opportunity is to build relationships earlier, before these customers select automation equipment,” he observed.

Siemens has a lead in simulation capabilities, according to Interact Analysis. PTC may narrow Schneider’s portfolio gap, but it must successfully integrate the technologies of recent acquisitions first.

“Schneider must absorb thousands of employees while aligning product roadmaps, sales incentives, and data architectures,” said Kulezak. “AVEVA’s experience within the group should help, but Schneider will also need to manage adjacent capabilities across AVEVA and Cognite without slowing innovation.”

PTC gives Schneider Electric a shortcut from industrial operations into product engineering, strengthening its challenge to Siemens and Dassault Systèmes. Source: Interact Analysis

Where PTC could deliver

PTC‘s ServiceMax platform for field service could deliver the earliest commercial gains, suggested Kulezak. The connection of product configurations, service histories, and operational data could support maintenance contracts, spare parts, and equipment upgrades. This could produce returns sooner than full integration from engineering to operations, he said.

“Rockwell adds an interesting competitive angle – the company invested $1 billion for approximately 8.4% of PTC in 2018, but sold all its shares by September 2023,” said Kulezak. “Its exit arguably left the door more open to another industrial buyer, although there is no evidence it directly enabled Schneider’s deal. Much of the original partnership centered on [industrial Internet of Things platform] ThingWorx and [IT/OT software] Kepware, which PTC subsequently sold to TPG.”

He cited the stock market reaction as a reflection of both the price and execution risk. Schneider Electric’s shares fell sharply following its announcement.

“The 42.3% premium, substantial financing requirements, and reliance on future synergies likely contributed to investor concerns,” added Kulezak. “In my view, the long-term strategic logic remains compelling; the question is whether Schneider can deliver enough commercial value to justify the price.”

Teradyne claimed that Elite Robots’ cobots (above) and software were similar to its own. Credit: Elite Robots

Teradyne Robotics and Elite Robots have reached a mutual agreement resolving a legal dispute over robots and software, bringing the case to an end without either company disclosing the terms of the settlement.

Teradyne Robotics, a subsidiary of Teradyne Inc. and parent company of Universal Robots A/S, announced the settlement on Oct. 1. The resolution aims to bring the dispute between the parties to a close and reflects their shared interest in avoiding the continued time and cost associated with legal proceedings.

Teradyne is the world’s leading developer of collaborative robot arms, having sold more than 100,000 robots since it was founded in 2005.

In a joint statement, Jette Withers, Teradyne Robotics’ chief legal officer, and Charles Xie, Elite Robots’ overseas sales director, said: “The parties have resolved their pending legal dispute by mutual agreement. The settlement does not constitute an admission by Elite Robots regarding liability, infringement, validity of intellectual property rights, or any other disputed issue.”

Neither company has said what the settlement requires of either side, and there is no public evidence of what Elite Robots agreed to do.

An intellectual property lawyer familiar with this type of litigation, who asked not to be identified and is not involved with the case, told The Robot Report that disputes that begin with an early injunction often end early. The general pattern is that the defendant agrees to stop using the disputed code and pays a fee, but that does not necessarily describe this case.

Inside the dispute

Teradyne Robotics sued Elite Robots Deutschland GmbH earlier this year, alleging copyright infringement involving Universal Robots software. Teradyne announced in April that the Regional Court of Hamburg had issued a preliminary injunction against Elite Robots Deutschland. The injunction restricted the company in connection with the allegedly infringing software and products containing it in Germany.

The preliminary injunction was not a final finding of infringement. Elite Robots also did not admit liability as part of the settlement. The companies ultimately agreed to resolve the dispute rather than continue the litigation.

Neither side has publicly disclosed the terms of that agreement. The lack of details makes it impossible to determine whether the settlement involved a financial payment or changes to Elite Robots’ software or products, licensing rights, or other conditions.

Universal Robots launches Gen 7

The Gen 7 platform is designed to enhances the cobot user experience, says UR. | Source: Universal Robots

The settlement comes shortly after Universal Robots unveiled its seventh-generation force- and power-limited platform. The Odense, Denmark-based company said the new system represents a broader redesign of its technologies, including new g-Series robot arms, the CB7 Core controller, the TP7 Core teach pendant, and the SP7 Smart Panel.

Gen 7 is built around PolyScope X, which Universal Robots described as the software platform for its new generation of robots. PolyScope X includes open APIs and an SDK designed to support AI applications, along with expanded connectivity and programming capabilities.

The Gen 7 launch is notable given the Teradyne-Elite Robots dispute involved Universal Robots software.

The Elite Robots dispute is not the only recent lawsuit involving Teradyne Robotics. In August, it filed a separate case that alleged Chinese cobot maker JAKA Robotics’ Germany subsidiary infringed on three patents. All three patents have a March 2006 priority date and are assigned to Universal Robots. That case remains ongoing.

Editor’s note: James Davidson, chief AI officer at Teradyne Robotics, will speak at RoboBusiness 2026. The event takes place Oct. 20 and 21 in Santa Clara, Calif., and attract 1,500+ attendees from the robotics development community.

]]> Crypto can mean very different things to a startup. For one company, it could make international payments easier. For another, it might become part of a new financial product. And for plenty of businesses, it could simply be something they have no real need for.

Watching the Bitcoin price gives founders a sense of what is happening in the market, but it does not tell them whether crypto belongs in their own business.

Bitcoin crossed €74,222 ($85,000) on September 22 after ETF inflows hit €539.9 million ($617.6 million) in the previous session, according to Reuters reporting published by The Economic Times. That kind of movement is hard to ignore. It is also not necessarily the information a founder needs when deciding whether to adopt digital assets.

The better question is much more practical: where, if anywhere, could crypto make running a startup easier?

Why are startups exploring crypto?

Part of the interest comes down to how blockchain networks operate. They can run continuously, and digital assets can move between countries without following exactly the same route as a conventional bank payment.

For a young company working internationally, that can be interesting. A customer could be based in one country, contractors in another and suppliers somewhere else. Add different currencies and banking systems to the mix, and moving money can become even more complex.

Crypto is also becoming less separate from the financial system around it. Binance Research’s September 2026 Macro and Market Insights report found that equity holders’ share of crypto exposure rose from 64% to 72%. That suggests traditional market participants are playing a larger role in digital assets, too.

Where might it actually help?

There’s no standard crypto package that makes sense for every startup. A fintech business could have a clear use case, while a small software company selling locally might struggle to find one.

International payments are one possibility. A business dealing with customers or suppliers overseas could use digital assets as an additional way to move money. There are other options. A company could accept crypto payments from customers, build a product around tokenised assets or use existing blockchain networks as the infrastructure behind a financial service.

Smart contracts could also automate certain transactions where the conditions are straightforward.

Where does it get complicated?

The obvious concern is volatility. A company holding digital assets has to account for changes in their value. Even when crypto is only being accepted as payment, someone still has to decide how it will be stored, converted and recorded. And then there are the rules.

A startup operating across several countries can’t necessarily assume that the same approach will work everywhere. Digital assets, payments and taxation can all bring different requirements depending on the market.

Security is another practical issue. Blockchain transactions can be hard to undo, so losing control of a wallet or exposing private keys is not something a business can afford to treat casually. But there is an even more basic question worth asking: why use crypto in the first place?

If a startup already has a payment system that works and its customers are happy with it, adding crypto could simply create another thing to manage. There is little point taking on extra cost and complexity for the sake of having a new technology on the website.

Which startups might have a reason to try it?

Fintech startups are the clearest fit. Businesses working with payments, financial products or digital assets can use blockchain infrastructure as part of what they already do.

Other startups have more specific opportunities. An international marketplace could accept crypto payments. A gaming company could use blockchain for digital ownership. A creator platform could build services around digital assets.

Stablecoins are another option for businesses that want to accept crypto payments without holding large amounts of more volatile assets.

The key is having a clear use case. Startups don’t need to adopt crypto across the business. They can test one application and see whether it delivers a practical benefit.

What should a founder work out first?

Before adding a digital-asset feature, it is worth getting back to the basics. Ask what the technology is supposed to improve. Find out whether customers actually want the feature. Check the rules in every market involved. Decide who will handle security and custody.

Think about what happens if an asset’s value moves sharply. And, perhaps most importantly, work out whether the new system can slot into the tools the business already relies on.

Those answers will vary from startup to startup. There is no reason for a company with no obvious crypto use case to force one into its operations.

Crypto does not have to be the whole story

The growing overlap between crypto and traditional finance gives startups more choices, but choice doesn’t mean obligation.

For some founders, digital assets could solve a genuine problem or open up a service that would otherwise be difficult to build. For others, conventional financial infrastructure will remain the simpler route.

That’s probably the healthiest way to look at crypto in the startup world. It is a tool to consider, not a strategy in itself. If it makes something work better, there is a reason to explore it. If it does not, there is no need to force it.

The post Could crypto give startups an edge? (Sponsored) appeared first on EU-Startups.

]]> Cambridge-based Undecimal Bio, a spin-out from Eleven Therapeutics advancing targeted delivery of siRNA therapeutics, today announced a €16 million ($18 million) Seed financing round to expand DELiveri, its proprietary AI-enabled platform for identifying conjugates that can direct RNA medicines to defined cell types.

The round was co-led by 4BIO Capital and IQ Capital, with participation from Verve Ventures, Harel Tech, Entree Capital, Kerna Ventures and Saras Capital. The funding will also be used to progress Undecimal’s renovascular programmes and enable expansion of the team at their laboratories based at the Cancer Research UK Cambridge Institute.

“The hard problem in RNAi was never the silencing, it was getting the molecule to the right cell,” says Dr. Yaniv Erlich, CEO and co-founder of Undecimal Bio. “Our in-vivo validated DELiveri platform can screen large chemical spaces at an unprecedented pace, generating massive data for our legions of AI agents to decipher the structure-activity relationship and score the best candidates. We are excited to bring these advances to develop the next generation of siRNA therapeutics for the benefit of patients.”

Undecimal Bio’s Seed financing comes amid a series of European investments in RNA-based therapeutics, targeted drug delivery and AI-enabled biotechnology platforms in 2026.

Related announcements include Dublin-based Aerska‘s €32 million Series A to advance RNA interference medicines targeting neurological diseases, Paris-based WhiteLab Genomics‘ €23.2 million Series B for AI-driven genomic medicine design and delivery, and Cambridge-based STORM Therapeutics‘ €47.5 million Series C to progress RNA-modifying cancer treatments.

In the UK, Thalia Therapeutics also secured €3.1 million to develop its RNA therapeutics portfolio, while London-based Helical raised €8.4 million for its AI-powered pharmaceutical R&D platform.

Alongside additional investments in Spain’s Gate2Brain, Belgium’s Sightera Biosciences and the UK’s Houdini Bio, these announcements represent approximately €125.9 million in 2026 funding, rising to €141.9 million including Undecimal’s round.

Founded in 2026, Undecimal pairs massive scale combinatorial chemistry with transformer-based AI to guide siRNA therapeutics into the tissues that need them.

According to the company, RNA interference has transformed the treatment of liver-expressed diseases, but reaching tissues beyond the liver remains a key obstacle limiting the broader potential of the modality. DELiveri addresses this challenge as a technology that screens massive-scale combinatorial libraries of candidate ligands, converting cells to act as molecular radars that detect productive delivery at single molecule resolution.

This high throughput data is analysed by agentic AI to decode the resulting structure-activity data and identify conjugates capable of carrying siRNA into target cells.

Undecimal is initially applying the DELiveri platform in renovascular diseases, which pose significant unmet clinical need. Existing treatments of these indications largely address symptoms rather than the underlying etiological factors.

Th company believes that targeted siRNA delivery holds the potential to bring the digital-like precision of genetic medicines, enabling durable, target-specific silencing of the disease-driving pathways.

The Board of Directors comprises representatives of 4BIO Capital, IQ Capital and Harel Technologies, together with co-founders Dr. Yaniv Erlich and Shaul Ilan. Alongside the financing, Verve Ventures joins the Board as an observer.

]]> AI is steadily being integrated further into the systems and workflows that run many European businesses. What was once a tool for analysing information and assisting employees with basic administrative tasks, is now an integral part of how many of these businesses operate. 

The problem with Europe’s growing dependence on AI, is that much of the technology they are dependent upon comes from elsewhere. 

The companies producing the most sophisticated AI models and supporting infrastructure are concentrated heavily in the US and China, giving them huge influence over the technology that is becoming so important to the global economy. That influence is becoming more significant as these nations continue to develop competing AI ecosystems, with their rivalry increasingly tied to their wider geopolitical interests. 

Recent reports suggest that the US is preparing to tell dozens of countries to choose between rival US and China-led AI ecosystems, and China last week called for countries to respect their “digital sovereignty”. AI sovereignty is no longer an abstract debate. We are watching AI divide along geopolitical lines in real time, and Europe is now at risk of becoming a customer of whichever superpower controls the intelligence it relies upon.

Europe needs choice, not complete self-sufficiency

The vulnerability this presents was arguably already demonstrated in June, when the US ordered Anthropic to restrict foreign nationals’ access to its most advanced AI models, prompting European concern about how reliant businesses and governments could become on American frontier AI. 

For Europe, the question is how much autonomy will it have to make its own decisions as this divide widens? 

Europe should be able to use the best models available, wherever they might be developed,  but it cannot build its economy on imported AI that might get cut off.  

This is not to say that Europe needs to be completely self-sufficient in AI, but it needs enough choice to switch suppliers and maintain viable alternatives. 

That choice becomes more important as AI continues to become embedded into the everyday running of businesses. 

In July, The European Commission launched a call for up to seven AI Gigafactories, backed by up to €10 billion in EU and national funding and intended to unlock at least €20 billion in private investment.

However, the question of sovereignty goes beyond the models themselves, it also extends to the knowledge businesses create through AI. 

Businesses risk renting back their own knowledge

Every time an employee uses AI, they are writing down how their work gets done, often for the first time. The companies that hold onto that knowledge can use it to fuel their AI transformation. But many risk handing it to their vendors, teaching them how to commoditise their businesses, and will end up renting back their own know-how.

The consequences of this extend beyond technology. AI will shape which companies become most productive and which industries adapt quickest. If European companies are importing these capabilities from foreign entities, the value created will likely flow outside of Europe, also. 

This creates a different type of dependency. A business might be able to switch model or supplier, but separating from a system that has spent years learning its processes and organisational knowledge is much more difficult. The longer a business spends building its operations around external AI providers, the harder it will be to separate themselves from it.

For startups and scale-ups, this is particularly important. Their advantage often lies in their specialist knowledge, their understanding of a problem and the distinctive way they carry out their work. If that knowledge becomes trapped within an external platform, they risk giving away part of what makes the business valuable.

This does not mean that European businesses need to stop using foreign AI. This is unrealistic, and also poses the threat of Europe falling further behind. 

Europe’s opportunity is applied AI

Europe’s opportunity instead lies in building on top of these models and turning them into systems that are designed around the needs of its own businesses.  This is where European businesses can build intellectual property and competitive advantage around AI, even if the technology is developed elsewhere.  

The opportunity is also in building the infrastructure that lets businesses use different models, without rebuilding their systems each time the market changes. This flexibility can help businesses avoid vendor dependency and maintain greater control over how they use AI.

This applied layer is where AI is connected to a company’s systems and put to work. It is also where businesses can govern what agents are allowed to do, monitor their actions, test their performance and investigate when something goes wrong. Europe may not lead every part of the race to build the largest model, but it can lead in making AI safe, accountable and useful for the companies deploying it.

Europe has a large industrial base, strong expertise across sectors, and businesses that understand their own processes better than any general-purpose model ever could.

Sovereignty means control and continuity: control over what AI agents can do, ownership of the workflows and knowledge they create, and the freedom to choose or change the underlying technology.

Europe has the talent, industry and trust to become a genuine power in AI, but that does not mean it has to be a distant third participant. 

It must be the counterbalance to this race: deploy its talent and expertise into the applied layer, and build systems that are safe, sovereign and equitable by design, for the benefit of everyone, not just those in Europe.

We need AI that works for us, not the other way around. Building a sovereign applied AI layer that can be deployed in good faith, creating productivity and lasting values for businesses across the globe, is Europe’s decisive opportunity in this race.

]]> From AI-powered diagnostics to technologies that help people live independently for longer, the Republic of Korea’s rapidly evolving healthcare system is creating new openings for European HealthTech startups.

The Republic of Korea combines a highly digitalised society and sophisticated healthcare system with one of the world’s fastest-ageing populations. By 2025, more than 20% of its population was aged 65 or over, making it a “super-aged” society.

At the same time, investment in AI, digital health and medical technologies is creating opportunities for European startups that can help manage chronic diseases, support independent living and reduce pressure on healthcare professionals. 

For European companies looking to explore these opportunities first-hand, the EU Business Hub – Japan and the Republic of Korea is currently recruiting up to 50 SMEs and startups for its EU Business Hub @ KIMES 2027 business mission to Seoul, taking place from 17 to 21 March 2027.

Selected companies will have the opportunity to showcase their solutions at KIMES 2027, meet potential Korean partners and customers, and receive tailored support to explore the market. Applications are open until 15 November 2026.

Here are five areas worth watching.

1. AI that solves real healthcare problems

The Republic of Korea’s strong digital infrastructure, advanced hospitals and expertise in artificial intelligence are creating opportunities for AI-enabled healthcare, from medical imaging and diagnostics to clinical decision support and workflow automation.

For European startups, however, simply adding AI to a product is unlikely to be enough. Hospitals need technologies that solve a specific clinical or operational problem and demonstrate measurable value.

Startup angle: Lead with the healthcare problem, not the algorithm. A clear explanation of how your technology improves outcomes, saves clinicians’ time or reduces costs is likely to be more compelling than an “AI-powered” label alone.

2. Remote care moves beyond the pandemic

The longer-term opportunity in telemedicine is the shift towards healthcare that can increasingly happen outside hospitals – particularly important for older people and patients living with chronic conditions.

This creates opportunities for remote patient monitoring, connected medical devices, digital therapeutics and platforms that help healthcare professionals follow patients between appointments. But the value proposition needs to go beyond collecting more data: it needs to help healthcare professionals make better decisions.

Startup angle: Show what happens after the measurement. Technologies that turn patient data into useful alerts, recommendations or clinical insights may have a stronger proposition than monitoring alone.

3. Healthy ageing becomes a technology market

As the population ages, demand is growing for technologies that help people remain healthier and independent for longer – from mobility and rehabilitation technologies to fall prevention, cognitive health, assistive technologies and digital tools for caregivers.

The strongest propositions may be those that address a very practical question: how can technology help an older person continue living safely and independently while reducing pressure on family members and care professionals?

Danish health-tech company Entertainment Robotics, which develops game-based technology for physical and cognitive training, joined EU Business Hub @ KIMES 2026 and connected with the Seoul Federation of the Korea Senior Citizens Association. The relationship developed into a strategic cooperation agreement aimed at expanding AI-enabled dementia prevention programmes across the country’s elderly welfare sector.

Startup angle: Think beyond the end user. In healthy ageing, the buyer may be a hospital, care provider, municipality, insurer or senior organisation rather than the older person themselves.

4. Smarter rehabilitation and assistive technologies

As populations age, healthcare systems need scalable ways to support recovery and maintain mobility. Advances in sensors, robotics, computer vision and AI are creating opportunities ranging from robotic and sensor-assisted rehabilitation to digital physiotherapy and movement analysis.

These solutions can augment the work of healthcare professionals, enable rehabilitation at home and provide clinicians with better information about patients’ progress. But clinical evidence and ease of integration remain critical.

Startup angle: Demonstrate how your solution fits into an existing care pathway. Saving clinicians’ time or enabling patients to continue treatment outside the clinic can be as important as the technology itself.

5. Connected healthcare needs better data

As healthcare becomes more digital, making different technologies and sources of health data work together is becoming increasingly important.

This creates opportunities for European startups working on healthcare interoperability, clinical data platforms, cybersecurity and tools that turn fragmented health data into actionable insights. Smaller companies do not need to replace an entire hospital IT infrastructure: solving one interoperability, security or workflow problem can provide a realistic entry point.

Startup angle: Integration can be a competitive advantage. If your solution can work with the systems hospitals already use rather than requiring them to rebuild their digital infrastructure, make that part of the pitch.

The opportunity is real – but market entry takes preparation

The Republic of Korea’s sophisticated healthcare market also sets a high bar for newcomers. European startups need to navigate regulatory requirements, clinical validation, reimbursement, data protection and localisation, while competing with established Korean and international players.

This makes the right local partner particularly important. A distributor, hospital or technology partner can provide access to customers as well as knowledge of regulation, procurement and purchasing decisions.

Neuroelectrics Barcelona joined two consecutive EU Business Hub healthcare missions to the Republic of Korea, establishing local distribution and reporting more than €50,000 in additional Korean revenue within a year of its first mission. According to the company, the programme shortened its market-access journey by more than a year.

From market opportunity to market entry

The upcoming EU Business Hub @ KIMES 2027 business mission will bring up to 50 European SMEs and startups to the Republic of Korea from 17 to 21 March 2027 to showcase their solutions at KIMES and explore opportunities across medical equipment, assistive technologies, digital health, remote monitoring, AI-enabled healthcare and regenerative medicine. 

Selected companies will receive market intelligence and business coaching, tailored B2B matchmaking, interpretation support and financial support towards accommodation.

For founders considering the Republic of Korea, this provides an opportunity to move beyond desk research: to see how the market responds to their technology, understand what Korean healthcare organisations are looking for and start building the relationships that can make market entry possible.

Applications for EU Business Hub @ KIMES 2027 are open until 15 November 2026!

“We know the problems of this industry firsthand, and we build reebuild together with our customers, extremely close to the day-to-day reality on site. The software many construction companies and developers still work with today has barely evolved in decades and has fallen behind rising expectations. We’re convinced that we can shake up this market with a team that combines deep construction and technology know-how. On its platform, delivery notes, invoices, and order confirmations are matched automatically, and the software progressively learns from the decisions of commercial managers, reducing repetitive administrative workload over time. On site, a foreman can photograph a delivery note with the mobile app and have it instantly embedded in the system.

With cost administration between departments still largely managed in spreadsheets and paper folders, invoices matched by hand, approvals lacking transparency and early-payment discounts routinely unclaimed, reebuild wants to fix this gap with AI agents preparing work, flagging repetitive tasks and recommending next actions, while keeping human teams in charge of final approvals.

The company says its platform has processed more than €530 million in invoice volume across over 120 construction companies and property developers, spanning more than 8,200 construction sites and projects. It has automatically handled more than 345k documents, counts more than 2,350 active users across its customer base, and includes Pittel+Brausewetter, 3SI Immogroup, Rödl & Herdegen, and Kratzert Gruppe. It also reports that invoice handling time has been cut from over 20 minutes to approximately three minutes, while customers have indicated a reduction in procurement costs by up to 20%.

“We believe now is the time for construction companies to digitise and automate their back-office processes with SaaS and AI. reebuild is the right team to execute on this, with the founding team having their family roots in the construction sector,” said Wouter Goossens, Partner at Fortino Ventures.

The funding will be deployed across three areas: geographic expansion beyond reebuild’s established markets in Austria and Germany, the development of new AI-native modules that fully automate contractors’ workflows from calculation to accounting; and team growth at its Vienna headquarters, where the company currently employs around 25 people.

For reebuild, AI-native modules are the first step, but the company intends to become the agentic back office for the construction industry, where AI agents independently handle routine tasks such as invoicing, on-site documentation, and project estimation, covering a contractor’s entire commercial workflow from calculation to accounting.

]]> CarbonFarm, a Paris-based ClimateTech startup specialising in rice decarbonisation, has closed an oversubscribed €7 million Series A funding round.

The round was led by Colam Impact, the impact investment arm of Colam Entreprendre, the holding company for the French family-owned group Sonepar. The round also saw participation from Proparco, Suma Capital, elea, Working Capital Fund, Albo, and BPI France. Existing investors Serena & make sense (via Racine²) and Technmind also renewed their support for the company.

“CarbonFarm is building the enabling infrastructure for one of the largest untapped decarbonisation opportunities globally. We believe its combination of project-development expertise, climate-finance capabilities and digital MRV creates a uniquely scalable platform in the rice sector,” said Benjamine Friderich, Investment Director at Colam Impact.

Founded in 2021 by Vassily Carantino and James Hastwell, CarbonFarm partners with rice producers, cooperatives, agribusinesses, NGOs, governments, and local project developers to develop, finance, and measure high-integrity rice projects. The company has developed proprietary technology in collaboration with leading academic institutions, including Cornell University, INRAE, and the European Space Agency, that uses AI-powered satellite imagery analysis, field-data collection tools and greenhouse-gas modelling to track farming practices and quantify emissions at the field level.

It currently operates in 19 countries across Asia, Europe, Africa, and the Americas, and counts major food and agribusiness companies including Mars Food, Diageo, Ebro, and Tilda, among its partners. The company also lists carbon-finance players like Livelihoods Funds and myclimate, development organisations such as the World Bank and Asian Development Bank, and tech giants including Google, as partners.

CarbonFarm says rice cultivation accounts for roughly 12% of global human-caused methane emissions, giving the crop a greenhouse-gas footprint comparable to that of global aviation while consuming up to 28% of the world’s freshwater resources. With improved water management practices, such as allowing fields to drain periodically rather than remaining periodically flooded, CarbonFarm says rice producers can cut emissions by as much as 50% and reduce water use by up to 30%, without affecting yields.

“Scale will not come from replacing local value-chain players; it will come from equipping them. They understand the farming systems and have the relationships needed to make change happen. Our role is to help turn this local knowledge into programmes that can attract finance and stand up to scrutiny,” said Carantino, co-founder and CEO of CarbonFarm.

The fresh capital will be used by CarbonFarm to expand its presence across Asia, Africa, and Europe while accelerating its push into Latin America. The company will also invest in expanding the technology and expertise required to develop, finance, and certify high-integrity rice projects, and to connect those projects with corporate supply chains and regulated carbon markets.

The funding, CarbonFarm says, will enable it to make high-integrity rice decarbonisation viable at global scale.

]]> 29aea361935aecd30ce0373f24bf62f8 Thu, 08 Oct 2026 14:25:00 +0200 Solar Orbiter tracks origin of mysterious magnetic switchbacks

The European Space Agency-led Solar Orbiter spacecraft has flown through an S-shaped kink known as a ‘switchback’ in the solar wind’s magnetic field. By fingerprinting the elusive particles within the switchback, Solar Orbiter has traced its origin back to the Sun’s surface and revealed more about solar magnetism – the unruly instigator of dangerous solar storms.

Meet Hera, our very own asteroid detective. Together with two CubeSats – Milani the rock decoder and Juventas the radar visionary – Hera is off on an adventure to explore Didymos, a double asteroid system that is typical of the thousands that pose an impact risk to planet Earth.

After their two year cosmic roadtrip, Hera and its little CubeSat companions have finally arrived at Didymos and Dimorphos – the very first Solar System object to have had its orbit shifted by human action.  Suitable for kids and adults alike, this episode of ‘The Incredible Adventures of the Hera mission’ explains what ESA’s asteroid detective and its CubeSat assistants will be up to once they arrive, and precisely how they are going to say goodbye to each other – letting the CubeSats begin their close-up exam of this historic space rock.

<!DOCTYPE html><html lang="en-US"><head><meta charset="UTF-8"><meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1"><link rel="pingback" href="https://www.studyineurope.eu/xmlrpc.php"> <style id="sie-lean-layout"> #sie-lean-main { margin: 0; }
 #sie-lean-main > *:first-child,
 #sie-lean-main .sie-field-page { margin-top: 0; }
 .et_builder_inner_content { width: 100%; }
 .et_pb_section { position: relative; }
 .et_pb_row { position: relative; width: 80%; max-width: 1080px; margin: 0 auto; }
 .et_pb_row_inner { width: 100%; }
 .et_pb_column { position: relative; } </style> <style id="sie-custom-header-inline">/* ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
 SIE Custom Header — v1.1.2
 Zero-CLS, no JavaScript layout shifts.
 No panoramic image — lean 64px nav bar only.
 backdrop-filter is intentionally NOT used on .sie-hdr__bar.
 Any element with backdrop-filter becomes a CSS containing block for
 position:fixed descendants, which would trap the user-ui mobile bottom bar
 (position:fixed; bottom:0) inside the header instead of the viewport.
 ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════ */
/* ── Root variables ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
:root {
 --sie-hdr-brand:       #0056b3;        /* SIE brand blue                      */
 --sie-hdr-brand-light: #1a6fc4;
 --sie-hdr-bar-h:       64px;           /* nav bar height — fixed, prevents CLS */
 --sie-hdr-bar-bg:      #0056b3;        /* solid — no backdrop-filter needed   */
 --sie-hdr-bar-border:  rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.15);
}
/* ── Wrapper ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr {
 width: 100%;
 display: block;
 min-height: var(--sie-hdr-bar-h);
 /* Own stacking context so dropdowns render above Divi page content */
 position: relative;
 z-index: 1000;
}
/* ── Navigation bar ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__bar {
 height: var(--sie-hdr-bar-h);
 background: var(--sie-hdr-bar-bg);
 /* NO backdrop-filter here — it would trap position:fixed children
 (user-ui mobile bottom bar) inside this element instead of viewport */
 border-bottom: 1px solid var(--sie-hdr-bar-border);
}
.sie-hdr__inner {
 max-width: 1280px;
 height: 100%;
 margin: 0 auto;
 padding: 0 24px;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 32px;
}
/* ── Logo ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__logo {
 flex-shrink: 0;
 text-decoration: none;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
}
.sie-hdr__logo-img {
 height: 54px;
 width: auto;
 display: block;
}
.sie-hdr__logo-text {
 font-family: -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, 'Segoe UI', Roboto, sans-serif;
 font-size: 17px;
 font-weight: 700;
 color: #fff;
 letter-spacing: -0.01em;
 white-space: nowrap;
}
/* ── Desktop navigation ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__nav {
 flex: 1;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
}
.sie-hdr__nav-list {
 list-style: none;
 margin: 0;
 padding: 0;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 4px;
}
.sie-hdr__nav-list li {
 position: relative;
}
.sie-hdr__nav-list a,
.sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle {
 display: inline-flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 4px;
 padding: 8px 14px;
 font-family: -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, 'Segoe UI', Roboto, sans-serif;
 font-size: 14px;
 font-weight: 500;
 color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.88);
 text-decoration: none;
 border-radius: 8px;
 transition: background 0.15s ease, color 0.15s ease;
 white-space: nowrap;
 min-height: 48px; /* WCAG touch target */
}
.sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle {
 background: none;
 border: none;
 cursor: pointer;
}
.sie-hdr__nav-list a:hover,
.sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle:hover,
.sie-hdr__has-dropdown:hover > .sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle {
 background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.12);
 color: #fff;
}
/* ── Resources dropdown ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__dropdown {
 display: none;
 position: absolute;
 top: calc(100% + 6px);
 left: 0;
 min-width: 240px;
 background: #fff;
 border-radius: 12px;
 box-shadow: 0 12px 40px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.18);
 padding: 8px 0;
 list-style: none;
 margin: 0;
 z-index: 9999;
}
/* CSS-only hover on desktop */
@media (hover: hover) {
 .sie-hdr__has-dropdown:hover > .sie-hdr__dropdown,
 .sie-hdr__has-dropdown:focus-within > .sie-hdr__dropdown {
 display: block;
 }
}
/* JS-toggled state (mobile / keyboard) */
.sie-hdr__has-dropdown.is-open > .sie-hdr__dropdown {
 display: block;
}
.sie-hdr__dropdown li {
 margin: 0;
 padding: 0;
}
.sie-hdr__dropdown a {
 display: block;
 padding: 10px 18px;
 font-size: 13.5px;
 color: #003B73;
 font-weight: 500;
 border-radius: 0;
 min-height: unset;
}
.sie-hdr__dropdown a:hover {
 background: #f0f7ff;
 color: #0b5394;
}
.sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle svg {
 transition: transform 0.2s ease;
}
.sie-hdr__has-dropdown.is-open .sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle svg,
.sie-hdr__has-dropdown:hover .sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle svg {
 transform: rotate(180deg);
}
/* ── Mobile hamburger ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__hamburger {
 display: none;
 flex-direction: column;
 justify-content: center;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 5px;
 width: 44px;
 height: 44px;
 background: none;
 border: none;
 cursor: pointer;
 padding: 0;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 margin-left: auto;
}
.sie-hdr__hamburger span {
 display: block;
 width: 22px;
 height: 2px;
 background: #fff;
 border-radius: 2px;
 transition: transform 0.25s ease, opacity 0.25s ease;
}
/* Animate to ✕ when open */
.sie-hdr__hamburger[aria-expanded="true"] span:nth-child(1) {
 transform: translateY(7px) rotate(45deg);
}
.sie-hdr__hamburger[aria-expanded="true"] span:nth-child(2) {
 opacity: 0;
}
.sie-hdr__hamburger[aria-expanded="true"] span:nth-child(3) {
 transform: translateY(-7px) rotate(-45deg);
}
/* ── User-UI icon bar integration ────────────────────────────────────────────
 user-ui.php's desktop bar uses position:absolute; top:20px; right:30px — that
 was designed for Divi's header context. Inside our flex .sie-hdr__inner we
 need it as a normal flex child instead.
 Fixed-position children (auth drawer, mobile bar, destinations panel) are
 unaffected — position:fixed is always viewport-relative provided no ancestor
 has backdrop-filter, transform, or perspective (we intentionally avoid all
 three on .sie-hdr__bar).
 ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr .se-user-menu-wrapper {
 position: static !important;
 top: auto !important;
 right: auto !important;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 margin-left: auto;
}
/* Align our mobile breakpoint (860px) with user-ui's desktop/mobile split */
@media (min-width: 861px) {
 .sie-hdr .se-user-menu-wrapper {
 display: flex !important;
 }
}
@media (max-width: 860px) {
 .sie-hdr .se-user-menu-wrapper {
 display: none !important;
 }
}
/* Leonardo icon in the nav bar.
 user-ui's default .se-ai-icon is 86×86 px (fine for the mobile bottom bar),
 but that overflows our 64px-tall nav bar. Override to a crisp 36px square —
 the webp source is already high-res so it stays sharp at 2× on retina. */
.sie-hdr .se-ai-icon {
 width:  36px !important;
 height: 36px !important;
 border-radius: 50%;
 object-fit: cover;
}
/* Icon colours inside the header.
 user-ui defaults: map icon is #2f6fed (dark blue) and heart is #F44336 (red).
 The map icon is nearly invisible on our #0056b3 bar — lift all icons to white.
 The heart keeps its red via the !important below so favourited items still pop. */
.sie-hdr .se-shortlist-link,
.sie-hdr .se-dest-desktop-btn,
.sie-hdr .se-user-icon {
 color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.85) !important;
}
.sie-hdr .se-shortlist-link:hover,
.sie-hdr .se-dest-desktop-btn:hover,
.sie-hdr .se-user-icon:hover {
 color: #fff !important;
}
/* Fav heart — keep the red so it reads as "save" */
.sie-hdr .se-fav-desktop-link {
 color: #ff6b6b !important;   /* slightly lighter red, readable on blue */
}
.sie-hdr .se-fav-desktop-link:hover {
 color: #ff4444 !important;
}
/* ── Responsive ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
@media (max-width: 860px) {
 :root {
 --sie-hdr-bar-h: 56px;
 }
 .sie-hdr {
 min-height: var(--sie-hdr-bar-h);
 }
 .sie-hdr__hamburger {
 display: flex;
 }
 .sie-hdr__nav {
 /* Hidden off-screen when closed — no layout shift */
 position: absolute;
 top: var(--sie-hdr-bar-h);           /* flush below the nav bar */
 left: 0;
 right: 0;
 background: var(--sie-hdr-bar-bg);
 /* NO backdrop-filter — same reason as .sie-hdr__bar */
 padding: 12px 0 20px;
 clip-path: inset(0 0 100% 0);       /* collapses upward — no CLS */
 transition: clip-path 0.3s ease;
 z-index: 9998;
 }
 .sie-hdr__nav.is-open {
 clip-path: inset(0);
 }
 .sie-hdr__nav-list {
 flex-direction: column;
 align-items: flex-start;
 gap: 0;
 padding: 0 16px;
 }
 .sie-hdr__nav-list a,
 .sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle {
 width: 100%;
 font-size: 15px;
 padding: 12px 8px;
 border-radius: 8px;
 }
 .sie-hdr__dropdown {
 position: static;
 box-shadow: none;
 border-radius: 0;
 background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.06);
 padding: 4px 0 4px 16px;
 margin: 4px 0;
 }
 .sie-hdr__dropdown a {
 color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.8);
 font-size: 14px;
 }
 .sie-hdr__dropdown a:hover {
 background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.08);
 color: #fff;
 }
}
@media (max-width: 480px) {
 .sie-hdr__inner {
 padding: 0 16px;
 gap: 16px;
 }
}
/* Hover-gap fix: invisible bridge spanning the 6px gap between the nav item
 and the dropdown panel, so the cursor never "leaves" while crossing. */
.sie-hdr__dropdown::before {
 content: "";
 position: absolute;
 top: -10px;
 left: 0;
 right: 0;
 height: 10px;
}
/* Anti-FOUC guard for body-rendered overlays: their own CSS arrives 20KB+
 later in the HTML stream, so on slow connections they paint fully visible
 (the destinations grid "opens" during load). Force the CLOSED state from
 first paint — each component's .open/.is-open rules override these. */
.sie-dest-panel,
#sie-auth-drawer,
#sie-lead-form-drawer,
.sie-finder-overlay {
 position: fixed;
 inset: 0;
 opacity: 0;
 visibility: hidden;
} </style> <style id="sie-etmodules-font-display">@font-face{font-family:"ETmodules";src:url("https://www.studyineurope.eu/core/views/sie-theme/css/base/modules.woff") format("woff");font-style:normal;font-weight:normal;font-display:swap;}</style><meta name='robots' content='index, follow, max-image-preview:large, max-snippet:-1, max-video-preview:-1' /> <style id="sie-hide-divi-header"> /* Hide Divi's header (Theme Builder + classic) */

<h1 class="title-h1 eac-page-title">Conference on the Future of Europe : the future is in your hands</h1>
<span><span>sandoel</span></span>
<span><time datetime="2021-12-07T08:55:30+01:00" title="Tuesday, December 7, 2021 - 08:55">Tue, 12/07/2021 - 08:55</time>
</span>
<div class="ecl"><h2><strong>What is the Conference?</strong></h2>

<p>The <strong>Conference on the Future of Europe </strong>is the first transnational discussion with Europeans on how to address Europe’s challenges together. This is an opportunity to think about what citizens and&nbsp; civil society want for the European Union.</p>

<p>&nbsp;</p>
</div>

  <div class="eac-body lc-stripe-wrapper-text"><h2><strong>How does the Conference work?</strong></h2>

<p>Europeans can share ideas via the <a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/?locale=en" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Multilingual Digital Platform</a>, and both national and&nbsp;<a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/assemblies/citizens-panels" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">European Citizens' Panels</a>. These contributions feed into the&nbsp;<a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/pages/plenary" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Conference Plenaries</a>.</p>

<p>The Conference&nbsp;offers a new public forum for an open, inclusive, and transparent debate with citizens around a number of key priorities and challenges.</p>

<h2><strong>How can you participate?</strong></h2>

<ul>
	<li><!--[if !supportLists]--><!--[endif]--><a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/processes?locale=en&amp;pk_source=pdf_document&amp;pk_medium=link&amp;pk_campaign=europarl" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">share your own ideas or support others’ ideas</a> on the multilingual digital Conference platform</li>
	<li><!--[if !supportLists]--><!--[endif]-->organise your own events and promote it by adding them to the <a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/?locale=en&amp;pk_source=pdf_document&amp;pk_medium=link&amp;pk_campaign=europarl" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Conference platform</a></li>
	<li><!--[if !supportLists]--><!--[endif]-->take a look at the <a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/meetings" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">events organised by people across the EU</a></li>
</ul>

<h2><strong>What will the outcome be?</strong></h2>

<p>All of the ideas gathered and reports on events are published on the platform openly and transparently. These reports will then directly influence the discussions in the European Citizens’ Panels as well as in the Plenaries, where citizens will enter into a dialogue with national and European decision makers.</p>

<p>By spring 2022, the Conference will provide guidance on the future of Europe to the European institutions</p>

<p><a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/pages/getinvolved" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Get involved and make your voice heard when it comes to education, culture, youth, sport, and more</a>.</p>

<p>Follow on Twitter at&nbsp;</p>

<item>
  <title>European Student Card Initiative at EAIE 2026 in Glasgow - main highlights</title>
  <link>https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/european-student-card-initiative/news/european-student-card-initiative-at-eaie-2026-in-glasgow-main-highlights</link>
  <description>
<h1 class="title-h1 eac-page-title">European Student Card Initiative at EAIE 2026 in Glasgow - main highlights</h1>
<span><span>holbobe</span></span>
<span><time datetime="2026-09-30T09:11:45+02:00" title="Wednesday, September 30, 2026 - 09:11">Wed, 09/30/2026 - 09:11</time>
</span>
<div class="ecl"><p>EAIE 2026 took place from 8 to 11 September, with this year’s theme being “The Rhythm of Revolution”. ESCI featured in five activities: two sessions in the main conference programme and three mini-sessions at the European Commission stand.</p><h2>Shaping the next phase of the ESCI</h2><p>The session “What’s next for the European Student Card Initiative?” brought together Victor Aguilar Mendez from the European Commission, Harpa Sif Arnarsdóttir from RANNIS and Sergi Martínez Rigol from the University of Barcelona to discuss the roadmap beyond 2027.</p><p>The discussion highlighted three main points:</p><ul><li data-list-item-id="ec04a08fab5a0a15faf6d0537ff166c1e"><strong>Build on strong foundations</strong>. Participants welcomed the ambition to further simplify student mobility and emphasised the importance of building on the progress already achieved. They also noted that digital transformation involves more than technical connections, requiring aligned processes, staff capacity and resources.</li><li data-list-item-id="ec8f6683d0b4c64c36760e88ede263ada"><strong>Give institutions clarity and time to prepare</strong>. Participants highlighted the value of clear information on the <a href="https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/european-student-card-initiative/about/esci-2028-2034/continuity-and-preparation?">future scope of ESCI+</a>, practical implications and transition arrangements. The European Commission indicated that 2028 and 2029 are envisaged as transition years.</li><li data-list-item-id="e8a2629faf233a9053a3e7c84c25e2248"><strong>Broaden engagement beyond international relations and IT teams</strong>. Participants highlighted the value of involving university leadership, national authorities, governance bodies and research and education networks.</li></ul><h2>Practical exchange at the European Commission stand</h2><p>Three mini-sessions created space for practical discussion and peer exchange at the European Commission stand:</p><ul><li data-list-item-id="ea46800eaa0963f636bf8742a636fe844"><strong>Digital Officers and ESCI Champions</strong>: “Meet and Greet” explored different opportunities for close collaboration and participants discussed faster communication channels, technical sub-groups and ways to strengthen the community of practitioners.</li><li data-list-item-id="e722608eb7be29071793748afb04db370"><strong>ESCI+ timeline: what to expect and when</strong>, focused on preparations in 2026 and plans for 2027. Participants asked for timely communication, hands-on training, transition arrangements and support to integrate future developments with existing systems.</li><li data-list-item-id="e4abeb75d22c4e87d628dd3a9174bdc0a"><strong>How to issue your first European Student Card</strong> introduced the practical tools available to card issuers, including the ESC Router and the ESC Service Manager for listing services available to ESC holders.</li></ul><h2>Poster session: “The European Student Card: Bridging borders for students”</h2><p>The poster attracted strong interest, with ESCI representatives Elodie Ham (EACEA) and Deborah Arnold (NTT DATA) engaging with participants on the ESCI components and discussing the implications of the ESCI+ timeline with those already involved in the initiative as well as with potential newcomers.</p><h2>Session by ESCI Champions: “Erasmus Without Paper: Getting on board with the digitisation of Erasmus+"&nbsp;</h2></div>
<div class="ecl-u-type-bold ecl-u-mb-m">Intro Text</div><div class="eac-hero"><p>We joined more than 7,300 international education professionals from over 100 countries in Glasgow to discuss what comes next for the European Student Card Initiative and share practical guidance with institutions.</p></div>
  <div>
    <div>Card image</div>
              <div>
<figure class="media-image">
    
            <div class="media-image--main">
            <div class="media-image--enlarge" aria-hidden="true">
                <a class="media-image--enlarge-link" href="#">
                    <i class="fa fa-expand media-image--enlarge-icon"></i>
                    <span class="media-image--enlarge-label">Enlarge</span>
                </a>
            </div>
            
                            <div class="field field--name-field-media-image field--type-image field--label-hidden field__item test">  <img loading="lazy" src="https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/sites/default/files/styles/oe_theme_medium_no_crop/public/2026-09/eaie-26-presentation.jpeg?itok=JSRs1Txp" width="991" height="743" alt="The ESCI team presents at EAIE conference, Glasgow">


</div>
            
                            <div class="media-image media-image--copyright media-image--copyright__visible">
                    
                            <div class="field field--name-field-media-copyright field--type-string field--label-hidden field__item test">© European Union, 2026</div>
            
                </div>
                    </div>
                    <figcaption class="media-image--caption">
                
                            <div class="field field--name-field-media-caption field--type-string-long field--label-hidden field__item test">From left to right - Harpa Sif Arnarsdóttir (RANNIS), Sergi Martínez Rigol (University of Barcelona) and Victor Aguilar Mendez (European Commission). </div>
            
            </figcaption>
            </figure>
</div>
          </div>
                        <div id="paragraph-8349" class="lc-padding-top-default lc-padding-bottom-half lc-background-color-white lc-contained lc-stripe-width">
            <div class="slider-text-wrapp ecl-container right-align">
                                            <div class="slider-text-body eac-body lc-stripe-wrapper-text">
            <div><p>In addition to the sessions organised by the European Commission, <a href="https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/european-student-card-initiative/community/esci-champions?">ESCI Champions</a> (Kristin Anderson, University of Galway, Ireland, Katherine Bruun Funch, University of Copenhagen , Denmark, and Dana Rocklin, Stockholm University, Sweden) ran a practical workshop entitled "Erasmus Without Paper: Getting on board with the digitisation of Erasmus+". The session was very well-attended and enabled participants to share good practices and challenges in using different mobility management systems, including the EWP Dashboard.</p></div>
        </div>
                    <div class="stripe-hero-header img stripe-hero-header__with-slider">
                                    <div class="swiper-slide">

                    <div class="eche-report-title-question-text-wrapper">
                        <div class="eche-officer-question">Your institution has a strategy and an overarching structure supporting internationalisation</div>
                        <div class="eche-report-button-js eche-report-detail-close"><i class="fa fa-plus-circle fa-3x"></i></div>
                    </div>
                </div>
                <div class="eche-officer-question-wrapper eche-report-question-wrapper-show">
                    <div class="eche-report-border"></div>
                    <div classs="eche-officer-must">
                                                <h3>Must have</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">The internationalisation strategy is available and prominently displayed on your website</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>Internationalisation is an important driver for institutional change, and has a great influence on the major activities of a higher education institution (HEI) i.e. education and research. The importance of internationalisation is recognised, and most institutions have a strategy for internationalisation. However, for a strategy to be efficient, and for it to drive the HEI's activities regarding internationalisation, there is a need for its acceptance from across the whole institution. In addition the strategy could also be accessible to external collaborative partners. It is highly important to have the institution's internationalisation and modernisation strategy published and easily accessible to all.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">The institution has a clear plan to implement the strategy</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The strategy and policy should include explicit allocation of responsibilities for its efficient implementation to individuals at all levels of the institution, from senior management to the heads of departments, schools and faculties, to academic and administrative staff. This will ensure acceptance and accountability for the strategy. The internationalisation strategy and policy should outline a specific implementation plan that sets out explicitly the financial and human resources available.&nbsp; For example, it is recommended to set up an International Relations Office (IRO) to implement mobility and other international projects.</p><p>As with any other activity, the institutional implementation of the internationalisation strategy is dependent on the people behind the activities. It is highly important for an institution to have staff with the right set of skills and knowledge driving the internationalisation agenda and liaising with international students and staff members. Therefore understanding the development needs of the staff and supporting their professional development should be a high priority for the institution. Such development should focus on both staff engaged in international activities as well as the supporting staff, ensuring the most efficient implementation of international activities and cooperative projects across the institution. For example, trainings/webinars/projects could be organised on intercultural competences and communication, project management, enhancement of internationalisation at home/intercultural, or other activities suggested by the staff and supported by the hierarchy.</p>                      </div>
                    <div class="eche-officer-best">
                                                <h3>Best practices</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">It promotes incoming and outgoing student and staff mobility</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>Mobility is important to the development of the institution as a whole as well as for the individual participants. Therefore the HEI should make mobility and international cooperation a central element in its institutional policies, and explicitly and consistently promote and support student and staff mobility. Non-discrimination policies and further emphasis on the promotion of mobility for under-represented groups should also form an integral part of the institutional support structures.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">It promotes engagement in European and international cooperation projects</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The institution's internationalisation strategy and policy should explicitly and consistently promote the development of cooperation with partners in other EU and non-EU countries. The activities and co-operation projects agreed by the HEI should be based on identified needs. In addition they should identify geographical and subject priorities of the internationalisation strategy.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">The implementation of the strategic plan is monitored</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>International activity, including co-operation projects and mobility should be carefully monitored. Clear and unambiguous monitoring of such activity are key to ensuring success. Explicit indicators should be developed to show specific success scenarios. The indicators should be SMART.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">Incentives are provided to staff involved in international activities</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>Participation in such international projects should be seen as an important aspect of the professional development of the staff and of the modernisation of the HEI. It should, therefore, be considered a key component in staff evaluation. As part of the institutional modernisation and internationalisation strategy, concrete support measures should be defined at both institutional and departmental levels to encourage and recognise staff participating in such projects, as well as allow adequate time to carry out this work.</p>                      </div>
                    <div class="eche-officer-case">
                                                <h3>Case studies</h3>
                                                <div><a href="https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/eche/the-effective-management-and-ownership-of-erasmus-for-internationalisation" target="_blank">The effective management and ownership of Erasmus +’ for ‘internationalisation’</a></div>
                                                <div><a href="https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/eche/internationalisation-at-the-university-of-helsinki" target="_blank">Internationalisation at the University of Helsinki </a></div>
                                             </div>

                        <div class="eche-officer-question">Your institution has established a framework of Inter-Institutional Agreements for Erasmus+ mobility</div>

                    <div classs="eche-officer-must">
                                                <h3>Must have</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">They are based on areas of mutual interest</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>It is vital that Inter-Institutional Agreements are based on areas of mutual interest. These agreements should identify shared quality requirements specific to the planned exchanges, including concrete proposals as to how these activities will contribute to the development of learning and teaching in participating institutions. The involvement of academic staff is key to ensuring that the selection of partners is based on sufficient knowledge of the area. Each HEI should decide who is responsible for initiating, signing and implementing these agreements and the list of responsible persons should be available on the website for contact and consultation purposes.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">They are based on the compatibility of study programmes</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>Inter-Institutional Agreements should be based on a comprehensive understanding of the partner HEIs, the compatibility of study programmes, quality levels and standards considered adequate for student and staff mobility activities. For example, selected partners should have learning, teaching and assessment procedures that can be accepted by the sending institution without requiring mobile students to do any additional work or take examinations upon returning from the receiving institution. The compatibility of the programmes should be reflected in the learning outcomes to be achieved.</p>                      </div>

                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">There are specific provisions e.g. in the general policies, rules and regulations of the institution</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>In signing the Erasmus Charter for Higher Education, the institution agrees to respect <strong>in full</strong> the principles of non-discrimination as set out in the Programme. The institution must clearly demonstrate through its policies, rules and regulations that equal access and opportunities to mobile participants from all backgrounds. Which means that all individuals or groups will be treated equally, irrespective of their characteristics. In accordance with Article 21 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union, there should be no discrimination "based on sex, race, colour, ethnic or social origin, genetic features, language, religion or belief, political or any other opinion, membership of a national minority, property, birth, disability, age or sexual orientation". For more information, see: <a href="http://www.europarl.europa.eu/charter/pdf/text_en.pdf">http://www.europarl.europa.eu/charter/pdf/text_en.pdf</a></p>                      </div>
                    <div class="eche-officer-best">
                                                <h3>Best practices</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">The principle - that extra fees are not being charged to incoming mobile students - is implemented</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The receiving institution must <strong>not </strong>charge any type of fees to incoming mobility students for the tuition, registration or examination of these students or for their access to laboratory, library and other facilities offered to local students.<br>In certain cases, however, mobile students may be required to pay small fees for insurance, student unions, use of miscellaneous materials (e.g. photocopies, laboratory products) on the same basis as these are charged to local students. Students should be made aware of these extra costs before the start of mobility. Fees may only be charged in the case of full degree mobility or for students registered in joint degree programmes.&nbsp;</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">All students and staff (incoming and outgoing) are treated equally in all academic and service matters</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>In accordance with equal access and opportunities, all students and staff should be treated equally in all academic and service matters. Clear appeal procedures should be in place to ensure equal treatment. There should be individuals - such as mentors and counsellors - available to offer support.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">It provides incoming mobile participants with access to the same services and facilities available to local students and staff</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>It is vital to ensure that incoming mobility participants have full access to the same services and facilities as local students and staff. For example, mobility participants with special needs can benefit from the support services that the receiving institution offers to its local students and staff.</p>                      </div>

                                                <h3>Must have</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">Ensuring that the mobile participant, sending and receiving HEI/organisation/enterprise (i.e. all three parties) sign the Learning Agreement before the start of the mobility</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The purpose of the Learning Agreement is to provide a transparent and efficient preparation of the study period abroad and to ensure that the student will receive recognition in his/her degree for the educational components or traineeship successfully completed abroad. The Learning Agreement:</p><ul><li>Sets out the learning outcomes for the mobility, including both the educational components or traineeship activities to be carried out by the student at the receiving institution/organisation/enterprise, which will be recognised by the sending institution upon successful completion of the study programme abroad and counted towards his/her degree.</li><li>Ensures full recognition for satisfactorily completed activities of study mobility and traineeships in terms of credits awarded, without the need for the student to take any further courses or exams, and documents these credits in the student records, so that they can be identified in a transparent way.</li></ul><p>The Learning Agreement is binding for all parties and constitutes the cornerstone of successful student mobility (for studies, traineeships, and combinations thereof), including quality assurances and the process for transparent transfer of credits. Therefore, it is essential to conduct mobility based on an agreed and signed Learning Agreement. The Learning Agreement should be agreed and signed by all parties (the student, the sending institution and the receiving institution/organisation/enterprise) before the start of the mobility. It is not compulsory to circulate papers with original signatures; scanned copies of signatures or digital signatures may be accepted, depending on the national legislation.</p><p>The EU official templates for Learning Agreements for studies and traineeships are available online: <a href="http://ec.europa.eu/education/opportunities/higher-education/quality-framework_en.htm">http://ec.europa.eu/education/opportunities/higher-education/quality-framework_en.htm&nbsp;&nbsp;</a></p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">Including allocation of responsibility to an academic who has the authority to approve, amend and recognise the Learning Agreements on behalf of the responsible academic body</span>
